the time of creation of user proﬁles, how many posts posted, etc. [9]. News creation,
posting, and temporal behavior includes the behavior of the user posting time patterns,
i.e., the time pattern between two successive posts, commenting, and sharing. The
user credibility features include the interaction of the online users with the news and
type of news and bias in the news that is shared or liked or commented by the user.
   In this paper, we conﬁne our work to content based fake news detection. In the next
part of this section the contribution of various machine-learning techniques and deep
learning models in fake news detection are explore. This study helps us to identify
the models we need to focus on in our study and propose the new model for content
based fake news detection.
   Granik et al. proposed a model using Naive Bayes classiﬁer for a BuzzFeed news
dataset [10]. Their model classiﬁed the data with high accuracy, but the recall metric
is very low because the dataset is skewed dataset. Fabricio Benevenuto et al., adopted
ﬁve supervised learning algorithms like K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Naive Bayes,
Random Forest, SVM, XGBoost [11]. They considered linguistic features of the
data and models were built with all the ﬁve classiﬁers. Out of all the ﬁve classiﬁers,
Random Forest classiﬁer shown high accuracy compared to the rest of the classiﬁers.
AUC (Area Under Curve) and F1-score metrics were also used for comparing the
detection performance of the models.
   Bennett Lefevre et al. built two fake news datasets, namely Fake News AMT and
Celebrity, using manual and crowd sourcing annotation approaches covering news
from seven different news domains [12]. From those datasets, different linguistic
features were extracted like, N-grams, punctuation using linguistic inquiry, and word
count software, psycholinguistic features, readability, and syntax. SVM classiﬁer
was applied to the datasets and accuracy of 76% was obtained. They also studied
the performance of models using the cross-domain approach, i.e., training using
one dataset and testing on the other dataset and found a remarkable reduction in
performance. They improved classiﬁcation performance by training the model on
ﬁve of the seven domains in the dataset, and testing on the remaining two.
   In recent years, deep-learning catches the attention of researchers with the
advancements in technology; researchers started using deep learning to enhance the
classiﬁcation accuracy of the fake news. In latest researches, variants of deep-learning
techniques are implemented by tuning different Hyper Parameters like learning rate,
dropouts, number of hidden layers, mini batch size, etc.
   In a recent research by Bilal Ghanem et al., Emotionally Infused Network model
(EIN) was proposed to detect false news on publicly available two datasets, News
Articles and Twitter data [13]. They compared the language features of false news to
that of real news from an emotional perspective. They considered propaganda, hoax,
click bait, and satire false information types of news from social media and online
news article sources. They used Google News Word2Vec 300-Embedding for pre-
trained word embedding, and tenfold cross-validation. The accuracy of the proposed
EIN model was 96% compared to LSTM 95%.
  Heejung Jwa et al. applied the Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Trans-
formers model (BERT) model considering the relationship between the news headline
and the body text to detect fake news [14]. They proposed an improved exBAKE

--- Page 74 ---
56                                                                 D. Haritha et al.

model by using pre-training based on a BERT model for deep understanding the
contents of such articles. Their results showed that the deep-contextualizing nature
of BERT is best suited for this task and improves the 0.14 F-score over the other
BERT models. Aswini Thota et al. used a ﬁnely tuned TF-IDF dense neural network
(DNN) model [15] and achieved an accuracy of 94.21%. They considered emergent
dataset created by Craig Silverman. The model was trained with three different vari-
ations, (i) TF-IDF vectors with dense neural network, (ii) bag of words vector with
dense neural network and (iii) pre-trained word embeddings with neural networks
and cosine similarity for ﬁnding similarity between article-headline. Unigrams and
bigrams were used for computing TF-IDF scores. By tuning hyperparameters the
model achieved utmost validation accuracy of 94.32% with the dropout rate of 0.1
by applying the Softmax activation function.
   Junaed Younus Khan et al. did a benchmark study on machine-learning methods
for fake news detection [16] on three different datasets namely LIAR [17], fake or real
news [18], and combined corpus [16]. Their study showed that the Naive Bayes with
n-gram can attain analogous results to neural network-based models if the dataset
is having less than 100 k news articles. The LSTM-based model’s performance
greatly depends on the information given in a news article and dataset size. Their
study emphasized the use of advanced models like the C-LSTM, Conv-HAN, and
character level C-LSTM that demands further attention on these models in fake news
detection. The literature study presented here inferences that the use of deep learning
techniques for fake news detection gives promising results.



3  Methodology


In this section, we discuss about the datasets used, the detailed sketch of multi-channel
hybrid model and the hyper parameters regarding to the model.



3.1  Datasets


In this paper, we tried working with two datasets, which are detailed in Table 1. First
one is, fake news dataset consists of the training set with 20,799 records and test set
with 5881 records. The training data are having four columns, namely, ID (unique
value assigned to that news article), Title (main heading of that news article), Author
and Text (body of the news article) and Label indicating whether it is reliable or
unreliable news. This fake news dataset collected from Kaggle contains the news
spread during the period of US Presidential elections, 2016. Second dataset is a
benchmark LIAR dataset [19]. The train dataset consists of total 10,240 records and
test dataset with 1267 records. This is a multi-labeled dataset with 6 different class
labels namely, false, pants-ﬁre, barely true, half-true, mostly true, and true.

3.2  Proposed Multi Channel Deep Neural Network Model


The proposed model comprises a deep neural network with multiple channels. Its
architectural diagram is shown in Fig. 4. The ﬂow diagram of the proposed model is
shown in Fig. 5. The input layer comprises the word embedding vectors obtained by
applying Glove embedding for the news articles in the dataset, followed by multi-
channel convolution layers with varied ﬁlter sizes (Zhong et al. 2019). Each channel
is constructed with a deep learning technique like Convolution layer, LSTM and
GRU layers. We have chosen hybrid multi-channeling concurrent application of three
models CNN, LSTM, and GRU to get the combined advantage of all three models of
neural networks in improving identiﬁcation accuracy. If we apply those three models
in sequential mode, we might lose some of the features discarded by a model and
that in turn might affect the accuracy of identiﬁcation. Every channel is followed
by a max pooling, ﬂatten layers, and concatenated. This is followed by a series of 4
dense layers with a ﬁnal output prediction layer. In the following sub-sections, the
details about each channel and techniques are discussed in depth.

Word Embedding: Word embedding is a natural language-processing technique to
represent the words in the given text in a numerical format, which can be under-
standable by machines. TF-IDF, Word2vec [20], and Glove [21] are the standard
word embedding models. TF-IDF represents a word with a score determined from
two frequencies; Term frequency, i.e., the number of times the word occurring in a
document and Inverse Document Frequency, the weight factor that gives higher value





Fig. 4  Architecture of the hybrid-multi-channel deep neural network (MCDNN) model

--- Page 76 ---
58                                                                 D. Haritha et al.





Fig. 5 Flow diagram of the hybrid multi-channel deep neural network (MCDNN) model


to words occurring in only a few documents. It ignores the semantic meaning and
relationship between the words. Word2vec and glove word embedding techniques
map semantic meaning and relationship between the words in the geometric word
space. All the words in the dictionary are represented by numerical vectors and the
distance between the vectors represents the semantic relationship between the words.
   For example the distance between the USA and Trump is nearly equal to that of
the distance between India and Narendra Modi but is much less compared with the
distance between the USA and Narendra Modi. This Glove model of word embedding
is improvement over Word2vec. The Glove model is a count based model and tries to
enforce the word vectors to capture sub-relationships in the vector space. This is done
by creating a global co-occurrence matrix of words by estimating the probability that
a given word will co-occur with other words from the entire corpus.
   In 2013 Tomas Mikolov et al. from Google proposed this Word2Vec [20] word
embedding technique. Word2vec is a predictive model and does not have any explicit
global co-occurrence information embedded in it by default. This model attempts to

--- Page 77 ---
Hybrid-Multi-channel Deep Neural Network for Fake News Detection                    59

train a neural network to predict the nth word for the given n-1 words. Word2Vec
can be obtained by Skip Gram and Common Bag of Words (CBOW) [22]. CBOW
method considers the context of every word as input and makes an attempt to guess
the corresponding word in the context. Skip Gram model works quite opposite to
CBOW model. In this, target word is at the input layer, context word at the output
layer. Skip Gram works well with a small amount of data, whereas CBOW works
faster and it can better represent most frequent words [23].
  The GloVe is available with different variations like 25d, 50d, 100d, 200d and
300-dimensional vector sizes. For our experimental purpose 100 dimensional vector
sizes is considered, with 6Billion tokens with 400 thousand vocabulary words
included. Figure 6 shows the screenshot of pre-trained GloVe that is considered
in the current study. GloVe is an unsupervised learning algorithm for converting
words to vector representation. Training is performed on collected worldwide word–
word co- event insights from a corpus, and the results are presenting the linear
relations of word vector space. The effectual method for computing the linguistic or
semantic relationship of the similar words is by calculating Euclidean distance or
cosine similarity.

Convolution Layers: Convolution layers are the basic building blocks in CNN [24].
Convolution layers convolve the input with an array of weights called ﬁlter or kernel.
The ﬁlters slide over the entire input and extract the local features. In this model, a
convolution 1D layer followed by three parallel convolution 1D layers are used each
with different ﬁlter sizes. Intuition is that convolution operation with ﬁlter size n is
equal to applying ﬁlter on n-grams of input sentence and hence with different ﬁlter
sizes, it can extract various n-grams information and can produce a new feature of
the input. In our implementation, we used 128 ﬁlters with kernel sizes 3 in layer,
which means 128 different ﬁlters each with length of 3 are created. It results with
128 different convolutions.

Pooling Layers: Pooling Layers in CNN are usually applied to the output of the
convolution layer to down sample the input. The most commonly used pooling is max

accuracy of the proposed
model using Kaggle dataset

pooling and it is a convolution process that the Kernel extracts the maximum value of
the area it convolves. Pooling layer reduces the output dimensionality without leaving
the important features in the sentence. Four convolution layers are followed by four
max-pooling layers in our model. Flattening is performed on the output of each max-
pooling layer to convert the two-dimensional feature map into a one-dimensional
format and is concatenated to deliver it to fully connected layers.

LSTM: An LSTM network k is a type of recurrent neural network (RNN) that
includes dedicated memory cells that store information over long time periods. A
speciﬁc conﬁguration of operations in this network, so-called gates, controls the
information ﬂow within the LSTM. An LSTM network works as follows: Given a
sequence data x = (x1, x2, …, xT) with T time steps, where each element x[t] is a
vector containing input features (model inputs) at time step t(1≤t ≤T), the following
equations describe the forward pass through the LSTM:

where i[t], f[t] and o[t] are the input gate, forget gate, and output gate, respectively,
g[t] is the cell input and x[t] is the network input at time step t (1 ≤ t ≤ T), h[t-1]
is the recurrent input, c[t − 1] the cell state from the previous time step. At the
ﬁrst time step, the hidden and cell states are initialized as a vector of zeros. W, U,
and b are learnable parameters for each gate, where subscripts indicate which gate
the particular weight matrix/vector is used for, σ (•) is the sigmoid function, tanh()
the hyperbolic tangent function and is element-wise multiplication. Though neural
networks are powerful in image related applications, they fail in remembering long-
term dependencies due to the absence of memory unit. LSTM is a special type of
RNN that learns long-term dependencies. In general, the news articles are long and
sequential text, LSTM works smart in such situations as LSTM cell has a memory
unit that can store previous time step information and this is how it learns. This
made us to choose LSTM in second channel in our hybrid multi-channel deep neural
network model.

GRU: GRU is another version of Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) and it looks bit
similar to LSTM. GRU uses hidden state for transferring the information. It is having
two gates, an update gate and a reset gate. The update gate decides the information
that need to be thrown away and the information that has to add. The reset gate is used
to decide the amount of past information that has to forget. The governing equations
of GRU are as follows:

                               z equals   sigmas

                                    a
                               r equ  ls   sigmas

                     h equals hyp erbolics


                              s S ubscript t Baseline equals1

  The reset gate is represented as r, and update gate is represented as z. Reset gate
makes the model to ignore the unnecessary information in future time steps. In every
batch the reset gate calculates the performance previous and new inputs and reset
the gate if needed for new input. Update gate determines the importance of previous
information in the current state. The sigmoid function used in the update gate results
the values between 0 and 1. Closer the value to 1 means include the past information
and the value closer to 0 means the only new information is considered. If the reset
gate is set to all 1’s and update gate to all 0’s it works like a plain RNN Model.
  The primary reason for choosing this in the third channel is, as few news articles
in our dataset are too long with thousands of words. GRUs can outperform LSTM in
this kind of situations by remembering only the important information and forgetting
the unnecessary information out of too long news articles.

Dense Layer or Fully Connected Layer: Fully connected layers connect all the
inputs from one layer to every activation unit of the next layer. In most popular deep
learning models, the last few layers are fully connected layers which compile the data
extracted by previous layers to form the ﬁnal output, i.e., the classiﬁcation decision.
The fully connected layer tries to ﬁnd out the most accurate weights by its own back
propagation process. Each neuron in CNN is given with the weights that prioritize
the most ﬁtting label. Each neuron is voted on the labels, the classiﬁcation decision
is made to the winner of the vote. The activation function used in dense layers is
ReLU except in the last layer, i.e., Softmax.
   In our proposed hybrid multi-channel deep neural network model we used both
CNNs and RNNs that helps to optimize the performance of the model by extracting
beneﬁts of both the models. In CNNs, convolutional kernels operates independent
of the other kernels, meaning that we can go over the entire input layer concurrently.
Convolutions result in a larger receptive ﬁeld as we stack more and more layers.
In our experiments we used 1D convolution to mix the words and extract relations
between the successive words.

--- Page 80 ---
62                                                                 D. Haritha et al.

   Recurrent Neural Networks (LSTM and GRU) are used for sequence modeling.
The LSTM units have the ability to add or remove information to the cell state, regu-
lated by gates to optionally pass the information. GRU controls the ﬂow of informa-
tion like the LSTM unit without using memory units. GRU learns useful information
in the historical data, and throws away the useless information by the forget gate. It
exposes the full hidden content without any control. GRU is computationally more
efﬁcient.
   This hybrid model combines the beneﬁts of both CNN and RNN (using LSTM
or GRU). RNN captures the long-range dependencies between words using memory
cells used in their architecture. CNN captures the local consequent words and extract
relations between them. So, our hybrid model focuses on capturing long-range word
dependencies as well as local word dependencies [25].
   In the architecture of Hybrid-MCDNN, the output from embedding layer is given
as an input for a convolution layer having 128 kernels each with a size of 3. It reduces
the input vector size from 1000 to 998. This layer is followed by a max-pooling, the
vector size further gets reduced to 499, i.e., 1/2 of 998, because the max-pooling
ﬁlter size is 2. Now this output is fed to three multi-channel layers. The ﬁrst layer is a
convolution layer which is having 64 kernels with size 5, this reduces the vector size
from 499 to 495. The second layer is LSTM with 256 hidden nodes. The third layer
is GRU with 128 hidden nodes. All these three layers are followed by a max-pooling
layer, the input for ﬁrst max pooling is 495 vectors and max-pooling ﬁlter size is 2,
the vector size is reduced to 1/2 of 495 resulted as 247. For second and third max-
pooling layers, the input vector size is 499 and the output is 249. A ﬂatten layer is
applied on the outputs and now they are concatenated. Now, the concatenated output
is passed through three dense layers, each with hidden neurons of 128, 64 and 64.
The ﬁrst dense layer is passed through a dropout of 0.1.



4  Hyper Tuning the Parameters of the Model


Activation Functions Activation function is a nonlinear transformation on the input
to get better desired output. It basically decides to deactivate neurons or activate them
to get the desired output. The performance of the deep learning models is mostly
determined by the selection of these activation functions. In our model, ReLu and
Softmax activation functions are used. ReLU (Rectiﬁed Linear Unit) is mathemati-
cally represented as y = max(0, x). In ReLU, the slope doesn’t saturate when the x
value gets too large. This solves vanishing gradient problem which is pertinent with
tanh and sigmoid activation functions. The Softmax function converts a vector of N
real values into a vector of N real values such that their sum is 1. The input values
can be any values, but the Softmax transforms them into values between 0 and 1, so
that they can be interpreted as probabilities that can be interpreted as output class
probabilities.

--- Page 81 ---
Hybrid-Multi-channel Deep Neural Network for Fake News Detection                    63

Drop Outs It is one of the simplest and most powerful regularization techniques for
deep learning models [26]. Few randomly selected neurons are ignored temporarily
during the training phase, and they do not contribute to the activation in the forward
phase as well as updating their weights in the back propagation phase. Dropout can
be applied on input layer and hidden layers as well. In development of the current
model, we used a dropout rate of 0.1 in the dense layers, which means 10% of the
neurons are randomly dropped. This results in a better generalized model and reduces
the chance of over ﬁtting on training data.

Batch Normalization During the training process of the neural networks, the
networks may face problem called as internal covariate shift. Generally, this problem
appears in the middle layers because of the change of the activations in the training
phase. This may slow down the training phase because a new distribution has to be
adapted in every layer during the training stage.

Learning rate A stochastic gradient optimization algorithm is used in training deep
network models. Back propagation is used in updating the weights of the model by
using examples from the training dataset. The learning rate is the amount of weights
that are updated during the training phase. It is one of the hyper parameters used
during the training of neural networks, whose value is small positive value between
0.0 and 1.0 in general. Learning rate of 0.001 is considered in the current model with
Adam as optimization technique.

Evaluation Metrics For  classiﬁcation problems, confusion matrix gives  the
summary of the model predictions. We can ﬁgure out True Positives, True Negatives,
False Positives and False Negatives from the confusion matrix. These values are used
to calculate the performance metrics Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-Score of
the proposed classiﬁcation model [26]. Confusion matrix with binary classiﬁcation
problem is represented in the Table 2.
   Accuracy is a measure that let know the overall model how often it is predicting
correctly on fake and real news. Recall is useful in estimating how much percentage
of predicted fake news matches with actual fake news. If Recall value is 0, this
means that the model is broken and cannot make even a single correct prediction
when actually it is real news. Precision is a measure that tells how many predicted
fake news samples are correctly predicted. F1 measure combines precision and recall
by taking harmonic mean. In the fake news detection, if the dataset is balanced in
terms of the ratio of fake news samples to real news samples in the dataset being
approximately 1. If the dataset is unbalanced F1 measure, Precision, and Recall are
of importance.

5  Results and Discussion


The performance of the proposed hybrid-multi-channel deep neural network is
compared with various other deep learning networks such as a simple multi-layer
perceptron (MLP) neural network [28], long short-term memory (LSTM) [29],
combined LSTM plus CNN network [30] and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) [29]. The
main reason for choosing deep learning over machine learning is that in machine
learning the features have to be extracted manually. However, in case of deep
learning the model automatically identiﬁes the features which play vital role in the
classiﬁcation process.
   First the simple neural network model Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) is imple-
mented with one input and output layer and a pre trained GloVE word embedding
method. This model achieved an accuracy of 54.01% on Kaggle dataset and 75.53%
accuracy on LIAR dataset. Evaluation measures like Precision, Recall, and F1-score
are shown in Tables 2 and 3. LSTM (long short-term memory) with GloVE embed-
ding which is tuned for different hyper parameters attained an accuracy of 95.97%.
The combination of LSTM and CNN achieved 98.83% accuracy. GRU (Gated Recur-
rent Unit) model with 4 epochs and Glove as word embedding attains 98.29% of test
accuracy for Kaggle fake news dataset and 80.15% accuracy for LIAR dataset.
  The proposed hybrid model can be signiﬁcantly beneﬁted from the optimization
of its hyperparameters. All the hyper parameters like activation function, dropout
rate, batch size, optimizer that were optimized using grid search method and used
for these models are listed in the Table 5. The proposed Hybrid-MCDNN model, with
Convolution Layer, LSTM Layer, GRU and max-pooling layers is implemented with
batch normalization to stabilize its learning process.
  The details of the hyper parameters (dropout, optimizer, loss function, batch size,
no. of dense layers) used in this proposed model are given in Table 6. This proposed
model has shown the testing accuracy of 99.80% for 4 epochs using Kaggle fake news
dataset. Table 2 infers that the proposed Hybrid-MCDNN outperformed the existing
deep learning techniques. The same Hybrid-MCDNN model applied on multi label
LIAR dataset and achieved an accuracy of 83.53%. In Tables 3 and 4, the accuracy
of MCDNN model is shown for 4 epochs. However there is no signiﬁcant change in
accuracy even after increasing the number of epochs.

  The results tabulated infer two major takeaways. First the RNN with GRUs outper-
formed with LSTM in the detection. Not only GRUs achieves the better accuracy but
also converged faster than LSTM. The better performance of GRU is likely that the
GRU exposes its full content without any control, given that dataset news items were
long having an average length of 500 words across both classes. The reason for faster
convergence might be the GRUs have fewer gates, and hence fewer computations
to generate the output. Some news articles in the dataset are having thousands of

words, and RNNs, even built with LSTMs or GRUs, cannot retain memory for more
than a hundred or so. However, RNNs could do well as its feed forward network
better performs as a classiﬁer and its input comprises the weight distributed across
the embeddings of all the words and the model takes salient words into account that
identify the news item. CNN performance can be observed to be much lesser than
RNN as it captures only salient words presence and their local features.
  Second takeaway is that the performance in hybrid approach is better than CNN,
LSTM or GRU methods used individually, as the hybrid design captures both local
and sequential characteristics of input data. In our proposed hybrid approach, the
local features extracted by the CNN are given as inputs for CNN, LSTM, and RNN.
This approach helps in extracting cumulative beneﬁts of CNN–CNN cascaded effect
and also extracting the long-term dependencies of the local features of news articles
that classify them as fake or real. The second dataset, Liar dataset contains news
articles whose average length is less than 100. That might be the reason that can
be attributed to the comparatively lower performance of all the individual models
as well as the proposed hybrid model. Second reason might be that the number of
samples is not signiﬁcantly sufﬁcient as it is the multi-class classiﬁcation problem
even though the dataset size is 10,239 records (Fig. 7).



6  Conclusion and Future Scope


In  this paper, a hybrid-multi channel deep neural network (MCDNN) model
comprising different deep learning techniques is proposed for fake news detection
using pre-trained GloVe embedding. This model is found to be useful in extracting the
long-range semantic dependencies between the words of the news content as well
as local dependencies and is evident from its performance in fake news detection
based on the content of the news. The performance of the proposed hybrid model
is evaluated for both the binary classiﬁcation and on the multi-class classiﬁcation.

--- Page 85 ---
Hybrid-Multi-channel Deep Neural Network for Fake News Detection                    67

The model achieved promising results with an accuracy of 99.8 and 83.53% in fake
news detection. Tuning of hyperparameters like dropouts, batch normalization, and
number of layers, optimizer and batch size helped in improving the performance.
This work can be further extended to explore the reasons for comparatively much
lower performance in the multi-class fake news detection and to improve it. This
model can further be applied for extracting hybrid features from both the content and
context of the news.

Integrated Gaussian—GLCM Butterﬂy
Optimization with CNN (IGGBOCNN):
A Hybrid Approach for Ovarian Cancer
Classiﬁcation in Medical Image Analysis


Monita Wahengbam and Tonjam Gunendra Singh



Abstract Cancer has become a common and often fatal illness. Ovarian cancer is
a particularly persistent and aggressive type of gynecologic cancer. Basic epithelial
ovarian cancer is classiﬁed into four different subcategories: mucinous, serous, clear
cell, and endometrioid. The four distinct types in the cytological pictures that the
pathologist’s eyes and intellect correctly identify are frequently difﬁcult to distin-
guish from one another. However, there is a great likelihood of inaccuracy if indi-
viduals evaluate and determine a large number of photos. Consequently, the inves-
tigation has used technological advances in pathology prediction to lower the risk
of error and acquire an accurate diagnosis. In this work, we suggest an extensive
approach for classifying ovarian cancer that combines conventional ML (machine
learning) approaches with optimization strategies. Butterﬂy Optimization (BO) is
used to optimize the model parameters for Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random
Forest (RF), and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) in particular. Moreover,
preprocessing methods are used to improve the quality of input data, such as feature
extraction with the Gray Level Co-occurrence Matrix (GLCM) and noise removal
with a Gaussian ﬁlter. The results of our experiments show that the suggested combi-
nation of methods—namely, classiﬁcation using CNN, the model parameter tuning
by BO, the texture feature extraction through GLCM, and the noise removal through
Gaussian ﬁlter—produces better outcomes in terms of accuracy of 91%, precision
of 0.90, and recall of 0.87, respectively. The Python programming language is the
analysis device.

Keywords Ovarian cancer classiﬁcation · Butterﬂy optimization · Gaussian
ﬁlter · Medical image analysis · Machine learning · Feature extraction · Image
preprocessing · Classiﬁcation accuracy · Precision · Recall · Early cancer detection

1  Introduction


According to Koray Aslan et al. [4], one of the most prevalent forms of cancer in
women is ovarian cancer (OC). In 2018, it was discovered that 295,414 women
had an ovarian cancer diagnosis and that the disease resulted in 184,799 deaths
globally. Since early-stage tumors usually cause minimal symptoms, the majority
of OC patients are suffering from advanced illness at the time of diagnosis, which
lowers their chances of survival over the long run.
  One of the main causes of cancer-related mortality for women globally is ovarian
cancer. A precise and timely diagnosis is essential for efﬁcient therapy and higher
survival rates. The ﬁeld of medical image analysis has improved signiﬁcantly since
the introduction of enhanced imaging technology, opening the door to the creation
of complex methods for classifying cancer. The combination of image-processing
techniques and machine-learning algorithms has produced encouraging outcomes in
this regard. Using the combined capabilities of SVM, RF, CNN, and cutting-edge
optimization methods like Butterﬂy optimization, this study focuses on a unique
methodology for classifying OC. Furthermore, the preprocessing stages are essential
for improving the caliber of medical photographs. The input data are further reﬁned by
adding GLCM for the extraction of features and a Gaussian ﬁlter for noise reduction.
Accuracy, precision, and recall are the three main performance criteria used to assess
the efﬁcacy of this integrated strategy, which aims to provide a reliable and accurate
system for OC detection.
   Ovarian cancer detection relies heavily on classiﬁcation models because of their
capacity to identify complex trends in patient data, which facilitate prompt and
precise diagnosis. These models are essential for the early identiﬁcation of cancer,
regardless of whether they are built on cutting-edge deep learning techniques or
conventional ML algorithms. These models can identify cases that are benign or
malignant, allowing for prompt treatment and better patient outcomes. They do this
by examining a variety of factors, including genetic markers, imaging data, and
clinical indicators.
  The urgent need for accurate and effective OC categorization techniques is
addressed by this study. Our goal is to improve the classiﬁcation system’s accu-
racy and dependability by fusing ML architectures, modern optimization methods,
and preprocessing techniques. A thorough examination of the input data is ensured
by the synergistic combination of SVM, RF, CNN, Butterﬂy Optimization, Gaus-
sian ﬁlter, and GLCM. This work not only advances the ﬁeld of medical image
processing but also has the potential to have a big inﬂuence on cancer diagnosis by
providing clinicians and scientists with an effective tool for early identiﬁcation and
better patient.

2  Related Works


According to the WHO, cervical cancer ranks fourth among malignancies that affect
women, accounting for 7.9% of all cancers in women. The absence of efﬁcient
early therapy proved to be one of the main contributors to this. Consequently, it is
critical to recognize cervical cancer as soon as possible. The main obstacle to early
cervical cancer identiﬁcation is the disease’s subclinical state. In numerous, medical
ML has proven to be extremely helpful. It could be employed as a classiﬁer for
identifying malignant cells in the cervical portion of the uterus earlier on. The research
paper compares all of the methods currently used for forecasting the development
of cervical cancer employing medical information and highlights the beneﬁts and
drawbacks of each. It also analyzes the different methods with ML the fact that have
been successfully deployed by Shetty et al. [2] for the recognition of cervical tumors.
  One of the most common causes of mortality for women is ovarian cancer. It
impacts women of all demographic and cultural groups and ranks ﬁfth in cancer-
related fatalities within them. It is critical to correctly differentiate it from tumors
to prevent inaccurate diagnoses of cancer and to appropriately address what the
individual needs. Aditya et al. [5] have developed an approach in this area that uses
various ML categories with varying approximation techniques, choices of features,
and DL from Kaggle datasets to distinguish between benign ovarian tumor and
ovarian cancer. It was clear that choosing characteristics signiﬁcantly improved the
ML model’s precision as well as effectiveness. RF with median restoration produced
the best results of all the categories. The DL algorithm’s performance was comparable
to that of the RF algorithm and did not signiﬁcantly outperform the conventional ML
approach.
   Ovarian cancer happens to be one of the most prevalent forms of tumor in women.
Currently, there remains no effective medication therapy available to treat this fatal
illness. On the other hand, early discovery may lengthen the lifespans of these individ-
uals. The primary goal of Md. Martuza Ahamad et al. [7] is to do analytical modeling
for early identiﬁcation by applying algorithms for ML and statistical methodologies
to health information collected from 349 affected persons. To identify the important
blood contaminants in the statistical evaluation, a test known as the Student’s t-test
and the log fold differences of both categories are employed. Moreover, classiﬁcation
frameworks are constructed using a collection of ML algorithms to separate patients
with moderate ovarian cancer from those with cancer. Furthermore, the statistical
evaluation outcomes demonstrate that the ML algorithms can distinguish between
malignant and benign cancer patients with up to 91% accuracy. ML recognition
may be crucial to the identiﬁcation of cancer considering the beginning predic-
tion is typically not possible. Furthermore, algorithms for classiﬁcation facilitate
the application of precision medicine strategies, enabling medical practitioners to
customize treatments according to the unique features of the malignancy. This indi-
vidualized approach to treatment reduces unneeded side effects for individuals while
simultaneously improving the efﬁcacy of medicines.

were able to identify a variety of genes that have been associated in terms of patient
outcomes and platinum resistance conditions. The algorithms performed better than
comparable strategies and attribute signiﬁcance assessment was used to identify
distinct genes.

the image. A 2D Gaussian function’s equation is as follows:

Feature Extraction

The process then moves on to feature extraction utilizing the GLCM after noise
reduction. By calculating the frequency of pixel pairs with particular intensity values
and distances, GLCM provides useful texture features that allow for the capturing
of texture information. These characteristics are critical for identifying minute
variations in the textures of ovarian tissue, facilitating more accurate classiﬁcation.

Gray-Level Co-occurrence Matrix (GLCM)

To examine the texture aspects of the image, GLCM was utilized to compute contrast,
energy, entropy, and homogeneity. Expressions (2) through (5) express the value at
the (i, j) position in a GLCM as the variable C(i, j). The four indices are indicative
of the surface characteristics of cancer cells and correlate with the disorder observed
in cell pictures. For instance, entropy indicated the amount of disorder, uniformity
indicated the smoothness of the pattern of distribution for the gray level, energy
indicated the orderliness, while contrast revealed the edges and 3D structures of the
cell [3].

Optimization

Butterﬂy Optimization

Arora et al. (2019) have created a population-based optimization technique called
BOA. It mimics how butterﬂies hunt for food and mate. The mathematical equation
for the scent in BOA is f  equalscupperISuperscripta, , where f stands for observed fragrance amount, c
for sensory modality, I for stimulus magnitude, and a for power exponent [8].

   Butterﬂy Optimization Algorithm (BOA) is an unmatched force in the ﬁeld of
ovarian cancer categorization, providing critical impetus for the quest for precise
and prompt diagnosis. BOA is essential in the complex world of medical imaging,
where the ability to discern minute details can mean the difference between life and
death. BOA makes sure that ML models such as SVM, RF, and CNN are optimized
to the maximum degree possible by carefully adjusting their settings.

Classiﬁcation

Support Vector Machine (SVM)

SVM is among the best classiﬁcation techniques available for the identiﬁcation of
cancer. A collection of appropriate variables and several signiﬁcant features are
critical to an SVM classiﬁer’s quality and effectiveness Rui Wang et al. [1]. One
important use of SVM) in medical image analysis is for the identiﬁcation of ovarian
cancer. SVM is a supervised ML technique that can be used to analyze medical images
since it works well with complicated and high-dimensional datasets. SVM can be
used in the context of ovarian cancer to differentiate between benign and malignant
ovarian tumors based on a variety of features taken from medical imaging, including
size, shape, and texture patterns. SVM looks for a hyperplane that divides the data
into two classes—benign and malignant tumors—in classifying ovarian cancer. This
represents the fundamental SVM classiﬁcation formula.

  A comprehensive strategy integrating SVM, RF, and CNN—each optimized with

Accuracy Analysis

To gain meaningful insights into the efﬁcacy of a model for classiﬁcation, accuracy,
precision, and recall are crucial measures in determining the type of ovarian cancer,
as well as any binary categorization problem. Accuracy is determined as the ratio
of successfully predicted occurrences to total instances and measures the overall
correctness of the forecasts made by the model. By dividing the number of accurately
predicted cases by the total number of instances, accuracy determines how accurate
the model is overall.

   Table 1 and Fig. 9 represent accuracy comparisons of proposed CNN + BOA.
Results show that accuracy of proposed CNN + BOA is 91% which is high compared
to RF + BOA is 85% and SVM + BOA is 88.50%, respectively.

Precision Analysis

Precision evaluates the model’s accuracy in making favorable predictions.  It
computes the proportion of true positive forecasts to all positive recommendations
(including true and false positives). The ratio of accurately anticipated beneﬁcial
ﬁndings to all predicted positive observations is known as precision. Precision is
signiﬁcant in the classiﬁcation of ovarian cancer since it gauges the accuracy of the
positive predictions. A high precision means that the model is generally accurate in
predicting ovarian cancer. When false-positive results—that is, results that indicate
cancer when there is none—have serious repercussions, such as needless medical
procedures or treatments, accuracy becomes essential.

Recall (Sensitivity or True-Positive Rate) Analysis:

Recall assesses the model’s ability to correctly recognize positive cases. It computes
the proportion of true positive predictions to all positive instances. The ratio of all the
actual beneﬁcial ﬁndings to all the correctly projected positive observations is called
recall. Recall is important in the categorization of ovarian cancer since it assesses
the model’s capacity to locate all pertinent cases within a dataset. A high recall
rate means that the majority of real positive cases can be identiﬁed by the model.
Because recall guarantees that the majority of true positive cases are identiﬁed, it is
particularly crucial in situations where false negatives—the failure to identify cancer
when it is present—can have serious repercussions.

                  Recall e                                                                                   PositivesOverTruePositivesplusFalseNegativesEndFraction
                            Recall equals StartFraction True

   In these formulas:

•  True Positives (TP): The number of correct positive predictions.
•  False Positives (FP): The number of positive predictions that were erroneous.
•  False Negatives (FN): The amount of times an event is anticipated as negative
   while it is positive.
•  Total Number of Predictions: True positives, false positives, true negatives, and
   false negatives are added together.

5  Conclusion


The combination of SVM, RF, and CNN with Butterﬂy Optimization, along with
preprocessing methods like feature extraction through GLCM and noise removal
with a Gaussian ﬁlter, constitutes a substantial advancement in the categorization
of ovarian cancer. In precisely recognizing ovarian cancer tissues from medical
photographs, our comprehensive assessment based on accuracy, precision, and recall
measures has clearly shown the superiority of the combination technique, Gaussian
ﬁlter + GLCM + butterﬂy optimization + CNN. We have enhanced precision and
recall rates in addition to achieving remarkable accuracy by combining the advan-
tages of deep learning, conventional ML models, and sophisticated optimization tech-
niques. The development of an improved categorization system has great potential
for accurate and timely detection of ovarian cancer, which is essential for bettering
patient outcomes. The accomplishments of this integrated approach highlight the
value of combining several approaches in the ﬁeld of medical imaging analysis,
opening the door to more accurate and efﬁcient cancer detection techniques. This
discovery offers hope for improved diagnostic tools and, eventually, better treatment
for patients with ovarian cancer by laying a solid platform for future developments
in the ﬁeld of medical imaging. Furthermore, by strengthening our knowledge of
ovarian cancer subtypes and assisting in the creation of targeted medicines, these
models complement ongoing research efforts that advance oncology and ultimately
save lives.

Abstract  In this investigation, we present a comprehensive analysis of deep learning
approaches employed in the detection of brain tumors. Our focus centers on eval-
uating the effectiveness of two distinct classiﬁcation models: a CNN sequential
architecture and a pre-trained VGG-16 model. Through a comparative review, we
shed light on the unique advantages and disadvantages of these methodologies. Our
study offers valuable insights into optimal deep-learning algorithms for diagnosing
brain tumors, derived from thorough experimentation and analysis. After assessing
multiple models, we observed that our proposed model exhibited remarkable accu-
racy compared to others. Analyzing a dataset comprising 7023 MRI images, our
CNN model achieved an outstanding accuracy rate of 96%. These ﬁndings contribute
signiﬁcantly to ongoing endeavors aimed at improving the identiﬁcation and treat-
ment of brain tumors, serving as a valuable resource for medical image analysis and
deep-learning researchers and practitioners.

1  Introduction


A brain tumor develops when abnormal cells begin to grow within the brain. These
tumors have a propensity to replicate and extend their presence across various areas of
the brain. In the context of medical diagnostics, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
stands out as a widely employed method for detecting and pinpointing the location
of brain tumors. The signiﬁcance of early detection of brain tumors cannot be over-
stated. Identifying and diagnosing brain tumors at an early stage is crucial for several
reasons. Firstly, it allows for prompt initiation of treatment, which can signiﬁcantly
improve a patient’s chances of successful recovery. Secondly, early detection can
help prevent the tumor from growing larger and potentially causing more extensive
damage to the brain or surrounding tissues. Moreover, it may lead to less invasive
treatment options, reducing the overall impact on a patient’s quality of life. Lastly,
early detection facilitates a better understanding of the tumor’s characteristics, aiding
in the development of personalized treatment plans tailored to the patient’s speciﬁc
condition. In summary, early detection not only enhances treatment outcomes but
also minimizes the physical and emotional toll on individuals facing brain tumors.
  Deep learning-based approaches for the analysis of brain MRI images for tumor
detection have garnered signiﬁcant attention and interest, primarily due to their
remarkable self-learning capabilities. Deep learning represents a robust and superior
approach within the broader realm of machine learning, ﬁnding valuable applica-
tions across various domains, including medical image segmentation. One notable
advantage of deep learning is its capacity to overcome the limitations associated with
inaccurate predictions in brain tumor detection. Traditional methods often struggled
with the complexities of brain MRI image analysis, leading to less precise outcomes.
Deep learning models, on the other hand, excel in handling intricate patterns and
nuances within the images, which are crucial for accurate tumor identiﬁcation. The
self-learning nature of deep-learning algorithms allows them to adapt and reﬁne their
performance over time as they are exposed to more data, making them particularly
suited for the evolving and intricate task of brain tumor detection. As a result, these
advanced techniques are contributing signiﬁcantly to improving the accuracy and
efﬁciency of medical image analysis, ultimately beneﬁting patients through earlier
and more reliable tumor detection and diagnosis.
   In our current study, we aim to bridge a critical gap by proposing and comparing
two distinct modeling methods with the primary objective of evaluating their perfor-
mance differences [1]. Understanding the importance of accurate and efﬁcient brain
tumor detection in health care is essential. Both benign and malignant brain tumors
pose signiﬁcant health challenges, and the potential life-threatening consequences
underscore the urgency to improve diagnostic methods, as highlighted by the National
Brain Tumor Foundation (NBTF) statistics. The invasive nature of brain tumor
biopsy, a current diagnostic procedure, not only carries inherent risks but also
places emotional and physical burdens on patients. Therefore, the development of
non-invasive diagnostic techniques, particularly advanced imaging modalities like
Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), is pivotal for enhancing early detection rates.

--- Page 106 ---
Enhancing Brain Tumor Detection Through Deep Learning …                          89

   In this research paper, we have conducted a comprehensive analysis of various
deep learning techniques employed in the realm of brain tumor detection. Speciﬁ-
cally, we have designed and evaluated two distinct classiﬁcation models. The ﬁrst
model is founded on a sequential architecture, while the second model leverages a
pre-trained VGG-16 model. CNNs play a pivotal role in the ﬁeld of medical image
analysis and tumor detection. Their signiﬁcance lies in their ability to automatically
learn and extract meaningful features from complex image data.
  A CNN sequential model is a general term for a type of deep neural network used
in image-related tasks, offering ﬂexibility in architecture design. In contrast, VGG16
is a speciﬁc pre-deﬁned CNN architecture characterized by its depth of 16 layers, with
a uniform structure. While a CNN sequential model allows customization, VGG16,
with its ﬁxed architecture, is known for simplicity and is often applied to image
classiﬁcation tasks due to its deep and uniform design [2–4].
   In the realm of brain tumor detection, the identiﬁcation of intricate patterns within
MRI images is paramount for accurate diagnosis. CNNs excel in discerning hierar-
chical patterns, edges, textures, and subtle intensity variations critical cues for tumor
identiﬁcation in brain images. Their adaptability and ability to learn from exten-
sive datasets make CNNs a potent tool for enhancing the precision and reliability
of tumor detection algorithms. Pre-trained models, such as VGG-16, have garnered
acclaim in the deep learning community for their capability to transfer knowledge
from vast datasets and domains. When applied to medical image analysis, particu-
larly in brain tumor detection, leveraging pre-trained models like VGG-16 expedites
development. These models have already acquired a rich hierarchy of features from
broad datasets (often in a general image classiﬁcation context), allowing for ﬁne-
tuning in speciﬁc medical imaging tasks with comparatively smaller datasets. This
transfer learning approach not only accelerates model training but also frequently
yields more robust and accurate models [5]. In the context of brain tumor detec-
tion, the use of pre-trained models enhances the efﬁciency and effectiveness of the
classiﬁcation process, contributing to early and precise diagnosis.



2  Background and Motivation


While traditionally, the identiﬁcation of brain cancers in MRI scans has relied on
the expertise of radiologists and medical professionals, this approach comes with
signiﬁcant drawbacks and limitations:

a.  Subjectivity: Varied interpretations among different radiologists may lead to
    inconsistent diagnoses and potential errors.
b.  Limited Efﬁciency: Manual examination of MRI images is time-consuming,
    especially when dealing with extensive datasets that require careful evaluation
    of each image slice.
c.  Error-Prone: Human errors, such as misdiagnosis or delayed diagnoses, can
   occur due to factors like fatigue, distractions, or variations in experience levels.

--- Page 107 ---
90                                                                 D. Barman et al.

d. Lack of Scalability: As the volume of medical imaging data grows, the scalability
    of manual interpretation becomes challenging, making it difﬁcult to meet the
    increasing demand for radiological services.

  On the ﬂip side, machine learning provides a viable method for identifying brain
tumors in MRI images, presenting numerous beneﬁts for medical imaging and health
care.

a.  Early Detection: Machine-learning algorithms can detect brain tumors at an
    early stage, often before symptoms manifest.
b.  Accuracy: Analysis of MRI images using machine-learning models achieves
   high accuracy, reducing the risk of misdiagnosis and consistently delivering
    reliable results.
c.  Efﬁciency: Automated brain tumor diagnosis through machine learning signiﬁ-
    cantly reduces the time required for analysis compared to manual inspection by
    radiologists.
d.  Consistency: Machine-learning algorithms, by minimizing the variability asso-
    ciated with human interpretation, produce consistent and accurate outcomes,
    ensuring that all patients receive precise diagnoses.
e.  Scalability: Machine learning is adept at processing and analyzing vast amounts
    of medical imaging data efﬁciently, making it scalable for health-care institutions.


3  Related Work


Khalil and colleagues [6] presented an innovative two-step dragonﬂy method speciﬁ-
cally designed for the segmentation of brain tumors from 3D MR data. The challenge
of detecting and classifying brain tumors in their early stages, given variations in size
and structure, was addressed by the researchers through a two-step dragonﬂy algo-
rithm, which aimed at accurately recovering the original contour points. Their study
utilized the BRATS 2017 3D MR brain tumors dataset, and notably, the proposed
model exhibited an accuracy approximately 5% higher than comparable investiga-
tions. The researchers utilized various techniques, including fuzzy C-means, SVM,
and random forests, to validate their ﬁndings. Assessment metrics such as accuracy,
precision, and recall were employed to evaluate the results. The outcomes indicated
superior performance of their model, achieving 98.20% accuracy, 95.13% recall, and
93.21% precision.
   In the realm of brain tumor identiﬁcation, Garg and colleagues [7] introduced a
diverse set of machine learning models, including Naive Bayes, Random Forest,
Neural Network, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and Decision Tree. They also
proposed a hybrid ensemble classiﬁer named KNN-RF-DT. To evaluate the perfor-
mance of these models, a dataset containing 2556 brain tumor images was utilized,
with 85% designated for training and the remaining 15% for testing. Thirteen distinct
features were extracted for the classiﬁcation task through methods such as Gray
Level Co-occurrence Matrix (GLCM), Principal Component Analysis (PCA), and

--- Page 108 ---
Enhancing Brain Tumor Detection Through Deep Learning …                          91

Stationary Wavelet Transform (SWT). Following a comprehensive assessment, the
recommended approach for brain tumor identiﬁcation and classiﬁcation demon-
strated impressive results. Speciﬁcally, the technique displayed a high level of reli-
ability at 97.72% and achieved an accuracy rate of 97.305%. Precision, speciﬁcity,
and sensitivity were reported at 97.73%, 97.60%, and 97.04%, respectively.
  Nayak et al. [8] introduced a dense Efﬁcient Net, CNN architecture designed
to detect brain tumors in MRI scans. In their study, the researchers conducted a
comparative analysis with ResNet-50, Mobile Net, and MobileNetV2. The ﬁndings
revealed that their dense Efﬁcient Net outperformed the other models. Following the
training phase, the dense Efﬁcient Net model exhibited exceptional results, achieving
an F1-score of 98.0% and an impressive accuracy of 98.78%. The study involved
employing four distinct categories of MRI images for the purpose of identifying
brain tumors, utilizing a total dataset consisting of 3,260 MR images.
  Almadhoun and colleagues [9] introduced a groundbreaking educational model
designed for the diagnosis of brain tumors using an MRI dataset. Alongside their
innovative educational model, the researchers conducted a performance comparison
with four other transfer learning models: VGG16, Mobile Net, ResNet-50, and Incep-
tion V3. The assessment utilized a dataset consisting of 10,000 MR images, each
with a resolution of 200 × 200 pixels. The dataset was partitioned into two main
categories: brain tumors and non-brain tumors, each comprising 5000 images. The
proposed deep learning model demonstrated superior performance in comparison to
the other models, achieving a test accuracy of 98%.
  Musallam and colleagues [10] introduced a DCNN model tailored for the iden-
tiﬁcation of brain tumors using MRI data. Their approach featured a lightweight
model with a limited number of max-pooling operations, iterative procedures, and
convolutional layers. In addition to their proposed model, the researchers incorpo-
rated a CNN-SVM method, along with VGG16 and VGG19, in their investigation.
The dataset encompassed a total of 3394 MR images, classiﬁed into four subgroups:
glioma (934 images), meningioma (945 images), no tumors (606 photos), and pitu-
itary (909 images). Notably, their recommended model demonstrated exceptional
performance metrics, achieving an overall accuracy of 97.72%. Furthermore,  it
displayed the capability to identify gliomas with a sensitivity of 99%, meningiomas
with a sensitivity of 98.26%, Pituitary tumors with a sensitivity of 95.95%, and
normal images with a sensitivity of 97.14%.
   In order to improve the early detection of brain tumors, Stadlbauer and colleagues
[11] developed a unique physiological MRI technique, integrating  it with nine
different machine learning models. Their assessment included diverse performance
metrics such as accuracy, precision, F1-score, AUROC, and classiﬁcation error. The
ﬁndings from their research suggest that machine-learning-driven radiophysiomics
has the potential to offer valuable support in clinical settings for the early diagnosis
of brain tumors. Concurrently, Aamir and collaborators introduced an automated
system designed for the identiﬁcation of brain tumors based on MR images. While
evaluating their machine learning model, they observed superior performance in cate-
gorization compared to previous methods, achieving an impressive accuracy rate of
98.95%.

   In their research conducted in 2009 [12], Rajeev Ratan, Sanjay Sharma, and

showcasing its effectiveness on both 2D and 3D MRI data. A noteworthy aspect
of this approach was its ability to function without the necessity of initialization
within the tumor, a requirement in other segmentation methods. Visualization and
quantitative assessments of the results conﬁrmed the efﬁcacy of this methodology.
The study went beyond the traditional manual segmentation for tumor identiﬁcation
by initially focusing on delineating the tumor’s area within a single MRI data slice

4.2  Classiﬁcation Model


In this study of Brain tumor, we are taken two classiﬁer model for the evaluation

4.2.1  Transfer Learning Model

Transfer learning is a commonly used approach in machine learning, especially for
tasks like image classiﬁcation and object detection. Models such as VGG16 and CNN
sequence are often employed for these tasks [13]. Transfer learning offers signiﬁcant
advantages in terms of both time and cost efﬁciency. Instead of starting from scratch,
which is time-consuming and demands substantial GPU resources and large image
datasets, pre-trained models are utilized to transfer knowledge and accomplish the
task efﬁciently [14–17].

Convolutional Neural Network

In our research, the CNN utilized speciﬁc parameters as follows: in the initial convo-
lutional layer, there were 16 ﬁlters with a 3 × 3 kernel size, succeeded by a 2 × 2
max-pooling layer; the second convolutional layer employed 32 ﬁlters with a 3 × 3
kernel size, followed by another 2 × 2 max-pooling layer; and the third convolutional
layer utilized 64 ﬁlters with a 3 × 3 kernel size, followed by a 2 × 2 max-pooling
layer. The fully connected dense layer comprised 4160 neurons, and the SoftMax
activation function was employed in the output layer [18–22].



VGG 16

The VGG16 architecture, introduced by Zisserman and Simona in 2014, is a member
of the VGG-NET family and is tailored for image detection and classiﬁcation, akin to
Alex Net [13]. Typically trained on the ImageNet database, VGG16 excels in precise
image recognition and categorization, particularly when dealing with large datasets
and intricate image recognition tasks. Boasting a total of 16 convolutional layers,
each featuring a 3 × 3 receptive ﬁeld, VGG16 incorporates ﬁve 2 × 2 max-pooling
layers. Beyond these layers, there are three fully connected layers following the ﬁnal
max-pooling layer. Activation of hidden layers in VGG16 is accomplished using the
ReLU activation function, while the SoftMax classiﬁer is applied to the output layer.

Janrhoni M. Kikon and Rubul Kumar Bania





Abstract The surging popularity of social media has yielded an abundance of
textual data, greatly enhancing its potential for analysis. Users freely express their
opinions and sentiments around the clock, irrespective of time or place. More-
over, the widespread dissemination of misinformation on social media platforms has
reached alarming levels. This study focused on the development of machine and deep
learning-based models, namely Random Forest (RF), Naïve Bayes (NB), Logistic
Regression (LR), a Majority Voting-based Classiﬁer, and Bidirectional Long Short-
Term Memory (Bi-LSTM). These ﬁve models are designed to analyze text data for
the identiﬁcation of fake news and the classiﬁcation of customer review sentiments.
Utilizing an 70–30% train-test split, the Bi-LSTM model demonstrated an impres-
sive accuracy of 97.11%, 92.01% in the classiﬁcation of fake news and customer
review sentiments, respectively.

Keywords Text data · Sentiment analysis · Fake news · Machine learning

In the digital internet age, social media has surged in popularity due to the user-
friendly interfaces, cost-effectiveness, and the ability to connect people globally
while facilitating the sharing of a vast spectrum of information [1, 2]. This encom-
passes product reviews, promotional campaigns, advertising, entertainment, and
much more. Conventional outlets such as daily newspapers and television broadcasts
have ceded their once-dominant position, with individuals now favoring the ease of

2  Related Work


In the era of digital communication, the widespread dissemination of misinformation,
commonly known as “fake news,” presents a substantial challenge. Effectively tack-
ling this issue necessitates inventive strategies for recognizing and countering false-
hoods. Sentiment analysis, a tool crafted to decipher the emotional subtleties within
text, has emerged as a valuable resource in this ongoing struggle. Despite researchers
starting to delve into the potential of sentiment analysis for detecting fake news, this
domain remains relatively unexplored. One noteworthy study [3] delves into various
text pre-processing techniques, including bi-grams and tri-grams, and employs the
TF-IDF method in conjunction with cosine similarity for evaluation, with accuracy
as the primary metric. This research emphasizes the integration of sentiment analysis
during COVID-19 periods. Another comprehensive investigation [4] examines the
utility of sentiment analysis in fake news detection. This study provides a summary
of systems demonstrating quantitative performance, as well as those that do not. It
also highlights future directions, such as analyzing content in multiple languages,
enhancing transparency in the detection process, mitigating biases in the analysis,
and effectively handling multimedia elements within fake news detection systems.
In the context of combating COVID-19 misinformation, [5] utilizes information
fusion to gather authentic news data from diverse multimedia sources like The New
York Times, Health Harvard. Their research work introduced sentiment features,
linguistic attributes, and named entity-based characteristics. DL models, including
Recurrent Neural Models (RNNs), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), and Long Short-
Term Memory (LSTM) networks, are deployed. The primary emphasis of this work
is on feature extraction from textual data, which is subsequently utilized in the fake
news detection process, rather than relying solely on the original text. Furthermore,
the study, as outlined in [6], explores the emotional content present in news headlines
and the sentiments conveyed in user comments on news articles. This investigation
delves into the intricate connection between these sentiments and the prevalence
of fake news within the Fakeddit dataset. To achieve this goal, a Bi-LSTM model
is employed to analyze textual characteristics. Collectively, these research efforts
illustrate the dynamic landscape of fake news detection, highlighting the pivotal role
of sentiment analysis in enhancing our ability to discern between veriﬁed facts and
fabricated information in the digital age.



3  Methodology


The methodology employed in this study is given in Fig. 1 as a block diagram, and it
consists of three distinct phases. Before delving into the detailed descriptions of each
phase, it is worth noting that the NLTK, a Python-based platform, plays a central
role in this study.

--- Page 119 ---
102                                                                                  J. M. Kikon and R. K. Bania

  The research methodology is organized into three primary phases. In the initial
phase, we undertake data collection and data preprocessing tasks. Data preprocessing
is of paramount importance, given that the data gathered from the Kaggle website
often arrives in an unclean state. This may entail the presence of numerous special
characters, hashtags, and extraneous symbols that do not contribute to the analytical
objectives. Moreover, the data may include punctuation marks, newline characters, a
mix of uppercase and lowercase text, and frequently occurring stop-words. Prepro-
cessing involves a series of transformations applied to the data before it is utilized
in machine learning algorithms.
  Moving to the second phase, for the processed restaurant review data assigned
sentiment scores are assigned, by considering polarity and subjectivity, using appro-
priate measures facilitated by Python libraries. To facilitate machine understanding,
the TF-IDF and word2vec word embedding technique is employed to convert words
into numerical format [3, 4]. The TF-IDF vectorized data are passed to the machine-
learning-based models and word embedding techniques are employed on LSTM and
bidirectional LSTM (Bi-LSTM) models (Fig. 1).
  Once the text data has undergone the process of vectorization or feature extraction,
the subsequent phase entails the selection of suitable learning models. In this investi-
gation, we draw upon insights gleaned from a variety of prior research endeavors [3,





Fig. 1 Work ﬂow diagram of the study

--- Page 120 ---
Towards Development of Machine Learning Models for Fake News …                   103

7–9] centered around text classiﬁcation and the classiﬁcation of social media data.
Consequently, we have opted for the utilization of three distinct supervised learning
models as our classiﬁers: Random Forest (RF), Naïve Bayes (NB), and Logistic
Regression (LR). These three models have been curated to form a diverse ensemble
classiﬁer based on Majority Voting. Furthermore, we have developed DL-based
models, namely LSTM and Bi-LSTM. The Bi-LSTM, an extended variant of long
short-term memory, constitutes a pivotal component of our approach. It comprises
two commonplace LSTMs: One that assimilates prior information and processes the
input sequence in the forward direction, and another that assimilates future infor-
mation and processes the data in reverse. This unique architecture empowers the
Bi-LSTM to concurrently capture both past and future contexts. The forward LSTM
comprehends the sequence from start to ﬁnish, while the backward LSTM appre-
hends it in reverse. The outputs from both LSTMs are harmoniously concatenated
to provide a holistic comprehension of the input sequence, encompassing informa-
tion from both temporal directions. This innovative design facilitates bidirectional
data ﬂow, enhancing the network’s ability to model long-term dependencies and
bolstering its predictive capabilities by accommodating data from both historical
and prospective perspectives. For the Bi-LSTM model employed in this study, we
have employed a stacked conﬁguration of Bidirectional LSTM layers. The initial
bidirectional layer is conﬁgured with 64 cells, and the subsequent layer is conﬁg-
ured with 32 Bidirectional LSTM units. Following this, we have introduced a dense
layer with 64 units and the ReLU activation function to further reﬁne the model’s
representations.

5  Conclusion


The progression of web and internet technologies has established an uncomplicated
landscape for individuals to freely share content. By leveraging text analysis tech-
niques, it becomes feasible to discern the emotions and perspectives of speciﬁc target
demographics. Concurrently, the proliferation of false information on social media
platforms has reached staggering proportions. In this research endeavor, we have
meticulously examined and scrutinized ﬁve distinct classiﬁcation models such as
RF, NB, LR, a Majority Voting-based Classiﬁer, and Bi-LSTM. These models have
been crafted to scrutinize textual data, facilitating the detection of fabricated news
and the categorization of sentiment in customer reviews. Notably, the Bi-LSTM clas-
siﬁer has demonstrated superior performance in our classiﬁcation evaluations when
compared to the other models. In future, we plan to extend this study to encompass
diverse languages, thus broadening the scope and applicability of our ﬁndings.

A Study on Measures Based
on Overlapping Area for Interval Data


Irani Hazarika and Anjana Kakoti Mahanta





Abstract  Interval data, a speciﬁc type of symbolic data, are increasingly widespread
across various ﬁelds, particularly in the domain of data mining. Evaluating the dis-
similarity or similarity between two intervals holds signiﬁcant importance in these
applications. This paper provides a comprehensive review of three distinct measures
commonly employed for interval data. Furthermore, it conducts a complete analysis
of these measures, shedding light on their respective properties and characteristics.

Keywords  Clustering · Dissimilarity measure · Distance measure · Interval data



1  Introduction


There are various popular applications in the ﬁeld of data mining like clustering,
classiﬁcation which are applied on various types of data like numeric, categori-
cal, text, interval etc. One key component of such applications is to measure the
proximity between two data. To ﬁnd proximity between the data different proxim-
ity measures are available as stated above. These proximity measures are broadly
categorized into two types—distance/dissimilarity measure and similarity measure.
Distance/dissimilarity measures are mainly used in numeric and interval data.
   Various real-world scenarios like weather forecasting, medical data analysis, and
stock market analysis produce data with interval-valued attributes. These situations
often involve challenges where it’s difﬁcult to obtain precise measurements or pin-
point exact attribute values. Uncertainty can also be a factor in observations. In such
scenarios, attribute values are represented as intervals. Again, sometimes values of
numeric attributes are converted into intervals to reduce size of the data or to uphold
conﬁdentiality (e.g., converting times to time slots). The data may also generate from

I. Hazarika (B) · A. K. Mahanta
Gauhati University, Guwahati, India

e-mail: anjana@gauhati.ac.in

I. Woungang et al. (eds.), Proceedings of the NIELIT’s International Conference
on Communication, Electronics and Digital Technology, Lecture Notes in Networks
and Systems 1022, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-97-3601-0_9

--- Page 126 ---
110                                                                                       I. Hazarika and A. K. Mahanta

intrinsically interval-valued random elements (e.g., daily temperature/humidity range
for a location, the daily ﬂuctuation of the blood pressure of a patient).
   Interval data extends the concept of single-valued data as it encompasses a range
of values bounded by two limits. Each interval within this data can be uniquely rep-
resented using a lower bound denoted as ‘l’ and an upper bound denoted as ‘r,’ often
referred to as the starting and ending points of the interval. Consequently, intervals
are denoted in the form of [l,r], encapsulating the range of values they represent.
If we consider any two intervals from the same domain in one-dimensional space,
then the intervals can be divided into groups as overlapping or non-overlapping. But
in case of numeric data there is no overlapping area between two data. But, it is
seen that several distance measures used for numeric data are also used for interval
data [ 1–4], in which the overlapping between the intervals may not be considered.
In [ 5], the authors studies about three distance measures L1-norm, L2-norm, L∞-
norm used for interval data. These measures are also used for numeric data. It is
seen that when L1-norm, L2-norm, L∞-norm are used for interval data then the
overlapping between the intervals is not considered. In this paper, we discuss three
different distance/dissimilarity measures available for interval data which consider
the overlapping between the intervals and also analyze some desirable properties for
the measures.
   In Sect. 2, preliminaries on interval data are given. After the preliminaries, in
Sect. 3 three existing distance measures for interval data have been mentioned and
also analyze of ten desirable properties for these three measures are discussed. In
Sect. 4, results and discussions are given, and in Sect. 5, conclusion statements are
given.



2  Preliminaries on Interval Data

2.1  Interval


Given a totally ordered discrete domain D, a non-empty subset I of D is called
an interval iff for all I −,I + ∈I and c ∈D, I −≤c ≤I + implies c ∈I. If for a
given interval I, I −≤c ≤I + holds for all c ∈D where I −and I + are two speciﬁc
elements in I, then I is denoted by [I −I +], and I −is the left end point (or lower
bound) and I + is called the right end point (or upper bound) of I. The intervals that
we consider are all closed intervals because for any c ∈I, I −≤c ≤I +.



2.2  Representations of Intervals

An interval I = [I −I +] can be represented in many forms such as—a line segment
in one-dimensional space, a point or circle in two-dimensional space. In line rep-

--- Page 127 ---
A Study on Measures Based on Overlapping Area for Interval Data                      111

resentation, each interval can be represented as line. Thus, in this representation
overlapping between any two intervals from the same domain can be seen. Any
two intervals from a domain are called overlapping, if Ix ∩Iy /= φ. In point repre-
sentation, intervals from same domain can be represented as a set of points where
overlapping between any two intervals is not seen. Again in circle representation any
interval I = [I −I +] can be deﬁned in terms of center and radius as follows:

                                           (I −+ I +)
                           Center, c =
                                     2

                                           (I + −I −)
                         Radius,r =                 .
                                     2


2.3  Arithmetic of Intervals


Some of the arithmetic concepts used for intervals are given below. The width and
midpoint of an interval I = [I −I +] are deﬁned as-

  Width, (|I|) = I + −I −
  Midpoint, (midI) = (I −+ I +)/2

   Suppose, Ix = [I x− I x+ ] and Iy = [I y− I y+ ] denote any two intervals then-
• Meet, Ix ∩Iy= [max(I x− , I y− ), min(I x+ , I y+ )]
• Meet, Ix ∩Iy = φ if I x+ > I y− or I y+ > I x−
• Join, Ix ⊕Iy= [min(I x− , I y− ), max(I x+ , I y+ )]
• Contain, Ix ⊆Iy iff I x− ≤I y− and I x+ ≥I y+
• Properly Contain, Ix ⊂Iy iff I x− < I y− , I x+ ≥I y+ or I x− ≤I y− , I x+ > I y+
• If Ix ∩Iy = φ, then Separation(Ix, Iy) = max(I x− , I y− ) −min(I x+ , I y+ )
  The Separation (Ix, Iy) increases when Ix and Iy are more apart from each other.
• vi.Suppose, the domain J contains n intervals I1, I2, …, In. Then width of domain
  J will be-

3  Materials and Methods

3.1  Measures Used for Interval Data


Several distance measures have been presented in the literature for interval data.
When the intervals are viewed as points, it becomes possible to measure the distance

--- Page 128 ---
112                                                                                       I. Hazarika and A. K. Mahanta

between any two intervals as the distance between two points [ 5]. But this measure
does not consider the overlapping between the intervals. So in this paper a study on
three existing distance measures has been done, which consider the overlapping area
between the intervals when measuring the distance between any two intervals from
a domain.

Measure Overlapping Interval Divergence (OLID) In paper [6], the authors intro-
duce a new proximity measure for intervals, called overlapped interval divergence
(OLID). This measure extends the existing distance measures by considering the
relationship between intervals and their overlapped area. The distance between two
intervals Ix and Iy can be measured by using overlapping interval divergence as-

                                          ∩Iy                 DOLID(Ix, Iy) = DHasym(Ix, Iy).(1 −Ix                        (1)                                                              |Ix| + 1).

    If an interval is considered as a closed continuous set, then the asymmetric Haus-
dorff distance between Ix and Iy can be measured as-

                      DHasym(Ix, Iy) = max {min D(a/, b/)}, ,                   (2)
                                               a/∈Ix b/∈Iy

where D(a/, b/) is a metric distance
   Suppose Ix = [I x− , I x+ ], Iy = [I y− , I y+ ] are two intervals for which cx, cy and
rx, ry denote the center and radii of Ix and Iy, respectively. If we consider the
relation between the intervals Ix and Iy, then DOLID(Ix, Iy) and DOLID(Iy, Ix) can
be expressed in terms of center and radius as follows:

•  Ix Before Iy :

  – DOLID(Ix, Iy) = DHasym(Ix, Iy)
  – DOLID(Iy, Ix) = DHasym(Iy, Ix)

•  Ix Overlap Iy:
    DOLID(Ix, Iy) = DHasym(Ix, Iy).(1 −(rx+ry)−|cx−cy|2rx+1     )
    DOLID(Iy, Ix) = DHasym(Iy, Ix).(1 −(rx+ry)−|cx−cy|(2ry+1    )

•  Ix Contain Iy:
    DOLID(Ix, Iy) = DHasym(Ix, Iy).(1 − 2rx+1)2ry
    DOLID(Iy, Ix) = 0


Measure by GK In [ 7], the degree of dissimilarity between two intervals Ix and Iy is
calculated based on their degrees of non-overlapping portion and the separability. The
intervals Ix and Iy may or may not overlap. If the intervals are overlapping, then the
degree of dissimilarity of Ix to Iy is deﬁned to be the ratio of non-overlapping portion
of Ix to |Iy|. On the other hand, in case of no overlapping the degree of dissimilarity
