of the pattern Ix to Iy is the ratio of the sum of |Ix| and the separability between Ix
and Iy to |Iy|. Hence, the degree of dissimilarity between Ix and Iy will be -

3.2  Analysis of Desirable Properties of Different Measures
    Used for Interval Data


In data mining, there are various applications such as clustering [9] and classiﬁcation
[10] where distance measures play a crucial role. Many real-life scenarios involve
describing objects using intervals and in some cases, one or more attributes of objects
are represented as intervals. For such kinds of applications, in this section some
desirable properties of distance measures used for interval data are stated [5, 11].
Also, it has been analyzed whether these properties are satisﬁed by the existing
measures discussed in Sect. 3.
  By considering the overlapping area between two intervals, intervals can be cate-
gorized as non-overlapping and overlapping. Suppose Ix = [ I x− I x+ ] , Iy = [ I y− I y+ ]
are two intervals. If Ix ∩Iy = φ, then they are called non-overlapping; otherwise
they are called overlapping intervals. In paper [12], the authors have considered the
possible relationships between any two intervals as Before, Overlap, Contains, while
discussing distance measures for interval data. In case of ‘Before’ relation, intervals

--- Page 130 ---
114                                                                                       I. Hazarika and A. K. Mahanta

are non-overlapping, and in case of ‘Overlap,’ ‘Contains’ relations intervals are over-
lapping. The mirror relations are after, overlapped by, and contained by, respectively.
By considering these relations, the desirable properties which should be satisﬁed by
the distance measures are discussed below-

Properties P1–P4 Suppose, Ix and Iy are two intervals and D(Ix, Iy) denotes the
distance between Ix and Iy. Then the measure D is called a metric or distance measure
if it satisﬁes the following properties [13, 14]-

• P1. D(Ix, Iy) ≥0; non-negativity
• P2. D(Ix, Iy) = 0; if and only if Ix=Iy
• P3. D(Ix, Iy) = D(Iy, Ix); symmetric
• P4. D(Ix, Iz) ≤D(Ix, Iy) + D(Iy, Iz); triangular inequality.

  A measure which partially satisﬁes these properties is called a divergence or
dissimilarity or semi-metric measure.

– Measure OLID is a divergence

  • P1: DOLID(Ix, Iy) ≥0, Hold.
  • P2: DOLID(Ix, Iy) = 0; if and only if Ix = Iy, Does not hold
    Suppose, Ix=[6 12], Iy=[6 17]. Here, Ix /= Iy and DOLID(Ix, Iy) = 0.
  • P3: DOLID(Ix, Iy) = DOLID(Iy, Ix), Does not hold
      It is calculated as a factor of Asymmetric Hausdroff distance and Asymmetric
    Hausdroff distance does not satisfy this property.
  • P4: DOLID(Ix, Iz) ≤DOLID(Ix, Iy) + DOLID(Iy, Iz), Does not hold
    Suppose, Ix=[10 30], Iy=[20 40], Iz=[100 120]. Then |Ix ∩Iy| = 10.


                                        =10 x (1–0.47) = 5.3       DOLID(Ix, Iy) = DHasym(Ix, Iy).(1 −Ix∩Iy|Ix|+1)
       DOLID(Iy, Iz) = DHasym(Iy, Iz).(1 −Iy ∩Iz|Iy| + 1) = 80 × 1 = 80
       DOLID(Ix, Iz) = DHasym(Ix, Iz).(1 −Ix∩Iz|Ix|+1) = 90 × 1= 90

    Now, DOLID(Ix, Iy) + DOLID(Iy, Iz) = 85.3 < DOLID(Ix, Iz)
    Thus, it does not satisfy triangular inequality.

– Measure by GK is a divergence

  • P1: DGK(Ix, Iy) ≥0, Hold
    But it does not satisfy properties P2, P3 and P4 (as shown below).
  • P2:DGK(Ix, Iy) = 0; if and only if Ix = Iy, Does not hold
      If Ix= Iy, then (3) can be rewritten as DGK(Ix, Iy) = 2|Ix||Ix| = Ix
    Thus, it does not satisfy property P2.
  • P3: DGK(Ix, Iy) = DGK(Iy, Ix), Does not hold
    Again, DGK(Ix, Iy) is calculated as a factor of |Iy|1 and DGK(Iy, Ix) is calculated
     as a factor of |Ix|.1
    Thus, the property P3 is not satisﬁed.

    Suppose, Ix=[10 30], Iy=[20 60], Iz=[100 120].
    Then |Ix ∩Iy|= 10.

Property P10 Let, Ix, Iy and Iz are three intervals. If Separation(Ix, Iy) = Separation

– Property P10 does not hold for OLID In property P10,  Ix ∩Iy = φ and

  Now, DOLID(Ix, Iy) = DHasym(Ix, Iy) = 20–10 = 10
  DOLID(Ix, Iz) = DHasym(Ix, Iz) = 20–10 = 10

– Property P10 holds for measure by GK Here, Ix ∩Iy = φ and Ix ∩Iz = φ.
  From (6), DGK(Ix, Iy) = |Ix|+Separation(Ix,Iy)|Iy|
  DGK(Ix, Iz) = |Ix|+Separation(Ix,Iz)|Iz|
  Now, if Separation(Ix, Iy) = Separation(Ix, Iz), then DGK(Ix, Iy) /= DGK(Ix, Iz)
  when |Iy| /= |Iz|.

– Property P10 holds for measure by IY Here, Ix ∩Iy = φ and Ix ∩Iz = φ.


From (7),

  DIY(Ix, Iy) = |Ix ⊕Iy| −γ (|Ix| + |Iy|) = |Ix| + |Iy| + Separability(Ix, Iy) −
  γ (|Ix| + |Iy|)
  DIY(Ix, Iz) = |Ix ⊕Iz| −γ (|Ix| + |Iz|) = |Ix| + |Iz| + Separability(Ix, Iz) −
  γ (|Ix| + |Iz|)

  From the above, it can be concluded that this measure satisﬁes property P10.


4  Results and Discussion


For the purpose of experimentation, three real-life interval datasets Car (https://
lhedjazi.jimdo.com/useful-links), Fish  (https://lhedjazi.jimdo.com/useful-links),
Water  (http://cpcb.nic.in/data2005.php), and  three  synthetic  interval  datasets
(SyntheticIntervalDataset1, SyntheticIntervalDataset2, SyntheticInterval
Dataset3) have been used. The Car dataset have of 33 samples with 8 interval fea-
tures and 4 different classes with 10, 8, 8, and 7 samples per class, respectively.

5  Conclusion


In this work, a study of three existing measures for interval data has been reported.
Also, different representations of interval data have been discussed. Based on the
representations, an analysis of ten desirable properties that should be satisﬁed by
the measures for interval data has been done. To know how these distances work on
the data, a comparative study of all the distance measures has been done by using
well-known K−Means clustering algorithm and 6 interval datasets.

Application of Secure Data Transmission
by Integrating QR Code with Visual

Anil B. Alde  and Vikas T. Humbe





Abstract A QR code is a quick response code, and it is a two-dimensional barcode
that can be read by a QR code scanner, a smartphone with camera or by a QR code
reader application. QR codes are often used to provide quick access to information
or to link users to a website or application which is often helpful for growing busi-
ness. With the wide application of QR code, the security problem of QR code is
serious, such as information leakage and data tampering. Anyone can scan the QR
code and access the data hidden in the QR code, which means access to the data is
public or global and not used for private purposes or for sharing conﬁdential data.
To solve all these problems, this paper proposed a methodology to secure conﬁ-
dential data as well as provide multilevel security while transmitting data through
communication channels by integrating QR codes with Visual Cryptography (VC).
By using the proposed methodology, QR codes can used for private purposes to
transfer conﬁdential information securely and hiddenly over the internet.

Keywords Mean square error (MSE) · Random grid visual cryptography scheme
(RGVCS) · Visual cryptography (VC)



1  Introduction


QR code stands for quick response code and was invented in 1994 by the Japanese
automotive company denso wave [1] to track vehicles and parts during the manufac-
turing process. It is a two-dimensional barcode that can be read by a QR code scanner
or by a smartphone with a built-in camera and a QR code reader application [2]. QR
codes are designed to be read quickly and accurately. They are made up of a grid
of squares that contain black and white modules, which can be arranged in various

1.1 QR Code


QR codes are becoming popular daily in the upcoming generation as they offer way
easier authentication than traditional old-fashioned user IDs and passwords. The
merits of QR codes are it has greater storage capacity and fast readability, it Offer
360° reading for scanning QR code, i.e., no need to place the scanner as per the
code symbol, different types of data that can be hidden in QR codes, small print
sizes take less space, error correction technique is used in QR code that enables
successful decoding even if up to 30% of the QR code is dirty or damaged, support
for more languages, scan the QR code for accessing WhatsApp, Wi-Fi, Zoom or
Google Meetings, Google Maps location. It can be used to make online payments. In
education, different book chapters are now molded in QR codes, just scan the QR code
to access all chapter contents and question-and-answer. The QR code technology
is easy to use, easy to access information, gives a fast response, access product
information and purchase it by scanning the QR code printed on that product.
  Due to all these qualities of QR codes, ﬁrms that are relatively new in the online
business tend to use these codes instead of the normal login process.

1.2  Motivation


If any user wants to hide information in the QR code and wants to access it for
private purposes is not possible. However, it can be possible if the QR code mech-
anism integrates with the visual cryptography scheme [6]. By using the proposed
methodology, security can also provide for transmitted data and have to utilize it for
private purposes also. This integrated approach adds an extra layer of security to the
QR code, as it ensures that the code can only be scanned and decoded if all the shares
are present and properly aligned.



2  Literature Review


Revenkar [7] describes that visual cryptography (VC) is a cryptographic technique
that allows Visual information (pictures, text, etc.) to be encrypted in such a way that
the decryption can be performed by human visuals without the aid of computers.
  Naor and Shamir [8] 1994 ﬁrst introduced visual cryptography and provided their
constructions of visual cryptographic solutions for the general k out of n secret
sharing problem in their paper.
  Chang [9] elaborates that in the present visual cryptography scheme, a Secret
sharing scheme is used to generate shares. Decoding operation includes XORing of
shares. It provides a low computation complexity method for the decryption process.
Shares are images of QR codes. It includes the reconstruction of secret images.
  Agrawal [10] illustrates that the visual cryptography (VC) scheme is a method to
encode a secret image into noise-like shadow images called shared images, and the
shared images need some processing to reconstruct the secret image.



3  Proposed Methodology


Due to the rapid development of networks such as an intranet, and internet, wireless
communication in digital media is a cheaper one for transferring any format of data
throughout the world within a second but the main thing is that it is not secure. It
may be secure if you have any mechanism or methodology that provides security to
data and has copyright protection, authentication, identiﬁcation, and secret sharing
information.
  To have security to conﬁdential and legal information hidden in the QR code and
also have private access to the QR code, we may integrate the QR code with visual
cryptography (VC) or visual secret scheme (VSS) [9, 11] as shown in Fig. 1.
  By the visual cryptography technique, the image of the QR code is split up into
two human unreadable encrypted forms of images called shares. As these shares are
sent toward the receiver side, the receiver can overlap these shares one above another

--- Page 144 ---
128                                                      A. B. Alde and V. T. Humbe





Fig. 1  Integrating QR code with visual cryptography (VC)


to reveal the original form of the QR code. After scanning the QR code with a smart
mobile or by any scanning device, hidden conﬁdential information within the QR
code can be revealed.
   But, the main problem is that while transmission these shares through a commu-
nication channel, over the internet if an unauthorized person or hacker succeeds in
accessing both these shares then he can reveal the original QR code image by super-
imposing these shares and access the hidden legal information by scanning the QR
code, which is again problematic one. Still, again we need more security mechanisms
to have security for legal data. The proposed methodology is more applicable to solve
all these problems and give more and more security to hidden data of QR codes as
shown in Fig. 2.
   In the proposed methodology, the original QR code image is divided into two
parts called shares which are in a human unreadable encrypted form built by using
the Visual Cryptography (VC) technique. To increase the security level, share 2 is
again divided into several parts called Cells (Tiles) and then all the Cells of Share
2 are randomly shufﬂed. After shufﬂing and randomization of all Cells, Cells of an
even number of rows are rotated by 180° anticlockwise and Cells of odd-numbered
rows are rotated in a clockwise direction by 90°. While randomizing, shufﬂing and
rotating all the Cells of share 2, a key is generated.
  Now share 1, shufﬂed share 2 and the key is sent towards the recipient side.
Recipient when receiving all the shares and key, a key is helpful to arrange all the
Cells of share 2 into their proper order form to reconstruct share 2. After that for
revealing the original form of the QR code, superimpose share 1 and share 2. After
revealing the original form of the QR code, it can be scanned by any smart device or
by smartphone to access secret data hidden in the QR code. In this way, integrating
the QR code with visual cryptography is helpful to access secured hidden information

stored in the QR code and also get success to access QR privately because publicly
it is not accessed due to encrypted QR code in the form of shares.
   In the proposed methodology, two main algorithms are used such as “Encryption”
and “Decryption”. “Encryption” Algorithm 1 is based on a Random Grid that helps
to generate encrypted shares.

 Input: M × N Binary image (secret image)
 k: Minimum number of participants to reveal a secret, where k = 2
 n: Maximum number of participants, where n = 2

 Output: Two Shares (Shadow image), one for each participant

 Step 1   Accept a secret binary image I of dimension M x N. If a secret image is a gray or color

this methodology and also increases the security ratio.

4  Experimental Result and Performance Analysis


The proposed methodology uses a Random Grid Visual Cryptography Scheme
(RGVCS), and it helps to overcome all the drawbacks of traditional visual cryp-
tography such as pixel expansion and low contrast. The mean square error (MSE) of
the resultant image in the proposed methodology is zero so the peak-signal-to-noise
ratio (PSNR) is inﬁnity and no change in aspect ratio because the height and width
of the resultant image remains the same as that of the original image which is shown
in Fig. 3.
   In studying different visual cryptography scheme, except the proposed Random
Grid Visual Cryptography Scheme (RGVCS), all schemes have the lossy resultant
secret image. However, the proposed methodology succeeds in overcoming this
problem and generates a lossless image at the receiver side which is shown in Table 2.
  The results of the proposed methodology are evaluated by different quality metrics
to check whether the resultant generated secret image is qualitative or not. All these
quality metrics values are shown in Table 3. The entropy value of the original image
and resultant image remain the same which implies exact matching of both the image.

4.1  Merits of Proposed Methodology


Integrating QR codes with visual cryptography enhances the higher level of security
and privacy that can be achieved at various levels ensuring that sensitive or conﬁden-
tial information such as government ﬁnancial reports and medical reports remains
protected and not accessed by unauthorized users. To access the information encoded
in the QR code, multiple shares need to be combined, ensuring that no single entity
has access to the complete code.
  The proposed methodology creates a multi-factor authentication system environ-
ment that is more secure and conﬁdential until all properties are matched with each
other as well and all necessary shares are overlapped with each one above the other.



5  Conclusion


The proposed methodology is a perfect application of secure data transmission by
integrating the QR code with visual cryptography (VC). The proposed methodology
uses the Random Grid technique which helps to generate a lossless image at the
receiver side, reduces the problem associated with pixel expansion, and generates
a high contrast noise-free image at the receiver side. Another main thing about the
proposed methodology is that it transmits the conﬁdential data hidden in the QR code
securely and offers a private mode of operation to the QR code. Lastly, the results
of the proposed methodology are analyzed by different quality measurement metrics
that give excellent results and generate a highly efﬁcient code that consumes less
battery power. This integrated approach adds an extra layer of security to the QR
code and adds a private mode for the operation of the QR code, as it ensures that the
code can only be scanned and decoded if all the shares are properly aligned.

Event Uncertainty for Twitter Data
Using Thematic Context Vector


Vaibhav Khatavkar, Swapnil Mane, and Parag Kulkarni





Abstract One of the critical steps in text mining is keyword extraction. Extracting
keywords along with their respective contextual events in Twitter data poses a sig-
niﬁcant challenge due to language informality, encompassing acronyms, misspelled
words, synonyms, transliteration, and ambiguous terms. The current systems for key-
word extraction rely on either pattern-based or event-based approaches. In this paper,
keywords are extracted using contextual events with the assistance of data associ-
ation. The thematic context vectors for events are identiﬁed using the uncertainty
principle in the proposed system. The system is tested on the Twitter COVID-19
dataset and proves to be effective. It extracts event-speciﬁc thematic context vec-
tors from the test dataset and ranks them. The extracted thematic context vectors
are then utilized for the clustering of contextual thematic vectors, improving the sil-
houette coefﬁcient by 0.5% compared to state-of-the-art methods, namely TF and
TF-IDF. The thematic context vector can be applied to other applications such as
cyberbullying detection, sarcasm detection, and ﬁgurative language detection.

Keywords Event identiﬁcation · Thematic context vector · Keywords extraction ·
Time series · Event clustering

1  Introduction


In the realm of text data, natural language processing is frequently employed to
develop systems for tasks such as named entity recognition, product ranking, sen-
tence ranking, and recommended systems. Data mining approaches for extracting
information from social media content have been discussed in [ 1], where researchers
emphasized the signiﬁcance of size, noise, and dynamism in social media content.
Khan et al. [ 2] provide a review of state-of-the-art machine learning approaches in
natural language processing, elucidating the utilization of part-of-speech tagging,
word sense disambiguation, and discourse analysis to address ambiguity in text pro-
cessing. Noteworthy developments in natural language inference aiming to infer
meaning from textual data are also reported [3]. A substantial volume of textual data
is accessible on the internet through social media, blogs, etc. [ 4]. Daily statistics
reveal the transmission of 500 million tweets, 294 emails, and 65 billion WhatsApp
messages, with around 300 million users identiﬁed as new users on social media
platforms [ 5]. This abundance of data is harnessed across various domains of text
mining to convert it into valuable information. Topic modeling algorithms like LDA
are commonly applied to Twitter data for topic extraction [ 6]. David and Martin [7]
introduce a topic model for Twitter data based on Author Topic Modeling (ATM).
Alvarez-Melis and Saveski ﬁnd ATM to be more effective than LDA, albeit consum-
ing more time. Additionally, data clustering produces similar clusters of tweets [ 8],
enabling the classiﬁcation of Twitter data into various categories [9]. Namugera et al.
[ 10] correlate topics using positive and negative sentiments in tweets, highlighting the
inﬂuential role of negative tweets in information dissemination on Twitter. Povinille
[ 11] applies time series data mining to temporal ﬁnancial data, deﬁning an objective
function to uncover hidden patterns and gain a trading edge over stocks in the ﬁnan-
cial market. The system’s efﬁcacy is tested on investment transactions from the New
York Stock Exchange. Makrehchi et al. [ 12] leverage events as market loss and gain
indicators in social media text, formulating marketing strategies. Xu [ 13] develops
a forecasting system for stock prices using Yahoo Finance and Google Trend data,
incorporating ARIMA time series analysis and correlating news with events. The
study concludes that news signiﬁcantly inﬂuences stock price predictions. Chavoshi
et al. [ 14] identify abnormal user accounts on Twitter using a lag-sensitive hashing
technique and a warping-invariant correlation measure, effectively recognizing and
correlating abnormal users.
   This study confronts the complexities of extracting keywords from Twitter data
and recognizing language informality issues, including acronyms, misspelled words,
synonyms, transliteration, and ambiguous terms. Diverging from prevailing pattern
or event-based methods, our approach utilizes data association to extract keywords
grounded in contextual events. By leveraging the uncertainty principle, we pinpoint
thematic context vectors for events. The subsequent sections of the paper follow
a structured progression. Section 2 delves into related work, offering insights into
existing research in the domain. In Sect. 3, our proposed methodology is detailed,
highlighting the distinctive aspects of our approach in contrast to prior methods.

Section 4 encompasses the experimentation phase, elucidating the methods and
datasets employed for validation. Section 5 articulates the results obtained from
the experimentation, emphasizing the effectiveness of our approach. Finally, Sect. 6
encapsulates the conclusion, summarizing the key ﬁndings and implications of our
work in the context of keyword extraction from Twitter data.



2  Related Work


Several studies have explored the mapping of Twitter data as a time series and its sub-
sequent analysis. Salvatore et al. [15] conducted qualitative and quantitative analyses
of social media content, using Twitter as a prominent example. They constructed a
timely socio-economic indicator based on social media data. Arias et al. [16] extracted
social, economic, and commercial indicators through Twitter time series analysis.
Alshaabi et al. [17] analyzed tweets related to medical, political, and COVID-19-
related topics across 24 languages over a year (March 2019 to March 2020). Notably,
they observed that the term ’virus’ peaked in all languages in January and February.
Cakit et al. [18] explored the use of supervised soft computing techniques—fuzzy
time series (FTS), artiﬁcial neural network (ANN)-based FTS, and adaptive neuro-
fuzzy inference systems (ANFIS)—to predict emotional states expressed in Twitter
data. Gonzalo et al. [19] identiﬁed critical events during natural disasters and social
movements using Bayesian networks, demonstrating the utility of tweet patterns for
classiﬁcation. Colette et al. [20] predicted Oscar winners using Twitter time series
data, employing logistic regression and time series decomposition. Raghuvira Pratap
et al. [ 21] focused on detecting and monitoring trafﬁc using classiﬁed and clustered
tweets. Arapostathis and Karantzia [22] utilized Volunteered Geographic Information
(VGI) and Twitter data for disaster management, successfully identifying, tracking,
and classifying ﬁre events. Chen and Terejanu [23] treated sub-event identiﬁcation
as an outlier detection problem, employing statistical methods such as Kalman ﬁlter,
Gaussian process, and probabilistic principal component analysis. Behzadan et al.
[24] detected events in social networks, particularly on Twitter, for cybersecurity
using a convolutional neural network (CNN). Hossny et al. [25] employed Naive
Bayes classiﬁers to predict future events based on historical and live events present
in tweets.
  Hasan et al. [ 26] combined random indexing with locality-sensitive hashing to
cluster tweets related to various events within a ﬁxed time. Katragadda et al. [27]
identiﬁed credible events by evaluating topics based on conversational patterns in
tweets. Kolchyna et al. [28] focused on the automatic identiﬁcation of optimum event
windows for Twitter data time series, followed by event clustering and quantiﬁcation.
Grindrod et al. [ 29] utilized event spikes in Twitter time series for their work, while
Lai et al. [ 30] modeled topics on Twitter data in the spatio-temporal time domain,
establishing relationships among them. Yadav et al. [31] modeled tweets related to
IPL T20 with temporal time series for event identiﬁcation and box ofﬁce revenue
trend analysis. Additionally, Arias et al. [ 17] analyzed and forecasted box ofﬁce

--- Page 153 ---
138                                                                        V. Khatavkar et al.

revenue trends using events in Twitter time series. Commonly, event-related data
acquisition involves using keywords as search patterns in available data. The size of
the data poses a signiﬁcant challenge. Some researchers [32] have reported success
in event detection with large Twitter datasets, proposing a method to retrieve more
events related to speciﬁc content using term frequency-inverse document frequency
(TF-IDF). Velankar et al. [ 33] represented audio and text data in time series form for
the identiﬁcation of contextual events. Zaman et al. [ 34] analyzed Twitter discourse
around Bitcoin discussions and events of Bitcoin price changes, performing sentiment
analysis and text mining on Elon Musk’s tweets from January 2021 onward. Singla
et al. [ 35] analyzed hashtags for INPST activities on Twitter from May 2021 to June
2021, concluding on the effectiveness of events using digital tools, particularly on
social media platforms like Twitter.
   In the proposed method, the thematic context is built on the available data, which
can be small or large. The thematic context comprises keywords and their association
for events. The events can be derived from the search patterns, which are queries on
the data. The theme of the document can be used to get thematic context vectors
[37, 38].

  As all words related to an event have the same term frequency (TF) value
(i.e., 1), TF alone does not provide a comprehensive understanding of the unique
events in the dataset. To address this limitation, TF-IDF values are calculated. How-
ever, Table 3 demonstrates that TF-IDF fails to adequately represent the importance
of words concerning speciﬁc events. Our proposed method overcomes this limitation
and provides a more effective measure of word importance in relation to events, as
shown in Table 2.
  The dynamic nature of the Twitter dataset, constantly evolving in real-time, poses
challenges for calculating TF-IDF scores due to the changing stream. Traditional
TF-IDF scores are computed for the entire dataset, lacking speciﬁcity for particular
events like medical or care-related discussions. To address this, we propose utilizing
thematic context vectors in the incoming data. These vectors provide a measure of
certainty for the occurrence of speciﬁc events based on words associated with those
events. We employ the apriori algorithm for association mining to identify thematic
associations among words in the data stream. This approach enables us to adapt to
the real-time increase in data and focus on the thematic context of events.

6  Conclusion


Essential knowledge in the times series of Twitter data is a set of keywords for con-
textual events. Thematic context vectors are derived from the Twitter data, which
gives the context of the event. The queries are used to ﬁnd the context of the event.
The uncertainty principle is used to rank the thematic vectors in the events. The
thematic context vector shows an uncertainty value of 0 for certain events in the
data that are associated with each other. When event clustering is performed using
the proposed method, the average improvement in silhouette coefﬁcient is achieved
by 0.5% over clustering performed with state-of-the-art methods such as TF and
TF-IDF. For contextual relation, conditional probability of keywords with respec-
tive events is used which proves to be effective. This can be applied to generate
automated events in the tweet. Our study confronts challenges from noisy data and
dynamic data streams. While we have addressed language informality in English,
extending our approach to diverse linguistic contexts is a future research priority.
We acknowledge the complexities of K-means clustering without predeﬁned clus-
ters and commit to ongoing efforts to address potential limitations. Future research
directions include exploring non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) for clustering
and integrating knowledge graphs to represent intricate word relations within events,
enhancing our understanding of contextual dynamics in textual data. In applications
like cyberbullying, sarcasm detection, language models, etc., the thematic context

--- Page 160 ---
Event Uncertainty for Twitter Data Using Thematic Context Vector                      145

vectors identiﬁed using the proposed system can be applied. The results also reveal
that contextual events can be used from social media platforms like Twitter for infor-
mation extraction and data mining.

A Brief Study of Prompting Techniques
for Reasoning Tasks


Satyavrat Gaur, Anjali Dagar, Aanchal Punia, and Pushpendra Kumar





Abstract  In recent times, there has been a growing interest in the capabilities of large
language models (LLMs). Prompting techniques give an efﬁcient way to guide the
LLM and get better results. The process of designing a prompt that can generate the
desired output is iterative. Here, we review different prompting techniques available
for solving complex reasoning tasks. It discusses how these techniques affect the
accuracy and efﬁciency of LLMs when they are used to address reasoning tasks.
Furthermore, this survey may work as a starting point for individuals who are new to
the ﬁeld of prompting. This work also contains a comparative analysis of the results
of different prompting techniques to assess their accuracy.

Keywords Natural language processing · Prompting · Reasoning · LLM



1  Introduction


Reasoning involves a scientiﬁc exploration aimed at assessing the capabilities of the
human mind. It serves as a guiding light for decision-making and offers a struc-
tured pathway to grasp complex problems [1]. Recognizing the signiﬁcance of this,
researchers are experimenting with large language models on different benchmarks
of reasoning to fully harness LLMs capabilities. Research in this ﬁeld has established

2  Related Work


In this section, we will discuss the evolution of LLMs, datasets, and prompting
techniques used for evaluating LLMs.



2.1 LLM


The evolution of LLMs can be traced back through a rich historical trajectory.
This development owes its progress not only to computer developers but also to
contributions from professionals across a spectrum of ﬁelds, including linguistics,
psychology, and philosophy, among others. These diverse inputs have played a pivotal
role in shaping the potential of LLMs. Beyond their core functions of language
understanding and generation, these models have demonstrated their versatility by
excelling in tasks such as word processing, text classiﬁcation, discourse analysis,
translation, text summarization, data analysis, text-based games, and more. A signif-
icant turning point in LLM development occurred in 2013 with the introduction
of neural networks in natural language processing (NLP). Subsequently, neural
network architectures such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs), convolutional

--- Page 164 ---
A Brief Study of Prompting Techniques for Reasoning Tasks                           149

neural networks (CNNs), and deep neural networks (DNNs) have gained prominence
in the realm of language models. Extensive comparative studies have been conducted
to identify the neural network architectures that offer superior performance, as
highlighted in references [2, 3].
  The introduction of transformers and attention mechanisms marked a revolu-
tionary phase, leading to the creation of multiple large language models like ChatGPT
[4], Falcon 7B, Falcon 40B, LLaMA [5], and BERT [6], each developed by different
organizations and characterized by substantial parameter counts. This advancement
has greatly broadened the scope of LLM and its applications across different domains,
contributing to continuous progress in the ﬁeld.



2.2  Dataset


For evaluating LLMs, datasets play a crucial role. Based on the test data, LLM
performance is scored based on exact match, precision, accuracy, recall, F1-score,
and BLEU. In the case of reasoning tasks, since the ground truth value is avail-
able, an exact match seems the best way to compare the LLMs’ performance. To
estimate the effect of prompting techniques, various datasets are required so that
changes exerted by prompting methods can be observed. Different types of datasets
are used by researchers to identify the capabilities of LLM. Mishra et al. [7] use arith-
metic reasoning to test LLM on procedural decision-making ability. In [7], symbolic
reasoning uses linguistic patterns to solve problems [8, 9] testing the common-sense
reasoning that requires humans to develop a lot of knowledge and time. Also, [10]
uses Logical Reasoning to measure LLM’s ability to analyze information, solve
problems, and make decisions in a coherent and structured manner [10, 11] uses a
Multimodal Reasoning dataset.
  The prompting technique’s evaluation used the following benchmarks  for
commonsense, symbolic, and arithmetic reasoning:

• CommonsenseQA

  – CSQA [12]
  – StrategyQA [8]

• Symbolic Reasoning

  –  Last Letter Concatenation [13]
  – Coin Flip tasks [13]

•  Arithmetic Reasoning

  – GSM8K [14]
  –  MultiArith [15]
  – AddSub [16]

2.3  Basics of Prompt Principles


With the development of more powerful NLP models, prompt engineering is evolving
concurrently. The prompt can be formulated manually as well as automatically [19].
In this section, we discuss how the prompting paradigm can effectively leverage pre-
trained models. Before moving forward to the advanced “prompting techniques”, it
is crucial to grasp the basics prompt formulations. To evaluate these basic prompts
(Role, Role with instructions, and Few-Shot Prompting), ChatGPT 3.5 is used.
  Role Prompting. This method may seem straightforward, but it is highly effective.
It narrows the model’s focus to a speciﬁc context [20]. In the ﬁgure below, an example
has been chosen to illustrate how the use of prompts can enhance the performance
of basic tasks.
   Figure 1 describes how the impact of role prompting can be seen by assigning 2
different roles to the model. In the poetic role, the model describes a beautiful and
tranquil picture of “stars twinkling in the night sky”. On the other hand, the scientiﬁc
role explains how the twinkling happens due to things like atmospheric refraction
and turbulence in clear, factual terms.
  Role Prompting with Instructions. Once a role is assigned, it is beneﬁcial to
include speciﬁc instructions as well. These instructions will inﬂuence the model’s
behavior, reﬁning its writing to produce more precise results tailored to the assigned
role.
   Figure 2 explains role prompting with instructions. In this example model is
assigned the role as well speciﬁc instructions are added in the prompt which has
shown better results.
  Few-Shot Prompting. In this approach, the model learns how to respond to ques-
tions through examples (1-shot, 2-shot, 3-shot, or more). “Few-Shot” describes a
scenario in which the model receives several task demonstrations during the infer-
ence process [21]. By providing examples or templates that demonstrate the intended
format or structure assists the model in generating improved results. The emergence

3  Prompting Techniques


In the realm of language models, a complex task typically involves a problem that
can be resolved through multiple sequential steps. When dealing with intricate tasks
of this nature, the signiﬁcance of Prompt Engineering is heightened, presenting an
even greater challenge. Indeed, variations in prompts across various critical aspects
can signiﬁcantly inﬂuence the accuracy and performance of large language models.

--- Page 167 ---
152                                                                                S. Gaur et al.

A fundamental prompt comprises four components: context, instructions, input data,
and output indicators. Various prompting techniques modify one or more of these
components to achieve more precise outcomes.
   Speciﬁcally, for reasoning tasks, the context often includes exemplars—a collec-
tion of related solved question answers that serve as references for the LLMs. To
demonstrate various prompting methods, we have chosen a standard example from
the GSM8K dataset. Through this example, the crafting of the prompt is explained.

  Example: {Question-Solution} Pair:
  Question: A garden has rows of flowers, with each row having 7
  sunflowers and twice as many tulips. How many tulips are there in the
  third row?
  Step-by-Step Solution:
  In the third row, there are twice as many tulips as sun-flowers.
  Since each row has 7 sunflowers, the third row has 7 * 2 = 14 tulips.
  Therefore, there are 14 tulips in the third row.
  Therefore, the Answer is 3.



3.1  Standard Few-Shot


When addressing a problem, an example is provided to facilitate better understanding
and solution development. In the same way, LLMs are provided a collection of
examples as context, and then the question is asked [22].
   Prompt- Example {Question–Answer}. Task



3.2  Chain of Thought (CoT)


This method aims to lead the LLM through intermediate reasoning steps before
generating a response. Consequently, the exemplars provided are manually drafted.
Alongside the target question, a pertinent question–answer pair is supplied as an
illustrative instance. In the provided example pair, the answer presents a step-by-step
solution to the problem [22].
   Prompt- Example {Question-Solution} (step-by-step Solution). Task



3.3  Zero Shot


As the name suggests, no similar example is given as context in the prompt. The
question is asked directly with the line “Let’s think step by step” as a preﬁx. “Let’s
think step by step” gives the highest accuracy among different possible options [23].
   Prompt- Task. Let’s Think step by step.

--- Page 168 ---
A Brief Study of Prompting Techniques for Reasoning Tasks                           153

3.4  Zero Shot CoT


The technique employs the phrase “let’s think step by step” in conjunction with the
question. This technique suggests two LLM interactions. During the “reasoning ex-
traction” phase, the LLM is tasked with generating the reasoning steps. In the subse-
quent step, prompts are furnished for “answer generation”. It merges the concepts of
CoT and zero shot techniques to improve the effectiveness of the prompt [23].

   Reasoning Extraction

   Prompt- Task. Let’s Think step by step.

  Answer Generation

   Prompt- Task. Let’s Think step by step. {Solution}



3.5  Self-consistency


The concept involves sampling diverse reasoning paths through the few-shot CoT
approach, utilizing the generated results to determine the most coherent response.
This approach enhances the efﬁcacy of CoT prompts, particularly in tasks requiring
arithmetic calculations and commonsense reasoning. Various distinct reasoning paths
are presented to the LLM using a few-shot method. The most frequent output is
subsequently deemed as the deﬁnitive answer. The study asserts an enhancement
in the precision of CoT prompts for tasks involving arithmetic and common sense
reasoning [24].
   Prompt- Example {Question-Solution}. Task



3.6  Least to Most


To solve a complicated problem, it is a good idea to start by breaking it into smaller,
simpler problems. These sub-problems are then addressed sequentially to ultimately
arrive at the solution. This technique employs two prompts. The ﬁrst prompt is used
to decompose the problem and generate the corresponding sub-problems. The second
prompt is employed to solve each sub-problem [25].
   Prompt- Break down the given problem into a series of sub problems to be solved.
   Task

--- Page 169 ---
154                                                                                S. Gaur et al.

3.7  Active Prompt


This technique emphasizes that human-designed exemplars are not always optimal.
The method proposed by this technique involves selecting the most pertinent and
valuable exemplars from a set of task-speciﬁc questions, utilizing uncertainty metrics
as a basis for selection. The objective of employing uncertainty-based question selec-
tion is to minimize the extent of human engineering required for question annotation
[26].
   Prompt- Task



3.8  Program of Thought (PoT)


This technique focuses on obtaining programming language statements, speciﬁcally
in Python code, to perform a reasoning task. These statements are subsequently
executed using a programming language interpreter, such as a Python interpreter.
The primary objective of this technique is to prevent calculation errors that can occur
within LLMs. The outcome of the executed program is then utilized as input for
the LLM to generate the ﬁnal answer. This approach can be applied in zero shot as
well as few-shot scenarios. For few-shot learning, exemplars are given to guide the
process [27].
   Prompt- Answer this question by implementing a solver() function.
   def solver():
   Let’s write a python program step by step, and then return the answer
   Task



3.9  Progressive Hint Prompting (PHP)


The technique comprises two stages. A foundational question and base prompt are
presented to the LLM in the First Stage. The resulting answer and PHP approach
are employed in the Second Stage. In the earlier stage, the LLM receives the initial
question. The answer acquired at this stage serves as a clue for the Second Stage
[28].
   Prompt- Task
   (Hint: The answer is near to ‘value’).
   A: We know the Answer Hints: ‘value’. with the Answer Hints: ‘value’, we will
answer the question.}

--- Page 170 ---
A Brief Study of Prompting Techniques for Reasoning Tasks                           155

3.10  Plan and Solve (PS)


It comprises two aspects: ﬁrstly, formulating a plan to divide the complete task into
smaller, more manageable subtasks, and subsequently executing these subtasks by
the plan [29].
   Prompt-Let’s ﬁrst understand the problem, extract relevant variables and their
corresponding numerals, and make a plan.
   Then, Let’s carry out the plan, calculate intermediate variables (pay attention to
correct numerical calculation and commonsense), solve the problem step by step,
and show the answer.
   Task



3.11  Tree of Thought (ToT)


The LLM is directed to explore multiple reasoning paths through various lines of
thought. Each thought is systemically broken down into simpler steps. For a given
problem, there can be multiple sequences of thoughts. These thoughts are structured
in a tree format, where each node symbolizes a partial solution corresponding to
the development of the thought sequence. This thought tree is then traversed using
either a Depth-First Search (DFS) or Breadth-First Search (BFS) algorithm to reach
the ﬁnal answer. A basic implementation of this ToT approach involves four distinct
steps: thought decomposition, generation, evaluation, and independent variation of
search procedures. This method demonstrates a signiﬁcant level of success, achieving
a high accuracy of 74 percent in solving the “Game of 24” problem, in contrast to
other techniques with accuracies below 10 percent [30].



3.12  Self-veriﬁcation


The initial phase, termed forward reasoning, closely resembles the standard CoT,
differing only in the generation of multiple candidate answers via sampling decoding.
In the subsequent phase, veriﬁcation scores are computed for each candidate’s
response through the self-veriﬁcation method. Subsequently, the answer having the
highest score is designated as the ultimate solution [4].

5  Conclusion


This paper offers an overview of prompting techniques applied to reasoning bench-
marks with large language models.  It encompasses accuracy comparisons and
explores various open questions and limitations associated with the prompting
technique. Here some points are observed while studying these techniques:

•  Increasing the model size has led to notable improvements in task accuracy.
   Enlarging language models offers advantages like enhanced performance and
  more efﬁcient sampling [21, 31], among others. However, merely increasing
  model size has not been enough to excel in demanding tasks like arithmetic,
  commonsense, and symbolic reasoning [32].
• The same prompts generate different results on different models.
• While the chain of thought prompting technique mimics human reasoning thought
   processes, it does not clarify whether the neural network is genuinely engaged in
   “reasoning”. This aspect remains an unanswered question, deliberately left open
   for further exploration.
•  Self-consistency [24] technique demands additional computational resources, and
    it may also generate incorrect reasoning paths. To enhance its accuracy, further
   reﬁnement is required.
•  In the least to most prompting techniques [25], tailoring prompts to speciﬁc
  domains is important as different problem types demand unique prompts to
   achieve optimal performance. Moreover, challenges can also arise within the same
  domain due to the difﬁculty of generalizing decomposition, potentially leading to
   varied results.
•  In ToT [30], the search can be expensive for certain tasks compared to simpler
   methods, and there is a limited scope as this technique might not apply to all tasks.

Comparative Analysis of Negative
Customer Review of Payment Apps:
A Data Mining Approach



Ranjit Singh    , K. Kajol    , Bhartihari Pandiya    , Lokendra Puri    ,
Lata Kumari Pandey    , Suman Agarwal    , and Sahiba Khan



Abstract The digital payment market is growing at unprecedented rates in India.
This can be attributed to the introduction of the Uniﬁed Payment Interface (UPI). It
has completely disrupted the digital payment space by effectively increasing the user
base of digital payments multiple times in India. However, any market innovation’s
success or failure is heavily inﬂuenced by how consumers perceive it. Therefore,
the study aims to know the perception of UPI users by using the sentiment analysis
technique. The data on consumer behaviour was scraped from the latest Google Play
Store reviews using Python scripts. After the data pre-processing, Exploratory Data
Analysis and Word Cloud Analysis were done. Interesting ﬁndings from the analysis
were found concerning the top three payment apps: GPay, Paytm, and PhonePe. The
research also presents a few managerial implications which could be applied for
better customer experience. The goal of these payment apps should be to convert
negative customer reviews into positive ones.

Keywords Payment Apps · Mobile payments · Negative reviews · Python ·
Exploratory data analysis



1  Introduction


Mobile payment apps have transformed emerging markets by offering convenient,
cashless transactions and faster processing speeds [32, 64]. In India, payment apps
have become a widely adopted payment method. The National Payments Corpo-
ration of India, a consortium of Indian banks, established the Uniﬁed Payments
Interface (UPI) to facilitate the widespread adoption of digital micro-payments.

Numerous payment platforms, including GPay, PhonePe, Paytm, and BHIM, utilize
UPI and compete in the market. Bhalla [12] reported a nearly 50% increase in trans-
actions through various digital wallets, such as PhonePe, Paytm, and Amazon Pay,
in India. Kajol et al. [31], Luna et al. [39], and Park et al. [49] stated the various
factors inﬂuence digital wallet adoption worldwide. These factors include percep-
tions such as perceived risk, perceived ease of use, perceived security, and perceived
innovativeness.
   User perceptions of a given product can provide valuable insights into the effec-
tiveness of its offerings [14, 15]. Reviews, whether positive or negative, can help iden-
tify areas that require attention. A negative review may indicate that the company’s
offerings need improvement, while a positive review may indicate user satisfaction
[29, 51, 58]. Businesses must understand customer viewpoints to effectively position
their products [48].
   Therefore, the ﬁrst objective of this study is to examine the relevance and popu-
larity of payment apps in India and explore the critical factors inﬂuencing their adop-
tion. The second objective is to perform an analytical comparison between payment
apps customers’ attribution strategies through their public reviews of three payment
apps—GPay, Paytm, and PhonePe—on the Google Play Store. As per the Reserve
Bank of India (RBI), UPI is the top most preferred method adopted by the bank
customers to complete the digital transaction [43]. GPay, Paytm, and PhonePe are the
top three chartbuster UPI payment apps used by customers to complete transactions
[47].



2  Literature Review


There are ample research works which have focused on the adoption factors of mobile
banking [6, 27, 33, 52] but only a few have focused on the negative experience of
the customers for the apps [36, 59]. Talwar et al. [61] identiﬁed six factors that
may impact the willingness to make both positive and negative recommendations for
mobile payment systems. Among these, security concerns, poor user experience, and
lack of reliability were the most common reasons for negative reviews [3]. Various
studies have worked on the text analyses of the reviews of products and services
which could be in qualitative text or quantitative ratings [20, 22, 42, 62]. Aldabbas
et al. [8] analysed ‘Google Play Store’ reviews semantics and compared the different
parameters with different machine learning algorithms to ﬁnd the best algorithm.
Gao et al. [23] develop a framework for understanding app reviews and addressing
emerging issues. Vanissa [63] aims to measure the competitive ability of social media
among ‘Internet Service Providers’ in Indonesia after data collection using crawling
techniques from Twitter. Several studies talk about data scraping, pre-processing,
classiﬁcation, and visualization [10, 21]; however, no such study has been conducted
till date in the context of India. The Central Bank as well as the Government of nation
is also working to encourage the digital payment mode that offers the cashless and
paperless transactions to complete the payment [53]. UPI-based payment takes only

--- Page 177 ---
Comparative Analysis of Negative Customer Review of Payment Apps …                163

a couple of seconds to complete the transaction while other payment methods like
cheque, bank cards take a couple of hours to settle the transaction that also make a big
difference in the adoption of UPI over the other payment methods [25]. Reviewing
the product allows the customer to provide their valuable input after the usage of
the product [2, 4]. Reviews of the product allow the new customers to know more
information about the product by the users who have used the product or using it
[9, 16]. Reviews are also responsible for the customers’ perception for the product
on the basis of available reviews; therefore, there should be accountability for the
customer reviews on the product as well as service [1].



3  Methodology


The study examines customer reviews of digital payment apps, comparing Gpay,
PhonePe, and Paytm for effective customer behaviour modelling. There are three
stages of data analysis followed in the study. The stages have been explained below.



3.1  Data Pre-processing


Data pre-processing overcomes redundancy and ensures analysis performance by
removing unusable data from raw sources.



3.2  Exploratory Data Analysis


This involves exploring statistical aspects of data using graphical methods like bar
charts and histograms. Python, along with tools like Google Colab notebooks, simpli-
ﬁes complex tasks and allows remote access to high-performance machines for
efﬁcient code management.



3.3  Word Cloud Analysis


It examines text data by ranking words based on their frequency and performing
intuitive visualizations. Customization options are available, with frequent words
displayed in a mixed mosaic form.
  The proposed methodology includes the extraction of 100,000 data points of
review data for each of the 3 payment apps Gpay, Paytm, and PhonePe respectively.
There are 9 attributes in the data as shown in Fig. 1.

later reduction, the reduced size of each ﬁle is 9061 reviews for GPay, 29,791 reviews
for Paytm and 41,092 reviews for PhonePe. The scraped reviews contain a lot of not
useful reviews that are either too short or non-textual for actual use. Accordingly,
all these kinds of reviews have been removed. The reviews which got a reply from
the company were deleted as all of the non-replied reviews were not useful. Figure 2
shows the review of the non-replied review by the three companies for the speci-

4.1  Data Pre-processing


First the outliers from the numeric columns are found from all three datasets. These
points were plotted on the graph. For the numeric columns to reduce noise, these
outliers are removed and the remaining data is further used. The following columns
were removed [‘reviewCreatedVersion’, ‘replied’] as this will not be used in future
EDA parts. Also adding a column called [“upi company”] to be later useful in joining
the datasets. All three datasets [‘Google’, ‘Paytm’, ‘PhonePe’] are joined to a single
dataset called ‘Data’. Since the distribution of data is not equal for example total
rows in the Google dataset is 9061 and in PhonePe it is 29729 and in Paytm, it is
41301, so, we took only 9061 rows to form each dataset and the study also used the
‘sample ()’ function so that it could get 9061 random data for all three datasets. The
review created at column was in standard type which converted it to ‘Date Time’
format and then extracted year and month from the ‘Date Time’ column and then
arranged the data accordingly. The framework of data pre-processing is depicted in
Fig. 4.



4.2  Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)


In the study, EDA was ﬁrst applied to each of the three datasets separately. The
relationships between scores and management-provided recipes, then between scores
and the number of thumbs up, were followed. After the accomplishment of EDA
separately, we move towards performing EDA on all three datasets together. EDA
helps to ﬁnd out which company has the maximum number of reviews in all score
categories. Which company has the maximum votes in all score categories? Which
company has the most feedback over the past months? Fig. 5 shows the analysis of
feedback given by the customer on different payment apps.

4.3  Word Cloud Analysis (WCA)


To create a meaningful word cloud from user reviews and replies, stop words were
removed to prevent unnecessary and unnaturally frequent words from appearing
in front. To do that Spacy’s word cloud stop word library is used (just for prac-
tical reasons). Also, we need words having a length of more than 3 which removes
unwanted small words like: ‘app, and, for’, etc. Using the remaining words, a word
cloud was created with appropriate accuracy showing words that represent the dataset.

6  Conclusion


Overall, Paytm now offers the best UPI payment services because it has the most
ratings, but PhonePe isn’t far behind with a bit more work. However, Google must put
up more effort to compete with these businesses given that it has the lowest rating
when compared to the other two. The mean of the combined number of negative
reviews on all 3 apps is around 2889 in the past 4 months. It also shows a variance of
nearly 367 reviews. According to the data, user complaints are remarkably constant
over a long period, exposing weaknesses in standard customer redressal through
review replies on the Google Play Store.
  Word Count Analysis results show customer satisfaction with Paytm is the worst.
While Google Pay seems ignorant due to the use of bots that translate towards the
redressal of problems. However, PhonePe still performs at a barely acceptable level.
The mean ratings of GPay, Paytm and PhonePe are 3.8, 4.0, and 4.3 respectively
from the extracted dataset. The study suggests PhonePe to be far ahead but these are
context-free ratings with objective quantiﬁcation and no real subjective signiﬁcance
in the case of customer issue redressal. From the above graphs, the problems relating
to ‘money’ are almost the same in all three apps. The word frequency of money
in the GPay dataset is 1827 (highest) and in the PhonePe dataset is 1452 (lowest).
Similarly, for account-related problems, where account word frequency is 1741 in
the GPay dataset (highest) and 1003 in the PhonePe dataset (lowest). Overall above
results suggest that each payment app customers face similar problems, but have
different redressal mechanisms.

A Transformer-Based Approach for Fruit
Spoilage Identiﬁcation


Mayuri Sharma    , Hemanta Chutia    , and Chandan Jyoti Kumar





Abstract One of the most signiﬁcant problems in the fruit industry is fruit spoilage,
which creates categories of losses across all fruit types. The main objective of the
current study is to develop a transformer-based system for identifying spoilage of fruit
and reducing waste. It employs vision transformer (ViT) to identify fresh and spoiled
fruit categories among eight types of fruit. The experimental ﬁndings indicate that
transformer-based fruit spoilage identiﬁcation system can attain a high performance
without the need for destructive analysis. With a high accuracy (99.89%) attained in
distinguishing fresh fruit from spoiled fruit, the proposed system may be useful for
improving real-time fruit quality and spoilage assessments, thereby improving food
management efﬁciency.

Keywords  Fruit · Spoilage · Transformer · Machine learning · Deep learning



1  Introduction


Fruits are a vital part of a balanced diet because they are rich in nutrients that are essen-
tial for human health, such as phytochemicals, vitamins, minerals, dietary ﬁber, and
antioxidants [1]. The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) advises consuming
at least 400 g of fruits and vegetables per day [2]. The demand for fruits and vegeta-
bles is increasing daily due to the growing population, and there is an emphasis on
reducing waste and assuring safety. Because of the country’s varied environment,

India offers a wide variety of fresh fruits and vegetables and is the world’s second-
largest producer of fruits and vegetables, after China [3]. According to the FAO
[2], India is the largest producer of bananas (26.45%), mangoes (including mangos-
teens and guavas) (43.80%), and papayas (39.30%). Fruit and vegetable losses are
the highest category of losses among all food types, and FAO found that fruit and
vegetable spoilage is a hidden contributor to losses of food and economy and under-
development, with up to 60% of all fruits and vegetables ending up in landﬁlls [4].
Despite its consequences for socioeconomic conditions, food quality, food security,
and spoilage of fruits and vegetables have received signiﬁcantly less study atten-
tion than produce-related foodborne disease and processing technologies [1]. Fruits
can be contaminated by spoilage microorganisms from the environment, handling
and processing after harvest, and a variety of agronomic and environmental factors
that have been linked to fruit microbial deterioration [1]. Several physical thermal
(hot water blanching, steam, hot sanitizing solution, sun drying etc.), physical non-
thermal technologies (pulse electric ﬁeld, ultrasound, high pressure, irradiation, pulse
light, cold plasma etc.), chemical (hypochlorite, chlorine dioxide, sulﬁte, ozone etc.),
cold treatments, and other treatments (use of antimicrobials, organic acid, essential
oil etc.) have been used as preservation techniques and treatment strategies for the
decontamination of fresh produce [1], but it is associated with high processing cost
and also spoilages are not recoverable. Again, the deterioration of a single fruit
directly affects the fruits nearby, so the removal of spoilage/rotten fruits from the
entire lot can be facilitated by early detection of the rotting and suitable action taken
for the purpose of aiding in keeping the fruits nearby from becoming spoiled. So,
proper (early) detection and monitoring of fruits are very important steps in fruit
spoilage prevention [4–7].
  Deep learning-based technological advancements help in automatically identi-
fying spoiled fruits and overcoming the above-mentioned drawbacks. The food
supply chain management can enhance fruit quality and shelf life by utilizing the
Internet of Things (IoT) to measure and monitor fruit conditions and exchange data
with customers. The IoT connects everything, everywhere, and at any time [8], and
also IoT indicators can be used to estimate how long a fruit can be stored. In recent
years, the discipline of deep learning has grown exponentially due to advancements
in theory and design. Another area of deep learning that has made great progress
recently is visual object detection from digital photographs. Visual object detection
has been able to precisely locate and identify a number of targets thus far. The moti-
vation behind the fruit product monitoring and analysis with machine learning is
to prevent fruit spoiling without the destructive analysis. Machine learning for fruit
deterioration monitoring and analysis saves time, yields reliable, consistent ﬁndings,
and maintains the socioeconomic condition and quality of fruits. Megalingam et al.
[9] introduced a novel approach to food degradation detection that combines artiﬁ-
cial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and photocategorization. In order to
identify food that was decaying, they used AI, deep convolutional neural network
networks (CNNs), computer vision, and ML techniques like the k clusters approach
for color classiﬁcations in photographs and its HSV values for spoiling detection. For
the recommended use, the study shows an extremely high accuracy rate. According

--- Page 196 ---
A Transformer-Based Approach for Fruit Spoilage Identiﬁcation                        183

to that perspective, AI is beneﬁcial in practically every industry today [9]. CNN
model was used to detect the type of fruit and vegetables by Sonwani et al. [8]. The
proposed system monitors the temperature, humidity, and gas emission levels of fruits
and vegetables in addition to measuring the degree of food degradation using sensors
and actuators. Furthermore, that would control the air and stop food from spoiling
whenever possible. Based on how fresh and undamaged the food was, a message
was also sent to the customer’s registered cell phone number informing them of the
extent of food spoilage. It was discovered that the model in use had a 95% accuracy
rate. Ultimately, the experiment was successful in adding two days to the shelf life
of some food categories [8]. At ﬁnal they suggested that the proposed smart device
could be improved by applying image processing and machine learning algorithms
to detect early spoilage. Compared with region proposal network of faster R-CNN
(region-based CNN), transformer is completely based on self-attention mechanism
[10]. The complexity of a transformer model ensures that the accuracy of the model
was found to be higher than that of R-CNN, observed by Xiao et al. [11]. Xiao et al.
[11] studied the accurate ripeness classiﬁcation of various types of fruits (apples
and pears as the representatives of fruits) by using vision transformer, Swin Trans-
former, and multilayer perceptron. They have found that at an average precision of
87.43%, the Swin Transformer model was achieved and can determine whether the
present fruit is in the “Ripe” or “Overripe” class by having their model precisely.
Additionally, the model manages to recognize objects quickly and accurately in 0.13
s [11]. A machine vision transformer system based on deep learning was suggested
to grade the fruits (apple, banana, guava, orange, lime, and pomegranate) according
to their external look. The main engineering component of that study was the design
of an image classiﬁcation problem as a sequential problem using image patches as
tokens and processing it by a transformer. In comparison with CNN models like
InceptionNet and EfﬁcientNet, the vision transformer model produced the highest
accuracy.
   Furthermore, while comparing the quality evaluation ﬁndings obtained from the
prior implementation of CNN-based models, it was discovered that the deployment
of the vision transformer-based technique was more accurate. Therefore, in order
to meet the demands of real-world applications, the proposed technique increases
the rate of fruit identiﬁcation and freshness detection [12]. However, there is still
a limited amount of research conducted on using vision transform systems for the
detection of spoilage in fruits. This study seeks to contribute by implementing a
transformer-based approach to effectively identify fruit spoilage in eight different
fruit varieties.

184                                                      M. Sharma et al.

2  Literature Survey


Spoilage in fruit has signiﬁcant impacts on the environment, the economy, and human
health. In recent years, fruit spoilage detection has become one of the most important
applications of ML techniques. This section provides an overview of the recent
developments in this ﬁeld.
  An efﬁcient method of detecting spoilage early on is by using machine vision
systems with cameras and image processing. The devices capture images of fruits
and use image processing methods to identify any that do not appear to be in good
condition [13]. It was found that using neural network classiﬁers to grade banana fruit
is highly successful [14]. The maturity of bananas was also determined by neural
networks utilizing RGB color components that were collected every day until the
bananas completely rotted [15]. Visual signals such as texture and color have been
used by researchers to identify spoilage. ML approaches and color-based features
were utilized to analyze color discrepancies in fruit images to identify rotten apples
[16]. SVM was used to classify different ﬂaws in monochromatic apple images [17].
  The use of deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) is one of the most funda-
mental methods for detecting fruit deterioration. In order to train these models,
datasets containing images of fruits at various stages of maturity and freshness are
used. To identify food degradation, a novel method combining computer vision, deep
CNNs, and artiﬁcial intelligence was presented which identiﬁed rotting fruits with
a high degree of accuracy [9]. Researchers have made signiﬁcant progress in distin-
guishing between fresh and rotten fruits [18]. It has been found that the CNN and
thermal imaging method is a viable data collection tool for identifying fruit ﬂaws
[19].
  CNN has been also integrating IoT devices and sensors to monitor several environ-
mental characteristics, including temperature, humidity, and gas emissions. These
methods were used by alert-based systems to provide early deteriorating signs in
fruits [8]. The real-time monitoring and tracking of fruit items in the supply chain was
investigated using blockchain technology and the Internet of Things [9]. Transformer-
based models, such as the Swin Transformer, have been utilized recently to accurately
classify the ripeness of fruits [11].
  A variety of deep learning techniques, including convolutional neural networks
(CNNs), as well as image analysis and sensor-based techniques, have been devel-
oped to provide a solution to the problem of fruit spoilage identiﬁcation. Despite
the increasing popularity of transformer models in natural language processing and
computer vision, they were not speciﬁcally examined in the context of fruit spoilage
detection. This suggests that future research may investigate the use of transformer
models for this purpose. A transformer-based approach could enhance the precision
and resilience of fruit spoilage detection systems.

3  Materials and Methods


The present study proposes a vision-based transformer approach for classifying
spoilage in eight types of fruits. Figure 1 shows the basic workﬂow of the proposed
work. The following sub-sections explain the experimental setup and methodology
in detail.



3.1  Dataset Preparation


The FruQ-DB dataset [6] is used in this study. There are images of various fruits,
including apple, banana, grape, guava, jujube, orange, pomegranate, and strawberry,
categorized into two categories: fresh and rotten. The fresh class contains a total
of 6,206 images. The rotten (spoiled) class consists of 6,141 images. All images
in the dataset share a common resolution of 1020 × 1040 pixels. Figure 2 shows
the distribution of the dataset used in the present work. The dataset had uneven
number of images for most of the classes. Hence, augmentation [20] was performed
to upsample the classes to have 800 images each, resulting in 12,800 images. Then
the augmented dataset of 12,800 number of images was splitted in the ratio 70:15:15
into train, validation, and test dataset.

3.2  Proposed Transformer-Based Spoilage Diagnosis System


In our experiment, we employed ﬁne-tuning for a vision transformer (ViT) [12]
model using PyTorch to classify the fresh/spoilage of eight different fruits. Initially,
we created an instance of the ViT model, utilizing pre-trained weights. Subsequently,
the model was transferred to a target GPU device. The base parameters were frozen
during training in order to prevent changes to them. In the ViT model, the classiﬁer
head was replaced with a linear layer, whose output size matched the number of
classes. For training, we set up an optimizer (Adam) and employed the cross-entropy
loss function to classify a total of 16 classes. Training was conducted for 10 and 20
epochs. Table 1 offers a summary of the ViT model, including details on the model’s
size. Different layers used in the proposed system are shown in Table 2.
   There were 12,304 trainable parameters and 85,798,656 non-trainable parameters.
It is worth noting that the model expects input images of size 224 × 224, which
necessitates resizing the images accordingly. The loss and accuracy values were
tracked while training the model. The performance of the vision transformer (ViT)
model was evaluated in terms of metrics like accuracy [20, 21], precision [21, 22],
recall [22, 23], and F1-score [24].

4  Results and Discussions


In this study, a vision transformer (ViT) model was applied to the task of classifying
fresh and rotten fruits. The model was trained separately for 10 and 20 epochs, and
the results obtained from both training phases provided valuable insights into its
performance.



4.1  Results of ViT for 10 Epochs


Figure 3 provides the training and validation curves for ViT model during the model
training for ten epochs. During the ﬁrst epoch, the training loss was relatively high
and the model showed the sign of overﬁtting on unseen validation data. In the second
epoch, training loss decreased signiﬁcantly to 0.2921 and the model had started to
generalize better. In the subsequent epochs, training/validation loss and accuracy
continued to improve. This suggested that the model achieved good generalization.





Fig. 3  Training and validation curves of ViT model with 10 epochs over a dataset containing fresh
and rotten classes of 8 fruits

Fig. 4  Confusion matrix of the transformer model (trained for 10 epochs) over a dataset containing
fresh and rotten classes of 8 fruits


   In the classiﬁcation process of fresh and rotten fruits using the vision transformer
(ViT) model, an accuracy of 99.17% was achieved. However, there were very few
misclassiﬁcations in some cases of rotten fruits. Figure 4 shows the confusion matrix
highlighting the model’s performance. Two samples of rotten apple were wrongly
classiﬁed as fresh or rotten pomegranate. One specimen of a rotten orange was
inaccurately categorized as a fresh orange. A single rotten pomegranate sample was
wrongly assigned as a fresh pomegranate. Six rotten grapes were misclassiﬁed as
fresh grapes. Two samples of rotten jujube fruits were erroneously labeled as rotten
pomegranates.



4.2  Results of ViT for 20 Epochs


Figure 5 shows the training and validation curves of ViT model with 20 epochs on
the dataset containing fresh and rotten classes of 8 fruits. In the ﬁrst three epochs, the
training accuracy increased from 0.9188 to 0.9940 and the training loss decreased

dramatically from 0.3728 to 0.0490. The training accuracy and loss improved over
the subsequent epochs, eventually approaching near-perfect training accuracy (nearly
1.000). Over the course of the training procedure, improvements were also observed
in validation accuracy and validation loss. A decrease in validation loss was recorded
from 0.1279 to 0.0062, while an increase in validation accuracy was recorded from

generalizes well to new data.
    It was observed that the classiﬁcation process with 20 epochs had a relatively
low rate of misclassiﬁcation with 99.89% accuracy. It is noteworthy that only one
fresh grape was mistakenly classiﬁed as rotten, and similarly, only one rotten grape
was erroneously classiﬁed as fresh. The results indicate that the model is effective
in distinguishing between fresh and rotten fruits, highlighting its efﬁciency in this
particular area of fruit classiﬁcation. Figure 6 shows the confusion matrix of the ViT
model after 20 epochs.



4.3  Comparison with Reported Work


The present work has shown that the ViT model is highly capable of predicting fruit
spoilage. The classiﬁcation process for fresh and rotten fruits using 10-epoch ViT
model resulted in an impressive accuracy of 99.17%.
  The longer training duration of the 20-epoch phase resulted in even greater gener-
alization and a lower rate of misclassiﬁcation. However, it is important to note that
there were a few misclassiﬁcations, particularly in the case of some rotten fruits.
Considering that ViT only accepts input sizes of 224 × 224 pixels, it may have
missed a few features. It was found that the ViT model was highly proﬁcient, with

5  Conclusion


The current study explored the potentiality of the ViT model in identifying fruit
spoilage. The proposed work showed remarkable accuracy when identifying fresh
and spoiled fruits, with a peak accuracy of 99.89%, thus outperforming some promi-
nent DL models. This work can be used in real-world scenarios to improve the
assessment of fruit quality and to drastically decrease food waste. Further investiga-
tion and reﬁnement endeavors could augment the efﬁcacy of the model and expand
its relevance to supplementary tasks associated with evaluating fruit quality.

A Study on Performance of Mathematics,

Among Female Students from Technical

Mousoomi Bora and Rupam Baruah



Abstract The Mathematics, Programming, and Practical courses are herculean task
for most of the students pursuing their study in the ﬁeld of engineering and tech-
nology. This study has explored the performance of female students in these three
categories pursuing Bachelor in Technology (B.Tech) in Computer Science and Engi-
neering (CSE). A deep learning (DL)-based prediction model is proposed to evaluate
the academic performance of students at the end of their B.Tech days measured by
cumulative grade point average (CGPA). The model is based on two deep learning
methods—convolutional neural network (CNN) and bidirectional long short-term
memory (Bi-LSTM). The overall predicted results are interpreted using an inter-
pretable supervised clustering framework. A comparative study is performed using
two baseline models—long short-term memory (LSTM) and gated recurrent unit
(GRU) to check the acceptability of the proposed model. The empirical results
conﬁrm that the losses encountered in the proposed model in terms of mean square
error (MSE) and mean absolute error (MAE) are less than the other two base-line
models that improve the overall performance. The results mirrored from the proposed
model has established the fact that the trend of female student’s performance in Math-
ematics, Programming and Practical courses is comparatively lower compared to the
male students.
