1  Introduction


The technocrats of a country play a vital role in its economic growth and develop-
ment. The success stories of economic development of a nation highlight the hard
work and dedication of the skilled workers. The technocrats have been the problem
solvers irrespective of their gender. To meet the requirement of energetic and knowl-
edgeable technical manpower in our society, there is always a demand for value added
technical programs in the educational institutions. It is reported that the proportion of
female technical persons and computer professionals varies with respect to different
engineering disciplines. Compared to 35% of environmental engineers, only 9% of
mechanical engineers are in the female category. On the other hand, in the computer
industry, 32% of computer and information scientists and 18% of software devel-
opers are women [1]. Looking at the statistics, there is always good scope for female
engineers in any interdisciplinary area in addition to the IT industry. The academic
performance of female students in the ﬁeld of technical courses is an important delib-
eration in terms of sustainability of retention and recruitment processes. To increase
the employability rate of the female engineering and other technical students, effort
must be given to increase the success rate in Mathematics, Programming, and Prac-
tical courses among such students. It would make them capable enough to clear the
interview rounds and also to improve their sustainability in their workplaces. Most of
the interview questions for CSE/ Information Technology (IT) graduates are based
on basic concepts on Programming and Practical courses. Our study is primarily
focused on analyzing the ﬁnal CGPA of the female engineering students and their
performance exclusively in Mathematics, Programming, and Practical courses. Most
of the time, students encounter challenges to acquire in-depth knowledge in these
subjects. The performance in Mathematics is explored in this study as it is found
difﬁcult by many students pursuing in any of the branches of engineering and tech-
nology. In recent years, deep learning (DL) has made remarkable changes in various
domains of research. An interpretable DL-based model is developed in this research
work to predict the academic performance of the female students in engineering.
The model is based on two DL methods—convolutional neural network (CNN) and
bidirectional long short-term memory (Bi-LSTM). The inclusive outcome of the
predicted model is interpreted using an interpretable framework based on supervised
SHAP clustering. A comparative study is performed using two baseline models—
long short-term memory (LSTM) and gated recurrent unit (GRU). The model is eval-
uated using mean square error (MSE) and mean absolute error (MAE) and compared
with two base line models—long short-term memory (LSTM) and gated recurrent
unit (GRU). The proposed model helps to analyze the knowledge and interest of the
female students pursuing their technical education in Mathematics, Programming,
and Practical courses. The model would provide insights that may be helpful for
persons imparting technical education. At the same time, the female engineering
students can gain valuable input for improving their performance in such subjects
and can make themselves more employable. Finally, the proposed model would bring
potential beneﬁt for technical education at large by improving the employment rate

of the female technocrats and they can go along with the male engineers with equal
importance in the society.



2  Related Works


While designing the proposed model, literature is reviewed to know the latest work in
performance of female students and also in educational data mining (EDM). Mansour,
H., Rees, D. I., Rintala, B. M. and Wozny, N. N. explored how the female students are
inﬂuenced by the female professors teaching Mathematics and Science in choosing
their career trajectory. The results conﬁrmed that there is a high prospect among
brilliant female students to either work or pursue their higher study in Science,
Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) [2]. Marshman et al. exam-
ined whether both male and female physics students have consistent self-conﬁdence
irrespective of different instructors and courses. Their ﬁndings claimed that lower
self-conﬁdence in female students compared to male students with similar results
can result in negative impacts on their short-term and long-term goals [3]. K. Krish-
nakumar and S. Dutt performed a study to determine the correlation between gender
and academic achievement as measured by Grade Point Average (GPA) at the end of
1st Year Engineering Degree Examination. As per their study, no signiﬁcant differ-
ence can be observed between male and female students, except their physical vari-
ances. Thus, both the genders possess equivalent levels of intelligence [4]. Y. T.
Badal and R. K. Sungkur have used Random Forest (RF) to predict student’s perfor-
mance by experiencing the learning level of a learner. [5]. S. Aydoğdu designed a
model with artiﬁcial neural network (ANN) that analyzes student’s behavior inside
the classroom and predicts their performance with the help of browsing history [6]. P.
Guleria and M. Sood developed an explainable machine-learning (EML) framework
to analyze educational features that assists students in their career development and
placement after graduation. [7]. C-M. Ricardo, O. Tiago, C. Mauro and J. Frederico
studied a Portuguese student dataset to carry out a comparative study of predic-
tive power between a multilinear regression model with a few base line models
such as ANN, support vector machine (SVM), RF, and extreme gradient boosting
(EGB) [8]. V. Realinho, J. Machado, L. Baptista and M.V. Martins analyzed a dataset
containing student’s demographic, socioeconomic, macroeconomic, pre-enrolment,
and academic records at the end of the ﬁrst and second semesters to estimate the
risk of dropout and failure [9]. M. Elmasry proposed a model using deep neural
network (DNN) and Decision Tree (DT) to predict students’ cumulative marks [10].
Fernandez et al. developed a recommended system to lower the dropout rate [11]. B.
Sekeroglu, K. Dimililer and K., K. Tuncal developed a DL-based model using long
short-term memory (LSTM), backpropagation (BP), and support vector regression
(SVR) for student performances prediction [12]. O. Saidani, L. J. Menzli, A. Ksibi,
N. Alturki, and A. S Alluhaidan developed a model that shows a strong correlation
between internship and employability of students [13]. T. T. Dien, S. H. Luu, I. N.
Thanh-Hai, and A. N. Thai-Nghe proposed a LSTM-CNN model to predict student

--- Page 210 ---
198                                                  M. Bora and R. Baruah

performance in next semesters based on their results from the previous semesters
[14]. S. Poudyal, M. Mohammadi-Aragh, and J. Ball built a hybrid 2D CNN model
for performance prediction [15]. S. Jung, J. Moon, S. Park, S., and E. Hwang proposed
a predictive model based on attention-based GRU [16]. Aljaloud et al. developed a
CNN-LSTM model to estimate the learning outcomes of students based on interac-
tive sessions with students using black board [17]. M. Cilínio, M. Pereira, D. Duarte,
L. Mata, and P. Vieira developed a boosting-based model for fault detection, and
TreeSHAP clustering is integrated with the based model for diagnosis part [18].



3  Proposed Works


The present study proposes a DL-based model to predict the performance of female
engineering students in Mathematics, Programming, and Practical courses. The
model is built on two popular DL approaches—CNN and Bi-LSTM and deployed
on a student dataset of a university. The independent and dependent variables of the
dataset are shown in Table 1. The dataset contains examination records of female
engineering students from a reputed university from India. As the problem statement
is formulated for evaluating the performance of female students in three types of
courses, the dataset has been prepared containing the student’s end semester exami-
nation marks in three categories of courses—Mathematics, Programming, and Prac-
tical. In Table 1, the CGPA is considered as the target variable and the grades in
various courses are used as independent variables of the prediction model. Although
the CGPA is calculated at the end of 8th semester based on partial percentage taken
after each semester, in the proposed work, an attempt has been made to predict the
ﬁnal CGPA with respect to only three categories of subjects. An exploratory trend
analysis is conducted on the performance of female students in above mentioned
courses to verify whether the different subjects exhibit a deﬁnite trend or pattern for
both male and female students.

  A derived column named “CGPA _GRADE” is used in this study. This additional
CGPA_GRADE column is derived based on the student’s overall percentage in their
4-year BTech curriculum as shown in Table 2. The grade division, as shown in
Table 2, helps us to analyze the students more profoundly. The data collected from
each student over a time period of 4 academic years is used to prepare the input
sequences for Bi-LSTM. The record of each student acts as one of the sequences.
Based on sequential data, the solution is developed by designing a predictive model.
  The proposed model learns about the student’s performance in the three courses
in the span of eight consecutive semesters. The serial number of each student is
considered as the index column and other courses are used as independent variables
that help in the model prediction. It was quite challenging to prepare the dataset as
Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN) like LSTM or Bi-LSTM accept only ﬁxed length
data input. However, the dataset used in this study is a multivariate sequential dataset
as number of courses vary in each semester and hence their marks and credit-hours
also vary. The issue was resolved by using two additional layers of padding and
masking in the DL model. Padding helps to align all the variable length sequences
and convert to sequences having ﬁxed length. The padded values are masked with the
help of a masking layer with any numerical values like “0” or “-1”. The masked input
is ignored by the DL model during its processing time. The functionality of the CNN
helps the model in automatic feature selection, whereas bidirectional long short-
term memory (Bi-LSTM) processes the input sequences using its Gate mechanism
with three types of gates—forget, input, and output gate. The role of LSTM is to
capture both temporal and long-term dependency from the input. The reason behind
using Bi-LSTM in the proposed model is that it leverages the power of processing
data in both directions. In Bi-LSTM, the information is processed in both forward
and backward directions. The past information is processed and manipulated by
the backward LSTM and future information is tracked with the forward LSTM.
As a result, the model can better understand the relationship between the student’s
past information containing examination grades in different subjects from different
semesters and CGPA as the future academic performance. The model is compiled
with three hyper parameters viz. loss function, optimizer, and performance metrics.

--- Page 212 ---
200                                                  M. Bora and R. Baruah





Fig. 1 Model used for performance prediction in mathematics, programming, and practical courses


“Mean Squared Error (MSE)” and “Mean Absolute Error (MAE)” are used as loss
functions for the regression problem that enables the model to learn from the errors
between actual output and predicted output. The proposed model is shown in Fig. 1.
  A popular stochastic gradient algorithm called “Adam” optimizer is used to auto-
matically adjust the weights according to the error encountered in the output layer of
neural networks [19]. Once the model is compiled, it is trained with the training data
provided that the optimum number of hidden layers and nodes in each hidden layer
are used for better performance. If validation error does not improve over the epochs,
“Early stopping” is used to stop the model training after a certain number of epochs.
Eventually, the inﬂuence of these subjects in ﬁnal CGPA can be evaluated using an
interpretable framework. The DL-based models are considered as black box models
for their lack of interpretability in terms of determining the most contributing input
in the model prediction. To enhance the model’s interpretability, a framework of
explainability is integrated with the proposed model that works on supervised SHAP
(SHapley additive explanations)-based clustering. SHAP helps to comprehend the
most inﬂuential features from the input dataset used in the prediction of the model’s
outcome. In this framework, the supervised task is accomplished by an ensemble
classiﬁer. The classiﬁer object is used by SHAP to generate SHAP values for each
data point exhibiting different values of input features present in the dataset. These
SHAP values are clustered using traditional clustering techniques and as a ﬁnal step,
the supervised SHAP clusters are reevaluated for further investigation.

The proposed model is implemented on a multivariate sequential dataset where both
the gender’s data are available in the form of their examination performance in
Mathematics, Programming, and Practical oriented courses. While such categories
of subjects act as independent variables, the role of target variable is played by their
ﬁnal CGPA. For easier analysis, the results of the proposed work are categorized as
given below

E.  Interpretation of the Most Contributing Course in Model’s Prediction with a
   Framework of Interpretability

After analyzing the Mathematics, Programming, and Practical courses for the girls’
students pursuing B.Tech in CSE, an attempt is made to interpret the DL-based model
with a framework of interpretability that is based on supervised SHAP clustering.
Fig. 9 shows the mean SHAP plot that determines the most important feature of the
model.
  As shown in Fig. 9, the most important subject among these three categories is
‘Compile design lab’ which is followed by PPS theory, Java theory, Data structure
theory, DBMS theory and so on. Figure 10 shows the results of supervised SHAP
clustering. In this study, the SHAP values corresponding to each data point are
segmented into three clusters. The SHAP summary plots are applied to interpret the
contribution of speciﬁc features that force the data points to be assigned in one of
the three clusters viz. Cluster 0, Cluster1, or Cluster 2. The positive SHAP values
indicate that the corresponding features are positively correlated with the predicted
CGPA and negative SHAP values indicate that the features are negatively correlated
with the predicted CGPA. The color of the data points signiﬁes the value of the feature
from high to low. By looking at the topmost features, the properties of the clusters
can be identiﬁed that have a positive impact on predicted outcome. For example, the
SHAP summary plot drawn for the Cluster 0 as shown in Fig. 10 indicates that the
female engineering students assigned to the Cluster 0 have good understanding in
Mathematics-II, followed by Mathematics-III, OOPS, Data structure, OOPS Lab,
DBMS, etc. All these high ranked features have the biggest positive impact on
deﬁning the cluster. However, they have not performed well in workshop practical.
Thus, the Workshop practical has a negative impact on the predicted CGPA. From

--- Page 219 ---

Fig. 10 SHAP summary plot for the data points from Cluster 0


this interpretation, it can be inferred that Mathematics-II, Mathematics-III, OOPS,
Data structure, OOPS Lab, DBMS—these are the most predominant features of the
model that belong to Cluster 0. Similarly, the other clusters can be also interpreted
using SHAP summary plot that may have some other set of features having positive
or negative correlation with the target variable that is CGPA.



5  Conclusion and Future Work


Student’s performance assessment at the time of graduation is a continuous evalu-
ation process. It needs constant tracking of the student’s academic performance in
every semester of a four-year degree program in the ﬁeld of engineering and tech-
nology. A DL-based model is developed as a part of our research that is intended to
predict the performance of female students measured by their ﬁnal CGPA. Consid-
ering the difference between the actual input and the predicted output, the model’s
performance is measured by calculating two types of losses—MSE and MAE. Both
the metrics conﬁrm that the performance of female students is lower in Mathematics
and Programming areas leading to lower CGPA compared to the boys. However,
they have better understanding in the Practical areas than the male students. An

--- Page 220 ---
208                                                  M. Bora and R. Baruah

interpretability framework is integrated with the model based on supervised SHAP
clustering. The framework infers that the compiler design laboratory is the most
contributing factor in the model’s prediction which is followed by PPS, Java, Data
structure, DBMS, etc. The model warns the students well in advance so that they
can work on their low-performing areas and improve their ﬁnal CGPA at the time of
graduation. The proposed model would be an inclusive roadmap for female students
pursuing their technical education. It would make the female students capable enough
to be employable and improve their sustainability in the work places. Currently the
model is implemented on only one dataset with the examination marks of both male
and female students. The same model can be used for other ﬁelds of education as
well with a new target audience. As a future scope, more emphasis would be given to
improve the performance of the proposed model. A metaheuristic algorithm would
be integrated with the model along with other hyper parameters like optimizer and
activation functions. The proposed model in this study would not only contribute to
the country’s economy by producing more female technocrats but also it would have
scope for generating more jobs as now a days Computer scientists or IT professionals
are very much demanded in most of the interdisciplinary areas.

Efﬁcient Handwritten English Word
Detection with Neural Networks


Subhrojit Saikia, Monita Wahengbam, and Jyotirmoy Deka





Abstract  In today’s digital era, the imperative to digitize documents is undeniable.
As the world transitions toward an increasingly paperless environment, the need
for accurate and efﬁcient methods of converting handwritten content into digital
format becomes crucial. This research addresses this demand through the develop-
ment of an Intelligent Word Recognition (IWR) model. Employing advanced deep
neural network architectures, including convolutional neural networks (CNN) and
long short-term memory (LSTM), the model is meticulously trained on a dataset
sourced from Kaggle. The outcome of convolutional bidirectional long short-term
memory connectionist (CBLC) IWR model endeavor is a highly effective system
that achieves a remarkable 96.71% word accuracy, showcasing its proﬁciency in
the accurate extraction of handwritten English words. This research contributes to
the ongoing efforts in enhancing document digitization processes, offering a potent
solution for handwritten word detection.

Keywords  Intelligent word recognition (IWR) · Convolutional neural networks
(CNN) · Long short-term memory (LSTM) · Connectionist temporal classiﬁcation
(CTC) · Neural networks · Deep learning · Convolutional bidirectional long
short-term memory connectionist (CBLC)



1  Introduction


Intelligent Word Recognition (IWR) is unconstrained handwritten word recognition.
IWR recognizes whole handwritten words and phrases, not character-by-character.
It is an advanced form of optical character recognition (OCR). IWR technology
matches handwritten or printed words beside user-deﬁned dictionaries. IWR elimi-
nates manual data entry of handwritten documents and creates an automated system.
IWR allows computers to recognize and convert printed or handwritten text into

machine-readable text. This technology has a wide range of applications, from digi-
tizing printing documents to assisting with data entry and enabling text-based search
in scanned documents. In cursive handwriting, letters are the various curves, shapes
and lines and IWR considers these various shapes and groupings as words and calcu-
lates a conﬁdence value associated with the word in question. Each word is analyzed
and the system breaks down the words into a sequence of graphemes, or subparts of
letters.
  IWR reduces the number of character errors associated with Intelligent char-
acter recognition (ICR) and OCR engines and it is ideal for processing real-world
documents that contain mostly unclear free-form data that is inherently unsuitable.
   In the past few years, deep convolutional neural network (CNN) techniques have
successfully performed their role in many ﬁelds, like, image recognition, object
detection, facial recognition, medical image analysis, self-driving cars, and more.
Many of the experimented problems are re-experimented using convolution neural
networks to acquire signiﬁcant results. The proposed model addresses the previously
deﬁned issues by developing an intelligent and efﬁcient handwritten scripts recog-
nition system. The development of such kinds of systems always demands extensive
image processing and pattern recognition techniques to be part of these systems. This
study reports the convolution neural network technique for ﬁltering images or hand-
written scripts. The convolution neural network consists of many layers, and these
layers comprise many neurons. An extensive dataset of 1,00,000 handwritten words
images is ﬁrst prepared to train, validate and test the proposed approach. Then, the
image is properly trained on the deﬁned dataset, then validated. A separate testing
phase applies to these images to check the accuracy of recognition. These images
are given to the recognition system, which requires proper segmentation of written
words. The proposed convolutional bidirectional long short-term memory connec-
tionist (CBLC) IWR model approach develops word-based segmentation algorithm
then convolution ﬁltering technique; hence, features are extracted. After extraction in
order to compress the features map max-pooling layers are used. Bi-directional long
short term memory (Bi-LSTM) for reading the pooled images from both sides, and
connectionist temporal classiﬁcation (CTC) for mapping and calculating the losses
of handwritten words. This proposed technique will generate a valuable contribution
to the ﬁeld of handwritten document recognition systems.



2  Literature Survey


Balci et al. [1], investigates two distinct approaches to handwritten text recognition
through deep learning methods: (a) In direct word classiﬁcation method, a convo-
lutional neural network (CNN) is trained for the direct classiﬁcation of handwritten
words. This training involves the utilization of a labeled dataset consisting of word
images, enabling the network to classify new word images effectively. In character
segmentation approach, ﬁrst involves the segmentation of handwritten words into
individual characters. Subsequently, each character is classiﬁed using a CNN. Various

--- Page 224 ---
Efﬁcient Handwritten English Word Detection with Neural Networks                    213

techniques, such as long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, can be employed for
the character segmentation phase.
  The study’s evaluation was conducted using the IAM handwriting dataset, which
encompasses more than 110,000 labeled words contributed by 650 writers. The
results indicated that the character segmentation approach achieved the highest
performance, with a word accuracy of 38% on the validation set. Furthermore, the
authors conducted an exploration of the impact of different CNN architectures and
hyperparameters on their model’s performance. The study revealed that the ResNet-
18 CNN architecture outperformed other options. Additionally, a learning rate of
0.001 and a batch size of 32 were identiﬁed as optimal settings. In summary, the paper
offers an extensive overview of employing deep learning techniques for handwritten
text recognition. The ﬁndings underscore the efﬁcacy of deep learning in achieving
accurate results for handwritten text recognition tasks, even when utilizing relatively
straightforward CNN architectures.
  The essential insights gleaned from the model that deep learning can be effectively
leveraged to attain high accuracy in handwritten text recognition tasks. And the
character segmentation approach surpasses the direct word classiﬁcation approach in
terms of accuracy. The ResNet-18 CNN architecture stands out as a preferred choice
for handwritten text recognition and the optimal hyperparameters for handwritten
text recognition include a learning rate of 0.001 and a batch size of 32.
  The review delves into the work presented by Chowdhury et al. [2] represents
a complex endeavor, characterized by the conversion of handwritten text into a
digital format. This complexity stems from the considerable variability in hand-
writing styles and the presence of noise within handwritten images. Chowdhury
introduced an innovative end-to-end neural model for HTR in their paper. Their
model ingeniously fuses a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) with a recur-
rent encoder–decoder network to transform an image into a character sequence. The
CNN serves to extract crucial visual features from the input image, while the encoder–
decoder network meticulously encodes these visual features into a concealed repre-
sentation, subsequently decoding them into a sequence of characters. This encoder–
decoder network boasts bi-directional long short-term memory (LSTM) components,
complemented by an attention layer. The presence of this attention layer empowers
the network to dynamically allocate focus to various segments of the input image,
thereby contributing to improved model accuracy.
  The training regimen for this model follows an end-to-end approach, employing
focal loss instead of the traditional cross-entropy loss. Focal loss is particularly
apt at addressing the class imbalance issue inherent in HTR, wherein negative
samples (representing non-text pixels) vastly outnumber positive samples (text
pixels). Further augment the model’s decoding proﬁciency through the applica-
tion of a beam search algorithm. This algorithm predicated on the joint distribution
of individual characters, efﬁciently identiﬁes the most viable character sequence
from a multitude of hypotheses. To substantiate the model’s efﬁcacy, the authors
conducted extensive evaluations using publicly available HTR datasets, IAM and
RIMES. The results were overwhelmingly positive, with their model surpassing the
state-of-the-art word-level accuracy on both datasets’ evaluation sets by 3.5 and

--- Page 225 ---
214                                                                               S. Saikia et al.

1.1%, respectively. It presents an effective, end-to-end neural model for HTR. It not
only attains state-of-the-art performance on two publicly accessible datasets but also
excels in computational and memory efﬁciency, rendering it suitable for real-world
applications.
  The scholar Vaidya et al. [3], introduces an innovative approach to the realm
of Handwritten Character Recognition (HCR). This study employs a convolutional
neural network (CNN) as the foundational framework for training a model designed
to identify handwritten characters using the MNIST dataset. The CNN architecture
adopted within this research comprises four convolutional layers, supplemented by
two fully connected layers. These convolutional layers are primarily responsible for
feature extraction from the input images, while the fully connected layers assume
the role of categorizing the extracted features. The experimental evaluation of the
CNN model took place using the MNIST dataset, encompassing 60,000 training
images and 10,000 test images of handwritten digits. The model exhibited remark-
able performance, achieving an accuracy of 98.6% on the test dataset, placing it on
par with the state-of-the-art results for the MNIST dataset. Additionally, the authors
extended their assessment to a dataset composed of handwritten characters gathered
from students. Here, the model demonstrated a substantial accuracy rate of 95%, thus
highlighting the efﬁcacy of their proposed approach in real-world HCR applications.
In summation, the paper introduces a deep learning-based paradigm for HCR that
strikes a harmonious balance between precision and efﬁciency. The CNN model,
meticulously trained by the authors, not only attained state-of-the-art performance
on the MNIST dataset but also exhibited commendable results when tested on hand-
written characters collected from students. The implications of this approach extend
across various real-world HCR applications, such as check processing, mail sorting,
and document digitization.
  The research work by Neche et al. [4], presents an innovative deep learning-based
methodology designed for the precise segmentation of Arabic handwritten docu-
ments into text-lines and words. The segmentation of text lines and words consti-
tutes a pivotal phase in the realm of handwritten text recognition, as it facilitates the
individual identiﬁcation and recognition of textual elements. However, this task is
profoundly intricate, particularly when dealing with Arabic handwritten materials,
owing to the diverse range of writing styles, the cursive nature of the text, and the
potential presence of overlapping and touching characters. It has devised a two-stage
approach to address the segmentation challenge. In the initial stage, they employ an
RU-Net for pixel-wise classiﬁcation, which effectively separates text-line pixels from
the background pixels. Subsequently, in the second stage, a BLSTM-CTC network
is utilized to execute word segmentation on the text-line images.
  The BLSTM-CTC network demonstrates an adept ability to discern the temporal
dependencies among pixels within a text-line, thereby ensuring precise segmentation,
even in cases of touching and overlapping characters. Moreover, the network exhibits
remarkable adaptability in accommodating various writing styles and the presence of
diacritic marks within Arabic text. The efﬁcacy of the proposed approach is metic-
ulously evaluated using the KHATT Arabic database, resulting in an impressive

--- Page 226 ---
Efﬁcient Handwritten English Word Detection with Neural Networks                    215

segmentation accuracy of 96.7% for text lines and 80.1% for words. This achieve-
ment marks a substantial advancement compared to previous state-of-the-art tech-
niques [5] employed in Arabic handwritten document segmentation. The approach
introduced by the authors embodies a promising stride toward the development of
accurate and resilient systems for handwritten text recognition in the context of
Arabic scripts.
   Yousef et al. [6] has an innovative neural network architecture designed for uncon-
strained text recognition, a challenging task in computer vision that involves the iden-
tiﬁcation of text within images without constraints on appearance factors such as font,
size, color, or orientation. The proposed architecture features a fully convolutional
neural network (FCN) without recurrent connections, rendering it highly efﬁcient
and amenable to parallel processing. This unique attribute allows the network to
accommodate input of varying sizes and generate text strings of arbitrary lengths. To
optimize its performance for sequence recognition tasks, the architecture is trained
using the connectionist temporal classiﬁcation (CTC) loss function. It conducted
comprehensive evaluations of their proposed architecture on seven publicly available
benchmark datasets, encompassing a wide spectrum of text recognition challenges,
including handwriting recognition, CAPTCHA recognition, optical character recog-
nition (OCR), license plate recognition (LPR), and scene text recognition (STR).
Remarkably, their model outperformed existing methods, achieving state-of-the-art
results across all seven datasets, showcasing its versatility and superiority in the
realm of text recognition.
   Moreover, the proposed architecture [7–9] exhibits data-efﬁciency, as the authors
demonstrated its capability to deliver comparable performance to state-of-the-art
models using signiﬁcantly less training data. This characteristic makes the architec-
ture particularly appealing for applications where obtaining labeled training data is a
challenging endeavor. It makes a substantial contribution to the ﬁeld of text recogni-
tion. The proposed architecture, characterized by its simplicity, efﬁciency, and data-
efﬁciency, consistently attains state-of-the-art results on a diverse array of benchmark
datasets. Hence, introduction of a fully convolutional neural network (FCN) architec-
ture devoid of recurrent connections, enhancing efﬁciency and parallelizability and
deployment of the connectionist temporal classiﬁcation (CTC) loss function, tailored
for sequence recognition tasks, to train the proposed model. Also demonstration
of state-of-the-art performance across seven public benchmark datasets, covering a
broad spectrum of text recognition tasks and highlighting the data-efﬁcient nature
of the model, capable of achieving competitive results with signiﬁcantly reduced
training data.



3  Problem Deﬁnition


New technology on character recognition such as OCR, recognizing both printed
and handwritten text remains a challenging task due to the high variability and
complexity of handwritten text. Handwritten text exhibits signiﬁcant variations in

--- Page 227 ---
216                                                                               S. Saikia et al.

terms of character size, shape, and spacing, rendering it a formidable challenge for
existing systems to accurately recognize and transcribe. Also often carries noise
in the form of smudges, scratches, and irregular handwriting styles. And certain
documents, such as intricate forms and detailed contracts, possess a high level of
complexity and contain extensive data. Existing models like tesseract, paddle [10],
Transformer OCR [9, 11] are struggling to accurately extract and process all the
data within these documents due to their intricate layouts and content structures.
It creates problems in applications such as digitizing historical documents such as
survey copies, scanned registration forms, attendance sheets, medical records and
ofﬂine forms, which typically contain both printed and handwritten text. In addition,
quality is not always ideal, that it may be time consuming and expensive, that it can
provide erroneous results, that it is mistake prone, and that it occasionally requires
proofreading.



4  Methodology


The methodology -convolutional bi-directional long short-term memory connec-
tionist (CBLC) IWR model for the development of the handwritten word detection
model revolves around the utilization of Intelligent Word Recognition (IWR) tech-
nology. The process unfolds through a systematic sequence of stages, beginning with
a meticulous data collection effort from diverse handwritten sources. Subsequently,
we engage in a comprehensive preprocessing phase to enhance the quality and rele-
vance of our dataset. The heart of our methodology lies in the design of the model,
wherein we leverage cutting-edge deep neural network architectures. The intrica-
cies of our approach encompass the stages of model training and testing, crucial for
reﬁning and evaluating the model’s performance. The post-processing phase ensures
the coherence and precision of the model’s output. The entire process is visually
articulated in the accompanying diagram, providing a clear and concise overview of
our methodology’s ﬂow (Fig. 1).



4.1  Data Collection


Data collection plays a pivotal role in the success of this research endeavor. This
crucial phase involved an extensive search for handwritten image data, culminating
in the discovery of a well-suited dataset on Kaggle [12], as designed by Budati et al.
[7]. This dataset is a rich repository of diverse handwritten words, with each image
encapsulating a single word, and the ﬁle name corresponding to the textual content
within the image. An intriguing facet of this dataset is its incorporation of various font
styles originating from different individuals, endowing it with a unique and diverse
character. While this diversity enhances the model’s adaptability, it is essential to
recognize the potential biases inherent in the dataset, such as variations in writing

styles that may be speciﬁc to certain demographics or regions. Acknowledging these
biases is crucial for ensuring the model’s fairness and generalizability. The inclusion
of diverse handwriting styles is a deliberate choice aimed at enriching the model’s
training data, ensuring its adaptability to a broad spectrum of real-world scenarios.
Below, we present a selection of sample images from this dataset, providing a glimpse
into the richness of our collected data (Fig. 2).



4.2  Preprocessing


In the initial stage of preprocessing, we address the variability in image sizes by
employing OpenCV’s resizing function, which uniformly scales all images to a stan-
dardized 64 × 256 dimension. Subsequently, a series of essential OpenCV oper-
ations are applied to enhance the quality and utility of the data. These operations
include grayscale conversion to simplify color information, dilation to emphasize
key features, division for contrast enhancement, and thresholding to reduce noise
and ensure that the images are primed for further analysis.
   In our data preprocessing pipeline, we encountered a crucial challenge—the model
cannot be trained directly on text data. To address this, we employed an embedding
technique speciﬁcally tailored for our label data. This involved the implementation of
a straightforward yet essential character-level embedding method, which efﬁciently
transformed our textual data into a numeric format. This meticulous preprocessing

step played a pivotal role in preparing our data for effective model training and
underscored the importance of proper data representation in our research.
   In the subsequent stage of preprocessing, our focus turns to the division of the
dataset to facilitate effective training, validation, and testing of our model. Initially,
we start with a dataset comprising 100,000 images. To optimize the machine learning
process, we allocate these images into three distinct subsets. Speciﬁcally, 80% of the
data, equating to 80,000 images, is designated for training the model, while 10%
(10,000 images) is reserved for validation to ﬁne-tune and assess its performance.
The remaining 10% (10,000 images) is set aside for rigorous testing to evaluate the
model’s accuracy and generalizability. This strategic division ensures that our model
is robust and capable of handling real-world scenarios effectively.

4.3  Model Design


The core of our architecture employs Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for
efﬁcient image feature extraction, which is crucial for our subsequent tasks. We
then pass these extracted features through a bidirectional long short-term memory
(LSTM) network, enhancing the model’s ability to capture temporal dependencies
in the data. Finally, we employ the Connectionist Temporal Classiﬁcation (CTC) for
mapping labels to the corresponding image sequences and calculating the loss. This
paper delves into a detailed explanation of our model’s architecture, including its
key parameters and their roles, offering a comprehensive understanding of its inner
workings (Fig. 3).
  The proposed model architecture for this research is designed to process input data
with a shape of (256, 64, 1) using a combination of convolutional layers and recurrent
neural networks. The model begins with a 2D convolutional layer (conv_1) with 16
ﬁlters, a kernel size of (3, 3), and ReLU activation is applied to the input. Padding
maintains spatial dimensions, and max-pooling with a (2, 2) window and stride of 2
is used. This process is repeated in conv_2 with 32 ﬁlters. Next, conv_3 and conv_4
both have 64 ﬁlters with a (3, 3) kernel, utilizing ReLU activation, followed by max-
pooling with a (2, 1) window in conv_4. Batch normalization is applied to conv_5 and
conv_6. Another max-pooling layer with a (2, 1) window is introduced after conv_6.
A smaller 2D convolutional layer (conv_7) with a (2, 2) kernel and ReLU activation
captures higher-level features. After the convolutional layers, a Reshape layer ﬂattens
spatial dimensions. Two bidirectional LSTM layers (blstm_1 and blstm_2) with 128
units each are used to capture long-range dependencies in the data. Finally, a dense
layer (‘outputs’) with softmax activation generates predictions for a character set
plus one additional class, suitable for tasks such as character recognition. The model
provides a comprehensive architecture combining convolutional and recurrent layers
for effective processing of the given input data.

4.4  Training, Testing, and Validation


In our research, the model training process was executed with a careful division
of our dataset to ensure robust and reliable results. Speciﬁcally, we allocated 80%
of our dataset, amounting to 80,000 images, for the training phase. This extensive
training dataset allowed our deep learning model to learn and adapt to a diverse range
of input patterns, facilitating the extraction of meaningful features. The remaining
20,000 images were split into two equal sets, with 10,000 images designated for
validation and the other 10,000 for testing. This partitioning strategy ensured that
the model’s performance could be effectively evaluated, with the validation set used
during training to ﬁne-tune hyperparameters such as epochs, batch size, image size,
learning rate, and feature extraction techniques. Optimizing these hyperparameters
allowed for a more nuanced and adaptive training process tailored to the intricacies of
the handwritten text recognition task. The test set reserved for assessing the model’s
generalization ability and accuracy on unseen data (Fig. 4).
   During the training phase, our model demonstrated remarkable proﬁciency by
achieving an outstanding 100% accuracy, indicating its capacity to effectively learn
from the training data. This impressive level of accuracy on the training dataset
signiﬁes that the model successfully captured the intricacies of the input patterns. In
the validation phase, it maintained a strong accuracy rate of 98%, underscoring its
ability to adapt to new and unseen data. Furthermore, in the rigorous testing phase,
the model showcased a commendable accuracy of 96.71%. These results reﬂect the
model’s robustness and suggest its potential to excel in real-world applications, where
it can accurately process and interpret data, making it a valuable asset for handwritten
text recognition.



4.5  Post-Processing


The post-processing procedure in our methodology is centered on the decoding of the
model’s output. This process is initiated during the model’s training phase, where a
character-level embedding technique is thoughtfully applied to the label data. Subse-
quently, during prediction, the model yields numeric values as outputs. To derive the
actual text labels from these numerical codes, the only requisite post-processing step

--- Page 232 ---
Efﬁcient Handwritten English Word Detection with Neural Networks                    221

involves decoding the model’s predictions. This uncomplicated yet critical decoding
process represents the sole component of our post-processing pipeline, ensuring that
the model’s output is readily interpretable in terms of the original text labels.



4.6  Evaluation Metrics


In our rigorous evaluation of the model’s performance, we took a meticulous and
comprehensive approach, considering the recognition of complete words as the
benchmark for success. This stringent criterion meant that any word lacking even
a single character was classiﬁed as an incorrect prediction. Within our substantial
testing dataset, which featured a total of 10,000 word images, our model exhib-
ited exceptional competence by correctly identifying 9671 word images. However,
there were 329 words where the model made incorrect predictions, marking them
as False Negatives (FN). This evaluation with 10,000 word images, the model
correctly identiﬁed 9671 words (true positives) but missed 329 words (false nega-
tives). Notably, there were no cases of incorrectly identifying non-existent words
(false positives) or correctly recognizing words it shouldn’t (true negatives). This
breakdown emphasizes the model’s strength in accurately spotting complete words
while highlighting areas for potential improvement, particularly in reducing instances
of missed identiﬁcations.
   This evaluation resulted in the following classiﬁcation of outcomes: True positives
(TP) equal to 9671, true negatives (TN) equal to 0, false positives (FP) equal to 0,
and false negatives (FN) equal to 329 (Fig. 5).

5  Future Work


This research presents a fundamental approach to tackling the given problem of text
detection, laying a strong foundation for future endeavors in this domain. Several
exciting avenues for further research and development have emerged from this work.
   Firstly, the ﬁne-tuning of hyperparameters stands as a crucial step forward. Opti-
mizing model parameters and architectural choices can signiﬁcantly enhance the
model’s performance and efﬁciency. Further exploration of parameter conﬁgurations
and training strategies could yield even more accurate results.
  Expanding the scope of this research to encompass multilingual handwritten text
detection represents another exciting avenue for future work. Adapting the existing
approach to recognize text in various languages opens doors to broader applications,
especially in diverse linguistic environments, and holds great promise for cross-
cultural communication and information retrieval.
   Additionally, the integration of a user interface for this model presents an exciting
opportunity. Enabling user interaction and real-time feedback mechanisms could
enhance the model’s adaptability and usability. Creating an intuitive and user-friendly
interface would facilitate practical deployment and cater to the needs of a wider
audience. These future prospects collectively contribute to the evolving landscape of
text detection and hold the potential to further elevate the impact of this research.



6  Conclusion


In conclusion, this research presents a remarkable approach for recognizing hand-
written text through the CBLC IWR model, achieving an impressive accuracy of
up to 96.71%. The ﬁndings of this study not only demonstrate the effectiveness of

--- Page 234 ---
Efﬁcient Handwritten English Word Detection with Neural Networks                    223

this model for single-language handwritten text recognition but also open the door
to the development of similar models for multilingual text detection. In the current
era, where the demand for digitizing documents is constantly growing, this approach
holds great promise and is expected to play a pivotal role in advancing ongoing
research in handwritten text recognition.
   However, it is crucial to acknowledge the limitations of the CBLC IWR model.
The accuracy of this model may vary when confronted with lower image quality or
increased noise in the input images. Additionally, it is important to note that the model
is designed speciﬁcally for recognizing letters and may not perform optimally when
tasked with recognizing digits. As we move forward, addressing these limitations
will be essential for ensuring the broader applicability and robustness of the model in
diverse real-world scenarios. As with any technological advancement, understanding
its constraints is key to unlocking its full potential.

MuBDA: Multimodal Biometric Data
Analysis for Gender Classiﬁcation Using
Deep Learning Techniques


Shivanand Gornale    , Sathish Kumar    , and R. Kruthi





Abstract  In recent years, technological advancements have led to an increased focus
on security measures for individuals due to the prevalence of inappropriate behavior
in society. Biometric applications play a vivacious role in the security authentication
and authorization of individuals in a day-to-day life activities. These applications
are used in a diversity of ﬁelds, including health care, forensic applications, and
in the court of law. The proposed work emphasizes the importance of multimodal
biometric traits in the demographic characteristic analysis of an individual. A total
of 3510 face and ofﬂine handwritten signatures were collected from 193 male and
158 female volunteers. Transfer learning models were used to analyze the features
and classify the data. The algorithms outperformed state-of-the-art techniques and
produced comparable results.

Keywords Face images · Ofﬂine handwritten signatures · Multimodal
biometrics · Transfer learning architectures



1  Introduction


Biometric technology is an emerging research topic in information security appli-
cations. Recent advancements in security domains point to intelligent biometric
systems. Biometrics have become one of the prominent and reliable systems for

person identiﬁcation. Biometric recognition  is based on visual and behavioral
biometric characteristics like Face, ﬁngerprint, hand geometry, voice, and signa-
ture [1]. In most of applications like border surveillance, medical data, and govern-
ment agencies, biometrics poses the most potent authentication system [2]. Every
human adheres to soft biometric characteristics such as gender, age, nationality,
hair color, body mass index, and so on. Identiﬁcation of the person using a single
biometric modality is said to be a unimodal biometric system [3]. These unimodal
biometrics may not completely identify the individual due to inadequate environ-
mental conditions, the effect of lighting, and improper data, which does not meet
fully the needs of existing system. To overcome these difﬁculties, a combination
of more than two biometric traits are used to identify the individual more accu-
rately. This method is called a multimodal biometric-based identiﬁcation system.
Even multimodal biometric models face the issue of lack of a combination of low-
reliability biometrics [4, 20]. In terms of robustness and defensive nature, multimodal
biometrics are preferred over unimodal. Face and signature biometrics are socially
accepted biometrics. Face is the biological trait which is vital part in the human body,
considered to classify the gender and other soft characteristics.
   However, with the rapid developments in the technology, face recognition system
is relatively improved. Due to variations in the illumination, facial expressions and
cultural differences, it is a challenging problem while classifying the face images. In
contrast, Ofﬂine handwritten signatures are said to be “written selﬁe” of an individual.
It is an evident behavioral biometric modality, which is extremely under the control
of individual’s hand action [5]. The signature dynamics vary in every session while
signing. These two modalities have been used in many application areas such as
law enforcement, border-security control, e-KYC, instant document veriﬁcation and
personal identity veriﬁcation and so on. An approach for classiﬁcation of gender from
face and ofﬂine handwritten signature images is a challenging task due to individual
cultural differences in appearance and variations in writing style. This proposed work
will investigate the multimodal biometric-based gender classiﬁcation through feature
base analysis using deep-learning techniques.
  The subsequent sections of the paper are arranged in following: a succinct
summary of the current works presented in Section II, the proposed methodology
elaborated in the Section III, Section IV investigates the experimental arrangement
and evaluation, and Section V concludes paper with future recommendations for
young technocrats and researchers.



2  Related Works


This section reveals the preceding work carried out by the researchers in the
multimodal biometric for gender classiﬁcation.
   Gornale et al. [6] proposes a deep-learning method for gender classiﬁcation using
multimodal biometrics. In this work authors have used pre-trained deep neural

--- Page 237 ---
MuBDA: Multimodal Biometric Data Analysis for Gender …                          227

network, i.e., Alex Net for feature extraction and classiﬁcation. For experimenta-
tion publicly available standard dataset SDUMLA-HMT is been used. A multimodal
biometric database of 15,052 images of 106 individuals (59 males and 47 females)
was constructed. The proposed method achieved a recognition rate of 99.9% on this
database.
   Patil et al. [7] investigated gender classiﬁcation using machine learning-based
multimodal biometric data analysis. BSIF and MB-LBP features were extracted from
ﬁngerprint, face and iris images of the SDUMLA_HMT dataset. To determine the
robustness of the proposed method, a feature fusion method was employed, achieving
an accuracy of 99.8%.
   In [8], authors have proposed a gender classiﬁcation using human face images.
Two standard datasets like UTK-Face and FERET datasets were employed for
the experiments. Histogram of Gradients, Gabor Filters, and SURF features were
extracted and reduced the dimensionality of the features via Principal Component
Analysis. The Multi-class Support Vector Machine (SVM) classiﬁer is used to clas-
sify the trained data. The proposed approach achieved 98.75% gender recognition
accuracy in the FERET database and 97.43% accuracy for UTK-Face database with
a runtime of 0.5 s.
  Song et al. [9] presented a novel approach to user identiﬁcation using multiple
biometric characteristics in their research. The study was to consider the efﬁcacy of a
deep learning (DL) model known as ResNet-50 for feature extraction from a dataset.
The experimental analysis involved utilizing a dataset comprising ECG, facial, and
ﬁngerprint data of 58 virtual subjects. The authors conducted a comparative analysis
of the fusion performance at both the feature extraction and score levels. Notably, an
impressive accuracy of 97.70% was achieved when integrating the information from
all three modalities.
   Bisogni et al. [10] worked on age and gender classiﬁcation using Periocular Data
Fusion. The authors studied periocular feature fusion of Iris data to derive demo-
graphic attributes of a person. Data fusion methods were used to improve the trustwor-
thiness of selected biometric features. The GANT dataset was used for experimen-
tation with four different machine-learning algorithms: ensemble classiﬁer, decision
tree, optimization, and instance-based algorithms. Experiments were performed on
periocular features, which achieved a recognition rate of 84.45% for age classiﬁcation
and an accuracy of 84.62% for gender classiﬁcation, respectively.
  Yadav  et  al. [11] studied the fusion of multimodal biometric features of
ﬁngerprints, irises, and handwritten signatures using deep-learning techniques. To
strengthen the framework, deep learning models were trained on iris, ﬁngerprint,
and ofﬂine signature data. The VGG-19 network was used to construct the model,
and Adam’s optimization technique was used to minimize the loss function. The
SDUMLA-HMT dataset is used for experimentation. Using different score-level
fusion strategies, an accuracy of 99.21% was achieved.
   Eskandari et al. [12] used ULBP for feature extraction and BSA for feature selec-
tion in gender based multimodal systems on face and ocular images. SVM with
RBF kernel was used for classiﬁcation. Their approach outperformed unimodal
approaches on MBGC and CASIA-Iris-Distance datasets. The accuracy for male

--- Page 238 ---
228                                                                             S. Gornale et al.

faces on CASIA-Iris-Distance was 84% and for female faces on MBGC was 83.34%.
The inclusion of both ocular regions improved female classiﬁcation accuracy by up
to 75%.
  Yaman et al. [13] developed a framework for age and gender classiﬁcation using
a deep CNN with multimodal and multitask capabilities. The framework was tested
on three multimodal biometric datasets. Three fusion methods were used, focusing
on ear and proﬁle face. VGG16 and ResNet50 CNNs achieved 99.11% accuracy
for gender classiﬁcation in both ear and face modalities. However, age classiﬁca-
tion accuracy was lower, with 67.59% using VGG16 on FERET and 66.44% using
ResNet50.
   Abhishek Garain et al. [14] designed a deep network model called GRA_Net
(gated residual attention network) to predict gender and age from face images.
They experimented with ﬁve different publicly available datasets, i.e., UTK-Face,
AdienceDB, Wikipedia, FG-NET, and AFAD. The results achieved for gender is
99.2 and 93.7% accuracy for age classiﬁcation.
  Han et al. [15] proposed a framework for age, gender, and race classiﬁcation using
unconstrained facial images. Their method extracts BIFs from input images and uses
3 SVMs with RBF kernel for age, race, and gender estimation. The results showed
that the method achieved 87.1% accuracy for gender and 68.1% for age classiﬁcation
on the LFW+ dataset, and 95.4% for gender, 66.7% for age, and 90.8% for race on
the FG-Net dataset.
  From, the related work, it is observed that, there is a scope to get the robustness in
the existing methods/models to improve the classiﬁcation accuracy using multimodal
biometric traits.



2.1  Motivation


The aim of work stems from the need for accurate gender classiﬁcation in various
real-world applications. Gender identiﬁcation plays a crucial role in security systems,
surveillance, personalized services, and human–computer interaction. Traditional
approaches to gender classiﬁcation often rely on individual biometric modalities,
which may have limitations in terms of accuracy and robustness. By employing
deep learning methodologies and conducting multimodal analysis of biometric data,
our objective is to enhance the precision and dependability of gender classiﬁcation,
thereby optimizing the efﬁcacy of these applications.



2.2  Signiﬁcance of the Work


Biometric systems have the potential to improve efﬁciency, security, and convenience
in numerous aspects of daily life while also raising important ethical and societal
considerations. The study of gender biometrics holds signiﬁcant importance across

--- Page 239 ---
MuBDA: Multimodal Biometric Data Analysis for Gender …                          229

various domains, including technology, health care, marketing, and social sciences.
Despite advancements, challenges persist in accurate age and gender classiﬁcation.
Variability in biometric data due to factors like lighting, facial expressions, cultural
and ethnic differences, and data quality can hinder precise classiﬁcation.
  By addressing limitations and exploring innovative approaches, the proposed
research work will provide new insights into the forensic science domain beneﬁt of
demographic attributes (age and gender) analysis, speciﬁcally on forensic biometric
data.
   Furthermore, this research work will provide valuable information for the future
research in exploring the biometric data. The following are the key contributions of
the proposed work:

•  Exploring the conventional and deep features to distinguish gender of an individual
   based on two different biometric modalities.
•  State-of-the-art methods were compared with existing works and presented
   transfer-learning methods and achieved a signiﬁcant result.
•  Identiﬁcation gender using a conventional classiﬁcation framework.
• Analyze the effectiveness of proposed study, and categorize its excellence in rela-
   tion to recent relevant research, and ultimately provide suggestions and hypotheses
   for future investigations.

   of biometric data as it captures the unique characteristics of the data. In this

   data. Figure 2 visualizes the feature map of the collected sample data in the neural
   network architecture.


Feature Fusion

Feature fusion is a technique for combining the features sets extracted from multiple
biometric traits. The main objective of concatenating the feature set is to improve
the system performance and recognition accuracy. In the proposed work, the features
were extracted from the deep models were fused to feature matrix and utilized for
the classiﬁcation system.



3.1  Transfer-Learning Architectures


Transfer-learning architectures are actively used in a variety of domains such as
image processing, speech recognition, and machine vision. These techniques can
improve the performance signiﬁcantly even if the training data is less. Transfer-
learning models acquire the knowledge gained from the pre-trained architectures

--- Page 241 ---
MuBDA: Multimodal Biometric Data Analysis for Gender …                          231

and allow the learned features to enhance the generalization and domain adaptation
across different tasks and databases. Ultimately, the transfer-learning models are
emerging techniques viz can overcome the challenges posed by limited training data
and improve accuracy and efﬁciency in deep-learning applications.

Vgg16

In 2014, Karen Simonyan and Andrew Zisserman, members of the Visual Geometry
Group (VGG) at Oxford University, proposed the VGG16 architecture. Their paper,
titled “Very Deep Convolutional Networks for Large-Scale Image Recognition,”
introduced a novel convolutional neural network architecture that achieved state-of-
the-art results on several benchmark datasets.
  The VGG16 architecture comprising 16 weighted layers. A notable characteristic
of the VGG16 architecture is its consistent utilization of 3 × 3 convolutional layers
with a stride of 1 and “same” padding. These convolutional layers are subsequently
followed by max-pooling layers with a window size of 2 × 2 and a stride of 2.
The authors of the VGG16 model deliberately chose this design to maintain a small
receptive ﬁeld while simultaneously increasing the depth, as they believed this to be
crucial for achieving optimal performance. For a visual representation of the overall
structure of the VGG16 model, please refer to Fig. 3 [16].

ResNet50

ResNet50, a convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture, which was proposed
by He et al. [17], and now it belongs to the family of ResNets (short for residual
networks).
  ResNet introduced a novel concept known as “residual learning”. In traditional
deep networks, adding more layers can lead to a problem known as the vanishing
gradient problem, where gradients become too small to effectively train the earlier
layers. ResNet addresses this issue by using residual blocks, which include skip
connections that allow the gradient to ﬂow directly through the network. With a 50
weight layers, it is considered to be a relatively deep CNN architecture that has shown

inviable performance on a variety of computer vision tasks, like image classiﬁcation,
image object detection, and image segmentation. Figure 4 demonstrates the general
architectural ﬁgure of ResNet50 model.



4  Experimental Results


This section discusses the dataset used, implementation details, and experiment result
analysis. The proposed work emphasis two different transfer-learning architectures,
which are been used for feature extraction and classiﬁcation.



4.1  Dataset Description


A literature review revealed that there are no publicly available standard image
datasets of handwritten signature images and face images that are both annotated
for gender. Additionally, either the face dataset or the handwritten signature dataset
is annotated, but not both. To address this issue, we created our own dataset to conduct
experiments with the proposed work.

Ofﬂine Handwritten Signature

Samples of signatures were gathered from individuals spanning various age groups.
The database comprises a total of 3510 signatures, obtained from 351 participants.
Among these, 193 were male volunteers, while 158 were female volunteers. All
individuals were duly informed about the objective behind collecting the signature
samples, and their participation was entirely voluntary. The dataset description was
derived from references [1, 19]. Figure 5 visually presents the collection of ofﬂine
handwritten signature samples.

Face Dataset

The face dataset was collected from various individuals using a Canon EOS 1300D
DSLR camera. We informed a total of 351 volunteers and asked them to face the
camera according to speciﬁc instructions. The photos were captured in different

--- Page 243 ---
MuBDA: Multimodal Biometric Data Analysis for Gender …                          233





Fig. 5 Ofﬂine handwritten signature samples





Fig. 6  Facial image samples of proposed work


lighting conditions (day and night), poses, and with neutral expressions. The dataset
contains 158 female and 193 male volunteers of varying ages, from adulthood (18)
to old age (65). We collected 10 different samples from each individual with minimal
head movements, for a total of 3510 facial images. The images are color and have
a resolution of 72 dpi and 5184 × 3456 dimensions in.jpg format. Figure 6 shows
some of the face images collected for the proposed work.

methodologies.

4.3  Results and Discussion


The study utilized extracted features of VGG16 and ResNet50 model and trained for
multimodal biometric images which are further been validated using CNN model
SoftMax layer for classiﬁcation on the collected dataset.

Algorithm

Input: Collected multimodal biometric image samples.

Output: Gender determination from collected multimodal biometric image samples.

     Step 1: Input the images from the dataset.

     Step 2: Normalize the image into 224 × 224 × 3 size.

     Step 3: Feature extraction using VGG16 and ResNet50 model.

     Step 4: Feature fusion and classiﬁcation using both transfer learning models.

Step 5: Feature map is trained and tested for validation.

Step 6: Performance metrics were analyzed for test data.

End.

obtained results are shown in Tables 2 and 3. It is been notice that the VGG16 model
has performed best for multi biometric trait, respectively.
    Initially, the experiments were carried on two datasets: Face and Signature. Each
dataset is evaluated on two different pre-trained models ResNet50 and VGG16.

models and weights were combined and used for image classiﬁcation among face
and handwritten signature images. Tables 4 and 5 show the obtained results for the
multimodal biometrics.

with the highest accuracy. To prove the efﬁciency of the proposed work, perfor-
mance evaluation metrics were calculated on two experiments. The f1_score, recall,
and precision metrics for facial images are computed to be 1.00, 0.99, and 0.9949,
respectively. Furthermore, the overall accuracy attained is 99.14%. Whereas, for
Handwritten Signature images the average precision value is 0.92, recall is 0.94 and
F1_score is 0.91. Overall accuracy is 90.88%. Hence, comparatively the obtained

5  Conclusion


Gender Classiﬁcation systems are the major contributors in addressing security
concerns, banking, document analysis and many more. The present study proposes a
gender based multimodal biometric data determination using deep models. The aim
of the study is to classify the demographic characteristics of individuals using their
physiological and behaviological biometrics. Combination of two transfer-learning
methods viz ResNet50 and VGG16 models were employed on self-collected multi-
modal dataset. To enhance the distinctiveness of the features, features extracted from
the both models were concatenated. The biometric data from each modality was
analyzed using these models, resulting in signiﬁcant improvements in classiﬁcation
accuracy. Further, this work may extend to utilize the more number of biometric
traits to achieve more robustness in the existing system.

Ethical Statement

The samples were collected from individuals who willingly participated after being
informed about the purpose of this study. These samples were exclusively utilized
only for research purposes.

Audio Data Feature Extraction
for Speaker Diarization


Vinod K. Pande, Vijay K. Kale, and Sumegh Tharewal





Abstract  In many applications, such as transcription, speaker identiﬁcation, and
audio indexing, speaker diarization—the process of dividing audio data into different
speaker segments—is crucial. The speaker diarization algorithms for audio data
utilising the Python Librosa module are the main topic of this research study. A
strong Python library for analysing audio and music is called Librosa. It offers a
number of features for extracting audio features, including MFCC, Spectrogram,
Chromagram, and Spectral Contrast. This study offers helpful advice on how to
extract features from audio data.

Keywords Speaker diarization · Spectral contrast · Feature extraction · MFCC ·
Chromogram · Spectrogram



1  Introduction


Speaker diarization is an approach used in computational linguistics and speech pro-
cessing in order to automatically divide an audio recording into segments belonging
to various speakers. Without prior information about the speaker, speaker diarization
attempts to recognise and distinguish the speech of various speakers throughout an
audio stream [ 1].
   There are various steps involved in speaker diarization. An audio recording is ﬁrst
divided into smaller segments, such as speaking turns or set periods of time [ 1]. Then,

3  Implementation Process


Implementation steps of each methodology explain below with a ﬂow chart.



3.1  Implementation of MFCC


 1. Load the audio ﬁle.

     (a) Use the librosa.load() function to load the audio ﬁle.
    (b) Specify the ﬁle path as an argument.

 2. Preprocessing (if necessary):

     (a) Apply any desired preprocessing steps, such as resampling or normalisation,
         to the audio signal.

 3. Compute the Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT):

     (a) Use the librosa.stft() function to compute the STFT of the preprocessed
        audio signal.
    (b) Specify parameters such as the window size, hop length, and window type.

 4. Compute the Power Spectrogram:

     (a) Compute the magnitude squared of the STFT to obtain the power spectro-
       gram, representing the distribution of signal power over time and frequency.

 5. Apply the Mel Filterbank:

     (a) Deﬁne the number of Mel frequency bands (nmels) desired for the MFCC
        computation.
    (b) Use the librosa.ﬁlters.mel() function to generate a Mel ﬁlterbank matrix.
     (c) Apply the ﬁlterbank to the power spectrogram using element-wise multipli-
         cation.

 6. Take the Logarithm:

     (a) Apply a logarithm (usually base 10) to the ﬁltered spectrogram.
    (b) This step compresses the dynamic range of the spectrogram.

 7. Apply Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT):

     (a) Apply the DCT to the logarithmically compressed spectrogram.
    (b) The DCT decorrelates the Mel-Spectrogram coefﬁcients and generates a
       compact representation.

 8. Select MFCC Coefﬁcients:

     (a) Choose a subset of the DCT coefﬁcients to retain as the ﬁnal MFCC repre-
         sentation.

--- Page 257 ---
248                                                                         V. K. Pande et al.

     (b) Typically, the ﬁrst few coefﬁcients (e.g. 1–13) are considered signiﬁcant and
         retained.

 9. Optional: Apply Scaling or Normalisation:

     (a)  If desired, apply scaling or normalisation to the MFCC coefﬁcients to ensure
        they fall within a speciﬁc range.

10. Plot or Use the MFCC:

     (a) Visualise the MFCC coefﬁcients using a plot or use them for further analysis,
       such as speech recognition or audio classiﬁcation.



   These steps outline the typical implementation process for computing MFCC
using Librosa. However, the speciﬁc parameters, such as the number of Mel bands
or the subset of DCT coefﬁcients chosen, can vary depending on the application and
desired level of detail captured in the MFCC representation.



3.2  Implementation of Male Spectrogram


1. Load the audio ﬁle.

    (a) Use the librosa.load() function to load the audio ﬁle.
   (b) Specify the ﬁle path as an argument.

2. Preprocessing (if necessary):

    (a) Apply any desired preprocessing steps, such as resampling or normalisation,
        to the audio signal.

3. Compute the Mel spectrogram:

    (a) Use the librosa.feature.melspectrogram() function to compute the Mel
       spectrogram.
   (b) This function takes the audio data as input and returns the Mel spectrogram
       as a 2D array.

4. Convert to log scale:

    (a) To improve the perceptual quality of the spectrogram, you can convert the
       amplitude values to the log scale.
   (b) Use the librosa.power_to_db() function for this purpose.

5. Visualise the Mel spectrogram:

    (a) use the matplotlib library to display the Mel spectrogram as an image.

3.3  Implementation of Spectral Contrast


1. Load the audio ﬁle.

    (a) Use the librosa.load() function to load the audio ﬁle.
   (b) Specify the ﬁle path as an argument.

2. Preprocessing (if necessary):

    (a) Apply any desired preprocessing steps to the audio signal, such as resampling
       or normalisation.

3. Compute the Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT):

    (a) Use the librosa.stft() function to compute the STFT of the preprocessed audio
        signal.
   (b) Specify parameters such as the window size, hop length, and window type.

4. Compute the Magnitude Spectrum:

    (a) Take the magnitude of the STFT to obtain the magnitude spectrum.
   (b) The magnitude spectrum represents the distribution of signal power over time
      and frequency.

5. Compute the Spectral Contrast:

    (a) Use thelibrosa.feature.spectral_contrast() function to com-
       pute the spectral contrast.
   (b) Pass the magnitude spectrum as an argument.

6. Optional: Apply Scaling or Normalisation:

    (a)  If desired, apply scaling or normalisation to the spectral contrast values to
       ensure they fall within a speciﬁc range.

7. Plot or Use the Spectral Contrast:

    (a) Visualise the spectral contrast using a plot or use it for further analysis, such
       as instrument classiﬁcation or audio segmentation.

1. Load the audio ﬁle.

    (a) Use the librosa.load() function to load the audio ﬁle.
   (b) Specify the ﬁle path as an argument.

2. Preprocessing (if necessary):

    (a) Apply any desired preprocessing steps, such as resampling or normalisation,
       to the audio signal.

3. Compute the chromagram:

    (a) Use the librosa.feature.chroma_stft() function to compute the chromagram
      from the audio signal.
   (b) This function uses the Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) to calculate the
      chroma features.

4. Visualise the chromagram (optional):

    (a) You can use the librosa.display.specshow() function to visualise the com-
       puted chromagram.



3.5  Implementation Steps for Tonnetz Feature


1. Load the audio ﬁle:

    (a) Use the librosa.load() function to load the audio ﬁle.
   (b) Specify the ﬁle path as an argument.

2. Preprocessing (if necessary):

    (a) Apply any desired preprocessing steps to the audio signal, such as resampling
       or normalisation.

3. Compute the Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT):

    (a) Use the librosa.stft() function to compute the STFT of the preprocessed audio
        signal.
   (b) Specify parameters such as the window size, hop length, and window type.

4. Compute the Harmonic and Percussive Components:

    (a) Use the librosa.effects.hpss() function to separate the harmonic and percus-
       sive components of the audio signal.
   (b) Pass the magnitude spectrogram obtained from the STFT as an argument.

5. Compute the Chromagram of the Harmonic Component:

    (a) Use the librosa.feature.chroma_cqt() function to compute the chromagram
       of the harmonic component.
   (b) Pass the harmonic component obtained from the HPSS decomposition as an
       argument.

6. Compute the Tonal Centroids:

    (a) Use the librosa.feature.tonnetz() function to compute the ton-
       netz representation.
   (b) Pass the chromagram obtained from the harmonic component as an argument.
