1  Introduction


In recent years, the escalating demand for high-speed and reliable communication
services, driven by applications such as the Internet of Things (IoT), wireless sensor
networks (WSN), vehicular ad hoc networks, and massive machine-type communi-
cation (mMTC) in beyond 5G (B5G) wireless networks [1], has necessitated highly
heterogeneous and reliable wireless networks. The future generations of wireless
networks are anticipated to be both architecturally and service-wise heterogeneous.
Traditional terrestrial networks alone struggle to meet these demands, particularly in
remote and challenging environments, such as disaster-prone areas, where reliable
and efﬁcient communication is critical. The integration of satellite and terrestrial
networks emerges as a promising solution, offering reliable connectivity [2]. This
integration holds the potential for seamless network coverage, global broadband
access, and heterogeneous user utility within a common network.
   Conventional terrestrial networks remain invaluable for providing low-cost, high-
speed services in densely populated areas, while satellite networks contribute global
coverage, high throughput, reliability, and boundary less propagation [3, 4]. The
integrated satellite–terrestrial network architecture combines the strengths of both,
aiming to provide global broadband access and enable ubiquitous network services
in future wireless communication generations. To overcome the limitations of terres-
trial networks, UAVs are deployed, offering wider coverage and improved Quality
of Service (QoS). Being highly mobile and resilient, UAVs function as plug-and-
play nodes, particularly in emergency situations, and can serve as relay nodes for
connectivity to mobile platforms [5]. The integration of UAVs and NOMA schemes
enhances the network’s potential, achieving higher levels of performance and relia-
bility [6]. NOMA’s efﬁciency in spectrum utilization proves beneﬁcial for bandwidth-
constrained applications like emergency or disaster management, positioning it as a
promising solution in 5G and beyond networks [1].
   In  addition, energy-harvesting technologies have emerged as a promising
approach to address energy efﬁciency concerns in wireless communication networks
[7]. Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) equipped with energy harvesting capabilities
can improve ﬂight endurance and ensure continuous communication. These UAVs

--- Page 381 ---
Energy Harvesting in a NOMA-Based Integrated …                                  381

can harvest energy from ambient sources, such as solar or wind power, to supple-
ment their on-board power sources, thereby extending their operational life. This
capability is particularly valuable in remote or disaster-prone areas where access to
traditional power sources may be limited or unreliable. In addition, the integration of
energy-harvesting technology with UAV relay nodes can contribute to the resilience
and sustainability of communication networks in harsh environments. The combi-
nation of energy harvesting and UAV-based communications offers a compelling
opportunity to improve the efﬁciency, reliability, and resilience of future wireless
networks.



1.1  State of the Art


In a NOMA-based ISTN, wide coverage for ground users is achieved through efﬁ-
cient bandwidth utilization using power domain multiple access [8]. In a two-user
NOMA-based ISTN, deep fading in the satellite-to-weak user link can lead to severe
outage conditions. To address this, suitable relays can be deployed, and maximal
ratio combining at the weak user proves effective [9]. While the relaying protocol
can be either amplify and forward (AF) or decode and forward (DF), the DF protocol
is preferable for its improved outage performance [9]. Studies have used terres-
trial relays with DF relaying protocols to enhance outage probability in hybrid
satellite-terrestrial networks transmitting satellite signals to terrestrial users via relays
[10, 11].
   In the context of NOMA-based ISTN with imperfect CSI, AF relaying has been
explored, and a power allocation algorithm proposed for outage minimization [11].
The application of AF-relaying protocol in NOMA-based heterogeneous satellite
terrestrial relay networks (HSTRN) has also been investigated [12]. In another study,
multiple terrestrial relays with partial relay selection have been employed in a decode
and forward cooperative NOMA-based ISTN with imperfect CSI, achieving coverage
enhancement [13]. A multi-antenna relay with a novel DF relaying protocol has been
considered to improve outage conditions in a two-user NOMA-based HSTRN [14].
  NOMA extends its application to cognitive hybrid satellite-terrestrial networks for
multi-user access and resource sharing [15, 16]. In a speciﬁc HSTRN scenario, AF
relaying in a cognitive radio overlay relay network has been used when the destination
lacks a direct link with the satellite source due to heavy shadowing [15]. Challenges
arise when the satellite shares its spectrum with small base stations, leading to co-
channel interference and degraded system performance [16]. Similarly, small cell
transmission under interference constraints with macro-cell users has been explored
[17].
   In scenarios where a terrestrial relay may not be feasible, UAVs serve as relay
nodes to reach hard-to-reach or hazardous areas. A hybrid satellite-UAV network with
DF relaying, based on NOMA, has been analyzed, demonstrating superior perfor-
mance compared to orthogonal multiple access schemes [18]. The potential of UAV
communication in speciﬁc applications like delivery, rescue, emergency services,

--- Page 382 ---
382                                                                    R. Tukaria et al.

and disaster management has led to ongoing research on integrating terrestrial and
satellite networks with UAVs [19]. Energy harvesting has emerged as a promising
solution to address the energy constraints in wireless communication systems [20].
Particularly in ISTNs, where seamless connectivity and reliable communication are
paramount, energy harvesting technologies offer the potential to enhance system
sustainability and resilience [21]. The major contributions of the paper are as follows:

•  In this paper, a UAV-based AF relaying network is used which serves two users
   based on the NOMA principle. The UAV relays information from the satellite
   to ground users. Existing literatures consider AF relaying from a terrestrial relay
  node [13], which often faces shadowed fading and dearth of the line of sight path.
  On using a UAV as a relay node, the satellite ﬁnds a direct transmission link
  from the satellite to the relay and hence the information delivery to the users is
   augmented.
•  In this paper, it is assumed that the UAV is in need of continuous power replenish-
  ment which is difﬁcult to be accomplished manually. Hence, this paper proposes
   energy harvesting at the UAV node. Energy is harvested from the transmitted RF
   signal from the satellite which is also the information signal.
• A rigorous analysis of the system performance has been presented in this paper
  by considering various system parameter dependence. Outage probability and
   throughput analysis has been considered as the performance parameters.

  The rest of the paper is organized as follows: In Sect. 1, the introduction along
with the literature survey and major contributions of the paper have been highlighted.
In Sect. 2, the system model and the channel models have been discussed. A hint of
energy harvesting has also been presented here. In Sect. 3, a discussion on the results
obtained is presented while the conclusion is presented in Sect. 4.



2  System Model and Channel Models


The system architecture proposed in Fig. 1 comprises a Low Earth Orbit (LEO)
satellite (S), an aerial relay node (U), and two terrestrial NOMA users, D1 and D2.
The satellite uses the UAV relay node to transmit a superposed signal to both users. A
direct link is established between the satellite and the near user D2, while the far user
D1 does not have a direct connection due to potential obstructions or severe large-
scale fading. Each node in the system has a single antenna, and the links between
the UAV and the ground users are characterized by Rayleigh fading. Imperfect CSI
is assumed for all links, with the S-U link exhibiting a Shadowed Rician fading
distribution. Operating in a half-duplex mode, nodes are constrained to either send
or receive data at a given time. The UAV relay node remains in a hovering mode to
ensure a consistent communication link between the satellite and the ground users.
The allocated bandwidth is intelligently divided into two orthogonal sub-bands: one
for the distant user D1 and another for the close user D2. The integration of energy
harvesting in the UAV is noteworthy. The harvested energy plays a pivotal role in

--- Page 383 ---
Energy Harvesting in a NOMA-Based Integrated …                                  383





Fig. 1 System model


subsequent power allocation phases. Power allocation coefﬁcients are determined
based on the channel conditions of each user. The energy harvested by the UAV
bolsters the power allocation for enhanced performance. This strategic approach
compensates for the diminished link quality between the UAV and the distant user
D1. The unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) maintains a constant altitude, denoted by h,
above the ground. This ensures stability in communication scenarios and facilitates
the intricate dynamics of the proposed system.

outage probability and throughput measurements as the performance metrics. Various
parameters of the system have been taken into account to thoroughly verify the
consistency and reliability of the network performance. Some of the results obtained
have been discussed here to prove the superiority of the proposed system setup.

Fig. 2  Overall outage probability versus SNR in dB with varying μ (imperfect CSI)


   In Fig. 2, the overall outage probability of the system has been illustrated with
varying SNR for typical values of the channel estimation error μ. As can be observed
from the results shown, the outage probability improves with increasing SNR.
However the imperfection in the channel estimation affects the outage performance.
Higher the estimation error, greater is the probability of system facing an outage
condition. For example, at SNR of 10 dB, the outage probability is as low as 10−4
for CSI estimation error of μ = 0.001, whereas it increases to 2 × 10−3 for μ =
0.002 and 5 × 10−4 for μ = 0.003. Hence, the CSI knowledge at the transmitter and
receiver ends is very important to have low system outage. In this simulation, the
overall outage can be deﬁned as the condition where either of the users (far user or
near user) faces and outage condition due to low SINR.
   In Fig. 3, the outage probability dependence on the energy conversion efﬁciency
parameter η of the energy harvesting unit has been illustrated. As can be seen from
the ﬁgure, the outage probability decreases with increase in the value of η. While the
far user demonstrates an increased outage probability under both SNR conditions,
due to the absence of the direct link for the far user, the outage probability decreases
with increase in the SNR value. A typical value of η = 0.9 has been considered in
the remaining simulations, indication 90% conversion efﬁciency.
   In this paper, the time-splitting protocol has been used and the fraction of time the
energy is harvested is indicated by the parameter τ. As the value of τ increases, the
energy harvested is more and that results in the decrease in the outage probability.
However, if τ is too high, there shall be limited time for actual signal transmission
and that can lead to loss of information or decrease in the actual data rate of the
system. The outage probability variation with τ has been shown in Fig. 4.
  Our investigation involved a thorough examination of the relationship between
throughput and near user target rate in Fig. 5, including three different sets of curves
with different far user target rates (0.5, 1 and 3). As expected, an increase in the near

user target rate corresponded to a signiﬁcant reduction in the probability of failure
and a consistent increase in throughput.
   This alignment with theoretical expectations reinforced the positive impact of
higher target rates on communication reliability and data transfer efﬁciency. Notably,
an unexpected drop in throughput was observed within the target rate range of 6–8,
which warrants further investigation. In addition, analysis of three sets of curves,
each associated with different far user target rates, highlighted a consistent positive

5  Conclusion


In this study, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of NOMA-enabled energy
harvesting in an ISTN with UAV AF relay, considering the impact of imperfect
CSI. The study covered various aspects of system performance and provided key
insights. The overall outage probability, shown in Fig. 2, improved with increasing
SNR, highlighting the importance of high SNR in reducing outage. However, the
presence of imperfect CSI affected the outage performance, emphasizing the key
role of accurate channel estimation for low system outage. Figure 3 explores the
dependence of outage probability on the energy conversion efﬁciency parameter
(normaleta), showing a decrease in outage probability as increases. Notably, the far user
showed a higher outage probability in both SNR conditions due to the lack of a direct
link, highlighting the importance of efﬁcient energy harvesting. The investigation
further explored the impact of the time-splitting protocol parameter   (normaltau), on outage
probability, revealing a delicate balance between energy harvesting and actual signal
transmission.
  Our investigation extended to the relationship between throughput and near-user
target rate, yielding interesting results as illustrated in Fig. 5. As expected, higher
near-user target rates correlated with a signiﬁcant reduction in the probability of
failure and a consistent increase in throughput, in line with theoretical expecta-
tions. However, an unexpected drop in throughput within the target rate range of 6

--- Page 391 ---
Energy Harvesting in a NOMA-Based Integrated …                                  391

to 8 prompted further investigation. Analysis of three sets of curves, each associ-
ated with different far user target rates, highlighted a positive correlation between
higher target rates and increased throughput. This study provides valuable insights
into the complex dynamics of NOMA-enabled UAVRNs with energy harvesting
in the context of an ISTN. The observed dependencies on SNR, imperfect CSI,
energy conversion efﬁciency and time-splitting protocol parameters provide a basis
for optimized system design. Future research could focus on reﬁning the system
model, addressing the unexpected throughput degradation, and exploring advanced
technologies such as machine learning for adaptive parameter optimization under
dynamic network conditions. This work contributes to the theoretical understanding
and practical considerations for the design and optimization of energy-efﬁcient
communication networks in evolving wireless landscapes.

KDSR: Hybrid Machine-Learning
Solution for Intrusion Detection in Fog

Partha P. Adhikari, Pawan Kumar Mall    , Abhinav Mishra    ,
and Swapnita Srivastava



Abstract Fog computing, that hip cousin of cloud computing, acts as the medi-
ator between cloud data hubs and our gadgets, providing computing, storage, and
network services. It is all about putting smarts right at the edge, speeding up those
on-the-ﬂy decisions, and cutting down the data trafﬁc to the cloud. Both fog and
cloud computing are susceptible to various types of cyber-attacks that could result
in unforeseen losses. For instance, malware, phishing, DoS and DDoS, SQL injec-
tions, and IoT-based attacks attack has the potential to obstruct veriﬁed users. This
research introduces an intrusion classiﬁcation model that harnesses the power of stack
machine-learning model by employing a combination of K-Nearest Neighbors, Deci-
sion Tree, Support Vector Machine, Random Forest (RF). Comparative analysis with
traditional machine-learning approaches highlights the superior performance of our
model. The model is intended for deployment in fog layer responsible for moni-
toring network trafﬁc and detecting cyber-attacks. This implementation ensures the
safeguarding of cloud servers and fog layer devices against malicious users, thus
ensuring uninterrupted service provision to IoT devices.

1  Introduction


Fog computing expands upon the idea of cloud computing, offering computing,
storage, and network services at the interface between cloud data centers and end
devices. Fog computing works in tandem with cloud computing through a control
plane and a data plane [1]. A fog node, comprising computing, storage, and network
capabilities, serves as a device supporting end devices. These nodes, which could
include switches, embedded servers, controllers, routers, and cameras, handle most
time-sensitive data from the end devices for immediate analysis. The response is
rapidly relayed back to the device from the fog node, while a condensed version of
the data and analysis is sent to the cloud for further scrutiny. Figure 1 depicts cloud
computing architecture.
   However, there are vulnerabilities to consider. Malicious users could inundate the
fog node with irrelevant data during communication, potentially executing a denial
of service (DoS) attack that disrupts the availability of both fog nodes and the cloud.
There are two major concerns in cloud architecture cloud security risk and threats.
Figure 2 depicts cloud architecture cloud security risk and threats.

Cloud Security Risks

• Unmanaged Attack Surface:

An unmanaged attack surface represents the overall exposure of your environment.
Embracing microservices can cause a surge in publicly accessible workloads, thereby
expanding the attack surface. Deprived of diligent oversight, this could inadvertently
expose your infrastructure in ways that remain unknown until an attack occurs,
leading to unwelcome late-night calls. The attack surface isn’t limited to overt vulner-
abilities but can also encompass subtle data leaks that pave the way for an attack.





Fig. 1 Cloud architecture

--- Page 395 ---
KDSR: Hybrid Machine-Learning Solution for Intrusion Detection …                   395





Fig. 2 Cloud security risks and security threats


Utilizing the public Internet or cloud inherently exposes an attack surface to potential
threats, even if vital for your business operations.

• Human Error:

According to Gartner, nearly 99% of cloud security failures until 2025 are anticipated
to result from some form of human error. The simplicity of the cloud may lead
users to unknowingly utilize unmonitored APIs, potentially creating vulnerabilities.
Managing human error involves establishing robust controls that guide individuals in
making sound decisions. It is crucial to avoid blaming individuals for errors; instead,
focus on reﬁning processes and implementing safeguards to steer people in the right
direction for improved security.

• Misconﬁguration:

As cloud service offerings expand, so do the complexities of cloud settings. Organi-
zations often use multiple providers, each with its unique default conﬁgurations and
service implementations.

• Data Breaches:

A data breach occurs when sensitive information leaves your control without consent.
Data are a primary target for attackers, and misconﬁgurations or inadequate runtime
protection in the cloud can expose it to theft.

Cloud Security Threats

A threat in the realm of cloud security refers to an assault on your cloud assets
that exploits vulnerabilities. What are four prevalent threats encountered in cloud
security?

• Zero-Day Exploits

Deﬁned as the utilization of vulnerabilities in widely used operating systems and
software that the vendor has not yet patched, zero-day exploits pose a signiﬁcant

--- Page 396 ---
396                                                                                      P. P. Adhikari et al.

risk. Despite robust cloud conﬁgurations, attackers can leverage these vulnerabilities
to inﬁltrate the environment due to the absence of patches.

• Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs)

APTs involve sophisticated, prolonged cyberattacks where intruders stealthily estab-
lish a presence within a network to pilfer sensitive data over an extended period.
Unlike swift attacks, APTs involve sustained presence, moving across workloads to
identify and seize valuable information, often going unnoticed for months.

•  Insider Threats

Internal threats stem from individuals within the organization—typically current or
former employees—with direct access to sensitive data, intellectual property, and
knowledge of business processes. These insiders leverage their access to potentially
carry out cyberattacks.

• Cyberattacks

Cyberattacks are attempts by cybercriminals, hackers, or digital adversaries to
breach a computer network or system with the intent of stealing, altering, exposing,
destroying information. These attacks, including malware, phishing, DoS and DDoS,
SQL injections, and IoT-based attacks, are commonly directed at companies.



2  Related Work


In [2], the author has evaluated the model’s predictive performance using UNSW-
NB15 dataset. After carefully assessing its reliability, a relevant section of the dataset
was chosen, prepped, and structured for training and evaluating neural networks.
Two models with dense layers were created, trained, and adjusted to enhance their
precision. Additionally, LSTM models were introduced and reﬁned in a similar
manner.
   In [3], the author has introduced a framework involving a three-tiered analysis.
Initially, a packet-level analysis is conducted to examine attack patterns. Subse-
quently, a graphical analysis is utilized to identify the attack ﬂow and discern whether
a node functions as an attacker or a victim, while also assigning a severity score
to the node. Finally, Forensics Exploratory Data Analysis (FEDA) is employed
to differentiate the distribution of various features during both attack and normal
scenarios.
   In [4], the author has introduced an ensemble learning approach for constructing
an intrusion detection model. The model outlined in this paper demonstrates superior
overall performance compared to its constituent classiﬁers. This ensemble model is
formed by incorporating lightweight machine-learning models—speciﬁcally, Gaus-
sian naive Bayes, logistic regression, and decision trees—as the base classiﬁers, with
stochastic gradient descent serving as the meta-classiﬁer.

--- Page 397 ---
KDSR: Hybrid Machine-Learning Solution for Intrusion Detection …                   397

   In [5], the author has introduced a two-phase Intrusion Detection System (IDS)
tailored for IoT. Initially, the data are segmented into four categories based on data
types (nominal, integer, binary, and ﬂoat) and classiﬁed using various Naive Bayes
classiﬁer versions. Subsequently, a majority voting system is employed to determine
the ultimate classiﬁcation result. In the second phase, data identiﬁed as behaving
normally or benign in the initial phase undergo classiﬁcation using an unsupervised
elliptic envelope method.
   In [6], the author has introduced an Intrusion Detection System (IDS) utilizing the
UNSW-NB15 dataset. The ﬁndings demonstrate F1-Score and Recall values: 76.1
and 85.3% for the Naive Bayes algorithm, 78.2 and 96.1% for Logistic Regression,
88.3 and 95.4% for the Decision Tree classiﬁer, and 89.3 and 98.5% for the Random
Forest algorithm.
   In [7], the author has introduced two Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) devel-
oped through the application of transfer learning (TL) principles using Convolutional
Neural Networks. The systems are constructed utilizing the VGG19 (Visual Geom-
etry Group 19) and a 152-layer Residual Network (ResNet152). The performance
evaluation of these models is conducted using the UNSW-NB15 intrusion detection
dataset.
   In [8], the author has introduced two distinct stacking machine-learning (ML)
models employing the Extra Tree (ET) Classiﬁer and Mutual Information Gain
feature selection methods to enhance the accuracy of the NIDS (Network Intrusion
Detection System). These models were tested on the UNSW-NB15 packet-based
dataset, encompassing the latest attack types. The experimental ﬁndings demon-
strate that the testing accuracy of the stacking models surpasses that of all individual
models.
   In [9], the author has introduced a hybrid technique and an innovative frame-
work model to tackle the issue at hand. Initially, four distinct sets of features
are extracted from the UNSW-NB15 dataset using random forest feature selection
techniques. Subsequently, in the aim of identifying potentially malicious network
activity, four effective machine-learning algorithms—speciﬁcally logistic regression,
decision tree, K-nearest neighbor, and random forest—are employed. The compar-
ison involves evaluating both the traditional machine-learning algorithm and the
machine-learning algorithm integrated with the synthetic minority oversampling
technique (SMOTE) for both binary and multi-class classiﬁcations. The objective
is to determine the most effective machine-learning approach suitable for detecting
vulnerabilities in IoT systems.



3  Proposed Methodology


In this segment, the detailed explanation of the newly introduced Intrusion Detec-
tion System (IDS) model, speciﬁcally designed for the cloud environment, known
as the KSRD-based ensemble classiﬁer, has been outlined, visually represented in
Fig. 3. Initially, the process involves loading the UNSW-NB15 dataset and conducting

--- Page 398 ---
398                                                                                      P. P. Adhikari et al.

necessary pre-processing steps. To further reﬁne the detection accuracy, a feature
selection process is executed using the ensemble classiﬁcation model, isolating only
the most relevant features. During the testing phase, it successfully identiﬁes various
attack types. Ultimately, the proposed KDSR-based ensemble classiﬁer undergoes
an evaluation using diverse performance metrics and is compared against different
existing models to demonstrate its efﬁciency.

•  Dataset

The UNSW-NB15 computer network security dataset, released in 2015 by Moustafa
and Slay, comprises a total of 2,540,044 instances that represent modern and realistic
normal as well as abnormal (termed as attack) network activities. Figure 4 shows
the count of normal and abnormal trafﬁc and type of attack. These records were
acquired using the IXIA trafﬁc generator through three virtual servers. While two

Fig. 4 Count of normal and abnormal trafﬁc and type of attack

--- Page 399 ---
KDSR: Hybrid Machine-Learning Solution for Intrusion Detection …                   399

servers were conﬁgured to simulate and distribute normal network trafﬁc, the third
server was tasked with generating abnormal network trafﬁc. The dataset includes 49
distinct features obtained from packet-based and ﬂow-based sources using tools such
as Argus and Bro-IDS. Packet-based features are derived from the packet header and
its payload, also referred to as packet data.

• K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN): KNN is a straightforward and intuitive machine-
   learning algorithm used for both classiﬁcation and regression tasks. In KNN,
   predictions for a new data point are made based on the majority class or average
   of its K-nearest neighbors in the feature space.
• Support Vector Machine (SVM): SVM is a powerful supervised learning algo-
   rithm used for classiﬁcation and regression tasks. In classiﬁcation, SVM identiﬁes
   the decision boundary that best separates data into different classes, maximizing
   the margin between classes.
• Random Forest (RF): RF is an ensemble learning method that constructs a
   multitude of decision trees during training and outputs the mode of the classes
   (classiﬁcation) or the mean prediction (regression) of individual trees.
•  Decision Tree (DT): Decision Tree (DT) is a simple yet powerful supervised
   learning algorithm used for both classiﬁcation and regression tasks. It creates a
   tree-like structure where each node represents a feature, each branch represents a
   decision rule, and each leaf node represents the outcome or a decision.
• KDSR-based ensemble classiﬁer: The model’s implementation in the fog layer is
   intended to fulﬁll its vital function of keeping an eye on network trafﬁc and spotting
   any cyberattacks. Its main goal is to protect fog layer devices and cloud servers
  from malevolent users so that IoT devices may receive services continuously
  and without interruption. Ensuring the integrity and functioning of the whole
   Internet of Things ecosystem, strengthening the security architecture, and boosting
   network resilience are all made possible by this implementation. The KDSR model
   utilized UNSW-NB dataset.

model. Accuracy gauges overall correctness, while sensitivity and speciﬁcity focus on
the performance for individual classes, particularly relevant in imbalanced datasets.
The F1-Score combines precision and recall, offering a more balanced evaluation of
the model’s effectiveness in classiﬁcation tasks.
   Accuracy: Accuracy measures the proportion of correctly predicted instances
among the total number of instances [10].

5  Conclusion


Fog computing extends cloud computing, providing computing,  storage, and
networking services between cloud data centers and end devices, enabling faster
real-time decision-making and reducing data sent to the cloud. It enhances IoT
capabilities, minimizing latency and improving service quality in applications like
augmented reality, smart grids, vehicles, and health care. However, both cloud and
fog computing are vulnerable to various attacks, such as malware, phishing, DoS,
DDoS, SQL injections, and IoT-based attacks, potentially disrupting networks and
causing data loss. This research presents an intrusion classiﬁcation model using This
research introduces an intrusion classiﬁcation model that harnesses the power of

--- Page 402 ---
402                                                                                      P. P. Adhikari et al.

stack machine-learning model by employing a combination of K-Nearest Neighbors,
Decision Tree, Support Vector Machine, Random Forest (RF). Comparative analysis
with traditional machine-learning approaches highlights the superior performance
of our model. The integrated KDSR-based ensemble classiﬁer model speciﬁcally
designed for Fog Computing Intrusion Detection achieves a high detection accu-
racy of about 99.76%, when tested on the UNSW-NB15 dataset. Comparative anal-
ysis demonstrates its superior performance over traditional and recent deep learning
approaches. The KDSR-based ensemble classiﬁer model is intended for deployment
in fog layer devices, enhancing security by monitoring network trafﬁc and detecting
attacks, ensuring the uninterrupted service provision of IoT devices on cloud servers
and fog layer devices.

MQFURP: An Overprovision Strategy
Supporting Performance Interference
Management in Cloud


Ayush Pandey, Nirbhay Chandorkar, Kumar Vaibhav, and Ajith K. John





Abstract Cloud computing has become a prevailing trend within the computing
landscape, enabling users to access computational resources on-demand through the
deployment of virtual machines on physical servers. To enhance resource utilization,
cloud administrators commonly employ a technique known as resource overprovi-
sioning, where more virtual resources are allocated to clients than what is physi-
cally available. This practice optimizes the utilization of computing resources and
is frequently adopted by well-known virtual machine monitors (VMMs) like KVM
to maximize the efﬁciency of cloud data centers. Resource overprovisioning strate-
gies are designed to support more virtual machines (VMs) with limited resources.
However, a challenge arises in the form of performance interference among VMs
co-located on the same physical host. This interference issue may be exacerbated by
resource overprovisioning, which aims to accommodate more VMs within the same
physical machine. The performance degradation results from contention over shared
resources among co-hosted VMs, leading to a violation of VM quality-of-service
(QoS) standards. Resource contention occurs when the demand for resources being
shared surpasses the incoming request as a result of co-hosting virtual machines.
In our paper, we introduce a resource overprovisioning strategy called the Multi-
level QoS Framework Using Resource Pooling (MQFURP). This strategy aims to
establish a multi-level QoS environment within a cloud by utilizing Linux control
groups. These control groups enable the differentiation of QoS levels for virtual
machines, allowing for better and more ﬂexible control over resource management.

other virtual machines on the same physical machine.

1  Introduction


Cloud computing has been made possible with the advent of virtualization tech-
nology. It enables sharing of physical resources of a single server into multiple
isolated execution environments called virtual machines (VMs), allowing multiple
applications to run in different isolated environments on a single physical server.
Cloud providers use concept of virtualization for consolidation of more VMs in
the same physical machine [1] to have better resource usage, so that each user in
the cloud efﬁciently utilize the precise amount of computing resources required for
running their applications. This allows cloud providers to dynamically scale resources
on-demand. Thus, along with resource utilization, we have better power saving as
consolidation of VMs leads to reduce the number of physical machines. However,
resource utilization by over provisioning and ensuring VM performance has some
tradeoff among them. While resource wastages can be mitigated through overprovi-
sioning, but sharing of physical resources causes unavoidable performance interfer-
ence among co-located VMs leading to performance drops which result in violation
of VM quality of service (QoS) [2]. Hence, the pivotal element for the effectiveness
of a server consolidation policy lies in the minimization of performance interference
among co-located virtual machines (VMs) in cloud computing platforms.
  Cloud systems traditionally have a single QoS level per physical node system as
shown in Fig. 1, which means single overprovision ratio (i.e., ratio of no. of virtual
resources demanded and no. of physical resources allocated) for whole cloud. As a
result, some nodes may stay underutilized, while others struggle to satisfy the needs
of resource intensive virtual machines. As a result, we require an environment in
which we can differentially prioritize hosted resources and accept extra requests
while minimizing the impact of other virtual machines on the performance of critical
virtual machines.
  The proposed Multi-level QoS Framework Using Resource Pooling (MQFURP)
as shown in Fig. 2 alleviates the challenge of performance interference among co-
located virtual machines within the same physical machine which preserves the QoS
(VM performance) provided to users based on its resource requirement and perfor-
mance need. Rest of the paper is organized as follows. We ﬁrst describe the previous
works related to VM interference management followed by the details of proposed

approach. The experimentation part describes our design and implementation. The
results and conclusion at the end complete the paper.



2  Related Work


Two established approaches for mitigating performance interference in co-hosted
VM environments are worth noting. The ﬁrst approach involves resource partitioning,
which directly allocates shared resources to each VM, preventing multiple VMs from
accessing the same resource concurrently. One example as observed by Zhang et al.

--- Page 406 ---
406                                                                A. Pandey et al.

[3] is that the partitioning of the last-level cache (LLC) of a physical machine (PM) to
prevent last-level cache sharing and contention among virtual machines is done using
page coloring. Each VM hosted on the same PM has its dedicated cache partition.
However, this method has certain drawbacks. While it can provide performance
beneﬁts by reducing interference, statically partitioning resources may not be the
most efﬁcient use of resources, and the overhead from the partitioning mechanism
needs to be considered.
   Similarly, another approach suggested by Podzimek et al. [4] involves the static
partitioning of resources using CPU pinning, which can enhance performance, isola-
tion, and reliability. However, it is essential to weigh the beneﬁts against the draw-
backs, as uneven workload distribution across CPUs can lead to reduced resource
utilization. The second approach is resource reservation, as explored by Nathuji et al.
[5]. In this approach, VM deployment agent has a resource “headroom” to dynam-
ically adjust resource allocation when a VM experiences more resource demands
than anticipated due to interference from co-hosted VMs.
   Nevertheless, determining appropriate “headroom” value often relies on empirical
evaluation, making it challenging to predict resource idleness and interference levels.
Some other strategies as suggested by Rodríguez et al. [6] such as “quiescing” VMs
and “live migration” have been explored to mitigate overload and provide dynamic
quality-of-service (QoS) management. These methods aim to reduce performance
interference by shutting down or migrating VMs on overloaded PMs. However,
quiescing VMs can result in reduced VM uptime.
   In summary, existing approaches have their respective limitations when it comes
to effectively addressing performance interference and QoS issues in overprovi-
sioned VM environments. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel over-
provisioned strategy that combines resource partition and resource reservation. This
approach allocates resources to VMs based on their performance requirements (QoS
needs) without requiring VM migration across physical machines. Our framework,
known as MQFURP, dynamically partitions resources based on user-deﬁned QoS
tolerance levels. This dynamic partitioning helps prevent QoS violations by ensuring
that VMs receive the minimum resources required to maintain their speciﬁed QoS
levels.



3  Proposed Method


In this chapter, we mathematically show, how our proposed framework is able to have
different QoS levels and ensure QoS requirement of different categories of VMs as
compared to traditional framework.

under various scenarios, we have used OpenStack Victoria version [8, 9] snd HPL

have taken a single node of 52 core in which we have created 58 virtual machines
categorized as high-, medium-, and low-priority VMs as shown in Table 3, each
having 2 vCPU cores, and on each, we have run Linpack benchmark which perform,
CPU intensive workload on it and observed the VM CPU core utilization and its
performance. The system speciﬁcation is shown in Tables 1 and 2.

5  Results


As shown in Figs. 3, 4, and 5, in terms of CPU utilization, the proposed framework
MQFURP outperforms traditional single-level QoS per node implementation, with
high-priority virtual machine performance improving from 40 to 90 GFLOPS and
medium-priority virtual machine performance improving from 45 to 49 GFLOPS
in terms of performance where we have 10 high-priority VMs, 16 medium-priority
VMs, and 32 low-priority VMs in single node, i.e., when all levels are overprovi-
sioned fully and resources are completed. For low-priority VMs, the performance
is enough which can help the VM carry out the low CPU intensive tasks. Through
this implementation, we are able to prioritize the need of VM based on its category
which was not possible in single-level QoS framework and provide similar perfor-
mance as we get in CPU pinning based. Our proposed framework outperforms the
CPU pinning-based Multi-level QoS when resources allotted to higher level QoS are
free as shown in Figs. 6, 7, and 8 as more no. of high-priority VMs becomes idle, and
CPU utilization of medium- and low-priority VMs increases in MQFURP which is
much greater than single-level QoS but remains same in CPU pinning-based method
where it leads to resource wastage because of its dynamic partitioning which allows
lower level to take up resources when higher level resources are free (Table 3).

6  Conclusion


Inherent assumption associated with CPU pinning and “head room”-based approach
pose limitation on dynamic optimization of utility of resources. Static premise of
CPU pinning leads to underutilization during idleness of critical VMs. While live
migration presents an internode optimization, MQFURP provides a strategy for
efﬁcient and dynamic intra-node resource utilization. Experiments and simulations
using MQFURP clearly indicate the increase in performance over existing strategies.
MQFURP is as easy to implement, pluggable solution based on Linux control group
which fulﬁlls the fundamental mandate of cloud systems.

Optimization of Computational
Efﬁciency of GP2U-Accelerated Grid
Applications on Non-dedicated Desktop
Grids: A Speed-Up Factor Analysis



Subrata Sinha



Abstract Phenomenal growth in the ﬁeld of biology has motivated computer science
to scale up high-performance computing (HPC) frameworks to cater the ever-growing
demand of today’s biologists. High cost of HPC hinders the progress of study in ﬁnan-
cially weak research teams, so non-dedicated desktop grid is makeshift arrangement
for such research groups, in which there is a set of existing desktop computers.
Gaining maximum possible performance out of such non-dedicated desktop grid is
a challenge. In this paper, an attempt has been made to gain maximum speed-up
of grid-enabled application deployed in a non-dedicated desktop grid. The grid-
enabled application developed has been GPU accelerated, and load balancing algo-
rithms’ performance parameters have been optimized along with node provisioning
resulting an overall speed-up of 16.01 with eight nodes only.

Keywords Grid-enabled application · Load balancing · Node provisioning ·
GP2U acceleration



1  Introduction


Biology’s immense complexity challenges our understanding  [1]. While fully
unlocking its secrets and modeling life remains a distant goal, there is hope for
progress in creating precise models and simulating organisms [2]. Building these
models requires rapid analysis of vast biological data [3] and has spurred various
computational approaches [4]. To meet the growing needs of biologists, computer
science has elevated high-performance computing (HPC) [5], which includes both
hardware upgrades and parallel algorithms [6]. HPC focuses on techniques like
parallel processing, cluster computing, and distributed systems.

   Recently, HPC has gained prominence in bioinformatics research [7, 8], signif-
icantly improving data processing speed. Yet, smaller research groups face chal-
lenges in obtaining HPC solutions due to funding constraints. In such scenarios,
non-dedicated desktop grids or clusters can be created from cost-effective computers,
optimizing performance. However, bioinformatics applications intended for grid
execution must be grid-enabled before deployment.
   This fusion of biology and HPC offers the promise of understanding and simu-
lating life’s complexities, providing a pathway toward more precise biological models
in a ﬁeld where comprehension is a constant pursuit.

(Intel® Pentium® D CPU, 2 cores running at 2.89 GHz), GPU (Intel GMA 950 with
4 Execution Units at 0.2 GHz), Memory—512 MB. Node 8: CPU (Intel® Pentium®
4 CPU, 2 cores running at 2.66 GHz), GPU (Intel GMA 900 with 8 Execution Units
at 0.4 GHz), Memory—512 MB.
  Communication Hardware: Interconnection Network: Utilizing Cat 5 cables with
Gigabit Ethernet running at 1000Mbps speed, facilitated by a D-Link 24-Port Switch
supporting 10/100/1000 conﬁgurations.
   Softwares and Libraries: Grid Middleware: JPPF 5.0.5; Java Development Toolkit
JDK 1.8; Aparapi Library [9]; GPU-Z [10].
   Protein structure: 10,842 protein structures derived from RCSB.

3  Method


Development  of  GP2U-Accelerated  Grid-Enabled  Application:  The GP2U-
Accelerated Grid-Enabled Application (design shown in Fig. 1) [11, 12] needs the
following packages: java.util, com.amd.aparapi, com.amd.aparapi,org.jppf.client,
org.jppf.node.protocol,org.jppf.node.protocol, and pBio library [13]. The applica-
tion consists of (a) GridEnabledApplication class which is main class of the entire
application, (b) ProtTask class, (c) pPeptideProperties_CPU class which executes
the task on CPU of grid nodes, by distributing the task among multiple cores of
CPU, (d) pPeptideProperties_CPU_GPU class which extends from the class Kernel,
which distributes the task in CPU and GPU of grid nodes. The GPU computation
in the application is managed through the Aparapi library [9], designed to offer
Java bindings for OpenCL [14]. When the grid-enabled application dispatches a
JPPF job containing one or multiple tasks to run on a GPU, these tasks consist of
code that adheres to Aparapi standards. At runtime, the bytecode undergoes intro-
spection to produce OpenCL [14] code. This resulting code is then compiled and
executed on an available OpenCL device. Additional conﬁguration adjustments are
necessary within the JPPF nodes. Speciﬁcally, since the Aparapi library relies on a
native library, the inclusion of the “aparapi.jar” ﬁle directly into the node’s classpath
becomes imperative.
   Performance Optimization: We have optimized performance of the grid by perfor-
mance parameter adjustments on various load balancing algorithms available in JPPF,
i.e., Manual, Autotuned, Nodethreads, Proportional, and Reinforcement learning
algorithms. For Autotuned, we have tested performance of grid application by adjust-
ment of samplesToAnalyse parameter from 50 to 500 with an increment of 50. For





Fig. 1 UML class diagram of GP2U-accelerated grid-enabled application

--- Page 420 ---
420                                                                                     S. Sinha

Nodethreads algorithm, we have tested performance of grid application with thread
conﬁgurations spanning from a minimum of 2, advancing to 4, then 6, 8, and a
maximum of 10 per grid node. For Proportional algorithm, we have adjusted perfor-
mance cache size from 100 to 500 with an increment of 100 for each value of
proportionality factor from 0 to 3 with an increment of 0.25. For Reinforcement
algorithm, we have adjusted performance variation threshold from 0, 0.001(default),
0.01, 0.1, 1, and 10 for each value of performance cache size from 1000 to 5000
with an increment of 1000. The performance of grid has been measured, and on the
best conﬁguration of load balancing algorithm, node provisioning has been done to
obtain even better performance.
   Performance Evaluation: We have submitted 10,824 protein structure analysis
jobs from a client (gc) directed to our grid server (gs). Upon job completion, we
meticulously recorded the overall job execution time (ΘTik) using the JPPF Admin
UI. Throughout the execution, we documented various network communication over-
heads: Lgsgk (delivery time from grid server gs to grid node gk), Lgkgs (task result
delivery time from grid node gk to server gs), Lgcgs (job submission time from client
to grid server gs), and Lgsgc (result delivery from server gs to client gc) for each iter-
ation of the grid-enabled application. The value /\L was computed as the maximum
of (Lgsgk + Lgkgs + ΘTik), and ΘES (job execution time on the grid) was calculated
as (Lgcgs + Lgsgc + /\L). Additionally, we recorded ΘE1, denoting the time required
to execute a job on a single processing unit. Finally, the speed-up factor (S), derived
from Amdahl’s law [15], was computed as S = ΘE1/ΘES, representing the ratio of
execution times for the single unit job to the grid-executed job [15].
   Monitoring CPU and GPU Load: The grid-enabled application (CPU only) and
GP2U-accelerated grid-enabled application (CPU + GPU) were executed on the
grid, and CPU load (%) has been measured by OpenHardWare Monitor [16] and
GPU Load (%) has been measured by GPU-Z [10] for the entire execution period of
the application.



4  Results


GP2U-accelerated grid-enabled application has been developed using Java which can
distribute the task between both CPU and GPU. The application processed 10,842
protein structures and was executed on a single node, and it produces the desired result
in 124,862,102 ms, i.e., 34.68 h. The same application was then made grid enabled
and deployed in a grid of various dimensions (2, 4, 6, and 8) and the execution
time in grid dimension 8 was found to be 17,246,146.69 ms, i.e., 4.79 h; hence, a
speed-up factor of 7.24 (approx..) has been achieved, which is quite satisfactory in
consideration with a 8-node grid.
  As additional processing nodes join, the anticipation for increased speed-up
grows. Yet, in practice, several critical factors inﬂuence this outcome. The deli-
cate equilibrium between communication overhead (client to server, server to node,
node to server, and server to client) and the effectiveness of job distribution and

--- Page 421 ---
Optimization of Computational Efﬁciency of GP2U-Accelerated Grid …                 421

result collection signiﬁcantly impact performance. Furthermore, considerations such
as job failure probability and the system’s recovery capability place a constraint,
preventing the speed-up factor from surpassing 8. In this regard, we must note that
un-optimized grid (with a static load balancing algorithm) distributes equal compu-
tational load in all nodes irrespective of their capability and availability. So in an
un-optimized grid we observed that speed-up ≤  grid dimension; ∀ grid dimen-
sion. We have optimized the rest of the load balancing algorithms, i.e., Autotuned,
Nodethread, Proportional, and Reinforcement Learning algorithms by adjustment
of various performance parameters like number of threads, performance cache size,
PVT, proportionality factor, MinimumSamplesToAnalyse.
  The speed-up of grid-enabled application using Autotuned load balancing was
found to be 2.75, 5.49, 7.31, and 10.96 in grid dimensions 2, 4, 6, and 8, respec-
tively. These results (shown in Fig. 2) are quite motivating with respect to static and
Nodethread load balancing algorithm as we achieved speed-up ≥ Grid Dimension;
∀ Grid Dimension but only for SamplesToAnalyse = 400; ∀ Grid Dimension.
  The speed-up of grid-enabled application using Nodethread load balancing was
found to be 3.56 (with 6/10 threads), 6.99 (with 8/10 threads), 7.88 (with 8/10
threads), and 9.89 (with 10/10 threads) in grid dimensions 2, 4, 6, and 8, respec-
tively. These results (shown in Fig. 3) are quite motivating with respect to static load
balancing algorithm as for the ﬁrst time we achieved speed-up ≥ Grid Dimension;
∀ Grid Dimension but only for thread count ≥ 6; ∀ Grid Dimension.
  The speed-up of grid-enabled application using proportional load balancing was
found to be 5.53, 9.19, 10.93, and 10.99 in grid dimensions 2, 4, 6, and 8, respectively.
The result (shown in Fig. 4) shows that a Autotuned performs better in lower grid

5  Conclusion


Non-dedicated desktop grids can provide a cheaper solution for researchers, but for a
more limited set of applications. Assuming that the computers making up a desktop
grid are already paid for, they can open up computational research to more scientists
at an even lower cost. However, mere construction of non-dedicated desktop grid
does not solve the purpose of computation, and we need to develop grid-enabled
application to solve a given problem. The application which is made grid enabled
may not achieve substantial performance out of the grid unless the grid is performance
optimized and the grid-enabled application made capable of exploiting the capability
underlying hardware resources of nodes. A grid-enabled application if deployed in
an un-optimized grid has resulted in horrible speed-up factor like 7.24, whereas
in optimized grid, same application has shown speed-up factor of 12.82 (without
node provisioning) and 13.88 (with node provisioning). The performance of the
grid-enabled application can further be enhanced if the application can be made
GPU accelerated. GPU-accelerated grid-enabled application has shown much better
speed-up, i.e., 15.90 (without node provisioning) and 16.01(with node provisioning).
Hence, it can be concluded with a remark that researchers with limited resource can
set up low-cost high-performance computing infrastructure and can achieve much
better performance in terms of speed-up factor with parameter optimization of load
balancing algorithm, node provisioning, and GP2U acceleration.

GPT Vision Meets Taxonomy:
A Comprehensive Evaluation
for Biological Image Classiﬁcation


Angsuman Das and Bhabana Das





Abstract This study assesses the proﬁciency of GPT Vision, a multimodal language
model, in the classiﬁcation of biological images across taxonomic ranks. Utilizing a
meticulously curated dataset from A–Z Animals, Wikipedia, and eLife Sciences, the
model’s performance was analyzed at various levels from Phylum to Species. Our
quantitative analysis, supported by Python libraries like Pandas, Matplotlib, Seaborn,
SciPy, and Statsmodels, revealed a trend of high accuracy at broader taxonomic
categories, with a notable decrease at more speciﬁc levels. The overall accuracy
peaked at 78.95% for Phylum but dropped to 11.58% for Species. Misclassiﬁcation
and null value analyses were conducted, indicating both the strengths of GPT Vision
in identifying certain taxa and its limitations, especially at narrower taxonomic levels.
The ﬁndings underscore the potential of GPT Vision in biological classiﬁcation
while highlighting the necessity for further model reﬁnement, particularly for lower
taxonomic ranks.

Keywords GPT4 · GPT vision · Biological image classiﬁcation



1  Introduction


1.1  Background on Image Classiﬁcation in Biology


Image classiﬁcation plays a pivotal role in a multitude of disciplines within the
ﬁeld of biology, encompassing genomics, computational biology, medical diagnoses,
drug discovery, biodiversity conservation, and ecological studies [1–3]. Automated,
image-based high-content screening serves as an essential tool for exploration in

the realm of biological science [4]. When it comes to the analysis of biological
images, the classiﬁcation of datasets is frequently executed employing specialized
techniques such as deep learning and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) [5].
These techniques have demonstrated remarkable progress in the realm of image-
based classiﬁcation, recognition, and detection tasks [6]. Furthermore, the utilization
of parallel neural networks and rule-based genetic algorithms has been investigated
for the purpose of image classiﬁcation in biology “(Binary Image Classiﬁcation using
Parallel Neural Networks”, 2020; Tseng et al. 2008).
  To achieve precise image classiﬁcation, a variety of methodologies and character-
istics are employed. For example, the proposal of combining multiple characteristics
and utilizing random subspace classiﬁer ensembles has been made for the purpose
of phenotype recognition [6]. Moreover, the utilization of indicator kriging error
comparison and texture analysis has been implemented to identify speciﬁc regions
within intricate intracellular spaces [6]. In the domain of stem cell research, image
analysis techniques have been employed to identify tenogenic differentiation using
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) [6]. Furthermore, the assessment of colony
and nuclear morphology has been utilized to evaluate human induced pluripotent
stem cells [8].
   In the context of animal taxonomy, automated image analysis techniques have
proven to be valuable tools for species identiﬁcation and classiﬁcation. These tech-
niques involve image processing and the extraction of relevant features from speci-
mens’ images, followed by the classiﬁcation of these features into correct categories.
By utilizing automated image analysis, scientists can streamline the process of species
identiﬁcation, saving time, and resources [9].
  The emergence of automated recognition algorithms exhibited a considerable
degree of precision in the identiﬁcation of plant species in the geographical region
of Northern Europe. These algorithms take into consideration diverse image char-
acteristics, including plant organs, background composition, and the concentration
of species being analyzed [10]. Furthermore, the quantity of training images acces-
sible for particular species inﬂuences the effectiveness of the automated recognition
algorithm (Pärtel et al. 2021). This clearly exempliﬁes the potential of employing
automated image analysis techniques to accurately discern and categorize various
plant species.



1.2  The Advent of Machine Learning and Its Implications
     for Biological Image Classiﬁcation


The advent of machine learning has had signiﬁcant implications for biological image
classiﬁcation. Machine-learning algorithms have shown great potential in analyzing
large and complex biological data [11]. The application of machine learning to
biological image processing has expanded with the development of deep-learning

--- Page 429 ---
GPT Vision Meets Taxonomy: A Comprehensive Evaluation …                        429

techniques [12]. These techniques have enabled the automated analysis of biolog-
ical images, leading to high-throughput measurement, identiﬁcation, and sorting of
biological entities [13].
   However, there are challenges in applying machine learning to biological image
classiﬁcation. Variations in cell densities and differences in low-level image features
can compromise the reliability of machine-learning methods [14]. Additionally, the
availability of data and the rarity of certain diseases can impede the application of
machine learning in musculoskeletal tumor imaging [15].
   Despite the obstacles, machine learning has garnered signiﬁcant acceptance
in the realm of medical image analysis, speciﬁcally in endeavors such as image
segmentation and classiﬁcation, as stated by Dai et al. [16]. Furthermore, machine
learning algorithms have demonstrated their efﬁcacy in detecting latent pathologies in
medical imaging, surpassing conventional image analysis techniques, as highlighted
by Ayubcha et al. [17].
  The ﬁeld of animal taxonomy has been impacted by the advent of machine
learning. Machine-learning algorithms have been utilized to aid in the classiﬁ-
cation and identiﬁcation of animal species. By extracting features from speciﬁc
image regions, machine-learning algorithms can classify these regions as either
animal or non-animal [18]. This methodology has the potential to streamline the
process of species identiﬁcation and contribute to the overall understanding of animal
taxonomy. Another such example is the app Merlin that speciﬁcally designed for Bird
identiﬁcation and classiﬁcation.



1.3 GPT Vision’s Potential in This Domain


GPT (generative pre-trained transformer) Vision’s integration of vast internet-scale
textual data with image processing capabilities holds considerable promise for
biological image classiﬁcation, particularly in the realm of animal taxonomy. Its
hypothetical advantages in this domain are grounded in the following attributes:
  Deep Contextual Understanding: The extensive scientiﬁc knowledge embedded
in GPT Vision’s training data can be used to provide context for visual features in
biological images, potentially leading to more accurate classiﬁcations [19].
  Advanced Feature Recognition: GPT Vision may excel at identifying subtle,
species-speciﬁc visual cues that are critical for taxonomic classiﬁcation due to
its ability to access and process large datasets of biological imagery and their
accompanying textual information [20].
   Efﬁcient Data Processing: The model’s ability to rapidly analyze large numbers
of images could support high-throughput classiﬁcation tasks, potentially speeding
up taxonomic workﬂows and research.
   Continuous Learning: By utilizing reinforcement learning from human feedback,
GPT Vision could iteratively improve its classiﬁcation accuracy, adapting to new
data and expert corrections over time.

--- Page 430 ---
430                                                              A. Das and B. Das

1.4  Objective of the Study


The primary aim of this investigation is to scrutinize the efﬁcacy of GPT Vision in the
classiﬁcation of biological images across various taxonomic levels. The study sets
out to (1) quantify the model’s accuracy and reliability, (2) understand its precision,
(3) identify the taxonomic ranks at which the model excels or falters, and (4) highlight
the model’s behavior in the face of non-classiﬁable data. This inquiry strives to not
only evaluate GPT Vision’s current capabilities but also to pinpoint areas for potential
enhancement, setting the stage for its application in the broader ﬁeld of biological
research.



2  Materials and Methods


2.1  Dataset Description


The dataset for this study was meticulously curated from a trio of reputable online
sources known for their extensive biological repositories. The primary source was
A–Z Animals (https://a-z-animals.com), a comprehensive database of animal images
spanning a wide array of species. Additional images were sourced from Wikipedia
(https://wikipedia.org), the renowned online encyclopedia that offers a vast collection
of wildlife photography contributed by its global user base. Lastly, eLife Sciences
(https://elifesciences.org) provided high-quality scientiﬁc images, supporting the
dataset with a scholarly perspective.
  Each image in the dataset was tagged with taxonomic information at multiple
levels, ranging from the broadest category of Phylum to the most speciﬁc designation
of Species. This multi-tier classiﬁcation enabled a granular analysis of GPT Vision’s
classiﬁcation capabilities, providing insights into its performance at each hierarchical
level. The categorization process was underpinned by the taxonomic data available on
the source websites, ensuring a scientiﬁcally grounded and accurate representation
of biological diversity.
   Categories and Taxonomic Levels: The dataset encompasses a diverse array
of biological categories, reﬂecting the rich tapestry of life. These categories are
organized according to the universally accepted biological classiﬁcation system,
spanning across several taxonomic levels. The broadest category included is the
Phylum, which groups organisms based on fundamental body plans and structures.
Within each Phylum, the images are further classiﬁed into Classes, Orders, Families,
Genera, and ultimately, Species.
  The Species level, being the most speciﬁc, denotes individual types of organisms
that are capable of interbreeding, while Genus groups together species that are closely
related. Family and Order represent higher levels of common characteristics, and
Class groups together those orders sharing key attributes. The dataset, therefore,

--- Page 431 ---

serves as a hierarchical map of biodiversity, capturing the complexity and nuances
of biological classiﬁcation.
  By leveraging such a structured and comprehensive dataset, the study aims to
dissect the performance of GPT Vision at each of these levels, delivering a thorough
assessment of its classiﬁcatory acumen. This approach not only challenges the model
across a spectrum of complexity but also mirrors the real-world application of such
technology in the ﬁeld of taxonomy and biological research.
  As the GPT vision is available in easy-to-use chat interface inside ChatGPT plus,
we input each image a simple initial prompt: “I will give you some photos return
me with only Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus and Species, if anything is
not know just write NA for that taxon. OK?”.



2.2 GPT Vision Overview


GPT-4 V is a language model developed by OpenAI that incorporates additional
modalities, such as image inputs, into large language models (LLMs). It is viewed
by some as a key frontier in artiﬁcial intelligence research and development. The
model enables users to instruct GPT-4 to analyze image inputs provided by the
user, expanding the impact of language-only systems with novel interfaces and
capabilities.
  The training process for GPT-4 V was completed in 2022 and was the same as
that for GPT-4, which is the technology behind the visual capabilities of GPT-4 V.
The pre-trained model was ﬁrst trained to predict the next word in a document, using
a large dataset of text and image data from the Internet as well as licensed sources of
data. The model architecture is not described in detail by the company (Open AI),
but it is a multimodal language model that possesses the limitations and capabilities
of both text and vision modalities.
   After the pre-training, the model was ﬁne-tuned with additional data using an
algorithm called reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). This algo-
rithm produces outputs that are preferred by human trainers, allowing the model to
learn from human feedback and improve its performance. The system card does not
provide further details on the model architecture and training, but it does describe
the safety evaluations, preparation, and mitigation work done speciﬁcally for image
inputs [19, 20]. Figure 3 explains the whole process of the experiment visually.

3  Results


Our study embarked on a comprehensive evaluation of GPT Vision’s ability to clas-
sify biological images across different taxonomic levels. The results varied across
the taxonomy, with the model exhibiting better performance at broader taxonomic
levels and a decline as the classiﬁcation became more speciﬁc.



3.1  Overall Accuracy Across Taxonomic Levels


To gain a deeper understanding of the model’s strengths and areas for improvement,
we computed analysis. In the presented Fig. 3, the classiﬁcation accuracy of GPT
Vision across different taxonomic levels is meticulously illustrated. Distinctively,
two scenarios are compared: One where null values are incorporated (represented in
blue) and another devoid of them (shown in red). At the broader levels of taxonomy,
such as “Phylum” and “Class”, the accuracy metrics are notably high, and there’s
a minimal disparity between the two scenarios. However, as we delve deeper into
more speciﬁc taxonomic categories like “Order”, “Family”, “Genus”, and “Species”,
a pronounced variability between the two conditions becomes evident. Particularly at
the “Order” and “Genus” levels, the inclusion of null values appears to signiﬁcantly
diminish classiﬁcation accuracy. Our results indicated that the model’s performance,
as measured by these metrics, mirrors the trend observed in the accuracy assessment,
with higher scores at the Phylum level and a decline at more speciﬁc classiﬁcations.

the domains that might beneﬁt from more specialized training or ﬁne-tuning.

even there in the whole sample (Figs. 6 and 7).

4  Discussion

4.1  Interpretation of the Results


The analysis of GPT Vision’s performance in biological image classiﬁcation has
yielded insights with signiﬁcant implications for both the model’s application and
the broader ﬁeld of machine learning in taxonomy. As observed in the results, the
model’s prediction accuracy diminishes as the taxonomic classiﬁcation becomes
more granular, with a notable decrease from broader categories such as Phylum to the
more speciﬁc category of Species. This trend suggests that while GPT Vision is adept
at discerning distinct, high-level biological features, its capability to differentiate ﬁner
taxonomic details is less robust.
   However, an intriguing pattern emerges when null predictions—instances where
GPT Vision abstained from making a prediction—are excluded from the analysis. The
exclusion of these null values results in a marked increase in accuracy across the lower
taxonomic levels. This observation points to a sophisticated aspect of the model’s
design; it appears that GPT Vision, likely due to the extensive and varied textual
context inherent in its training, possesses an inherent caution in its predictive process.
Rather than risking incorrect classiﬁcations, the model opts to withhold judgment
when the available visual data does not sufﬁce for a high-conﬁdence prediction.

--- Page 437 ---
GPT Vision Meets Taxonomy: A Comprehensive Evaluation …                        437





Fig. 6  Confusion matric of phylum level


   This behavior may reﬂect a form of “artiﬁcial intuition”, akin to a seasoned
taxonomist who recognizes the limits of their expertise under conditions of uncer-
tainty. From an academic standpoint, this self-regulating mechanism within GPT
Vision’s algorithm is a notable departure from the often-criticized “black box” nature
of many machine learning models. It opens avenues for discussion on the integration
of such models in scientiﬁc workﬂows, where the cost of misclassiﬁcation can be
high.
   Further discussions could explore the implications of these ﬁndings for the deploy-
ment of machine learning models in critical ﬁelds. The self-awareness exhibited by
GPT Vision in “knowing what it doesn’t know” could lead to more reliable appli-
cations of AI in biological research and conservation efforts. It also raises questions
about the training process for such models and the potential for incorporating explicit
measures of uncertainty or conﬁdence in their outputs.
   Moreover, the ﬁndings stimulate a conversation about the balance between the
breadth and depth of knowledge in machine learning applications. As machine
learning continues to intersect with diverse domains, the ability of models to gauge
their predictions’ reliability becomes paramount. This study’s insights into GPT

Vision’s performance across taxonomic levels offer a valuable case study for such
interdisciplinary dialogues.



4.2  Implications for Biological Research and Taxonomy


The potential of GPT Vision to revolutionize biological research through future
enhancements is substantial. As the model’s predictive accuracy at ﬁner taxonomic
levels improves, it could become an invaluable tool for rapid species identiﬁca-
tion, aiding in biodiversity monitoring and ecological studies. The model’s cautious
approach to classiﬁcation, opting to provide no prediction rather than an incorrect one,
sets a precedent for developing AI with a built-in safeguard against the propagation
of errors.
   Future iterations of GPT Vision could beneﬁt from augmented datasets that
include more varied and detailed images, coupled with robust metadata, enhancing
the model’s learning. Integrating feedback loops from taxonomic experts can reﬁne

--- Page 439 ---
GPT Vision Meets Taxonomy: A Comprehensive Evaluation …                        439

its algorithms, enabling the model to approach the discernment of a seasoned biol-
ogist. With these advancements, GPT Vision may offer unprecedented support
in cataloguing species, tracking invasive populations, and monitoring changes in
biodiversity.
  The  implications  for conservation biology  are  particularly promising. By
automating the identiﬁcation process, researchers can allocate more time to conserva-
tion efforts rather than the manual cataloguing of species. This increase in efﬁciency
and accuracy, especially in remote or highly biodiverse regions, could accelerate
conservation strategies and policymaking, ultimately contributing to the preservation
of ecosystems on a global scale.



4.3  Limitations of the Study


This study, while expansive in its scope, is not without limitations. The dataset, though
diverse, is limited to animal images and thus, the ﬁndings may not be entirely gener-
alizable to plant species or microorganisms, which exhibit different visual character-
istics and classiﬁcation challenges. Additionally, the comparison with other models
was beyond the ambit of this research, presenting an opportunity for future studies
to benchmark GPT Vision against existing classiﬁcation algorithms. The current
assessment focused solely on GPT Vision’s capabilities and did not explore a multi-
model or ensemble approach that might yield improved results. These limitations
underscore areas for further research, suggesting a broader application potential and
inviting comparative analyses with alternative machine learning solutions.



5  Conclusion


5.1  Key Findings


GPT Vision demonstrates high accuracy in classifying images at broader taxo-
nomic levels, particularly at the Phylum level, indicating robust recognition of
general biological features. Accuracy declines at ﬁner taxonomic resolutions, with
the Species level showing the lowest accuracy, suggesting challenges in distin-
guishing subtle, species-speciﬁc traits. Excluding null predictions reveals an increase
in accuracy, highlighting the model’s ability to self-regulate and avoid overconﬁdent,
potentially incorrect classiﬁcations. The model’s conservative approach in predic-
tion mirrors the caution of expert taxonomists, indicating a sophisticated level of
“artiﬁcial intuition” about its knowledge boundaries. Misclassiﬁcation patterns, as
visualized through confusion matrix, suggest speciﬁc areas where GPT Vision may
require additional training or reﬁnement. The study identiﬁes a potential “artiﬁcial
intuition” in GPT Vision’s design, where it demonstrates a form of self-awareness in

--- Page 440 ---
440                                                              A. Das and B. Das

its predictive capabilities, a promising feature for AI applications in scientiﬁc ﬁelds.
The research outlines the promise of GPT Vision’s future application in biolog-
ical research, with possible expansions into plant and microbial taxonomy, and its
potential role in enhancing biodiversity monitoring and conservation strategies.



5.2  Recommendations for Further Research


Based on the study’s ﬁndings and limitations, here are several recommendations for
future research:

1.  Algorithm Benchmarking: Benchmark GPT Vision against other state-of-the-
    art image classiﬁcation algorithms, including convolutional neural networks
   (CNNs) and other machine-learning models, to contextualize its performance
    in the broader ﬁeld of computer vision.
2.  Artiﬁcial Intuition Exploration: Research the underlying mechanisms that enable
    the model’s “artiﬁcial intuition”, and how this can be further developed or reﬁned
    to enhance decision-making in AI applications.
3.  Cross-Domain Generalization Studies: Conduct research to test and improve
  GPT Vision’s classiﬁcation capabilities across different domains, such as plant
    species and microorganisms, to assess the model’s generalizability beyond animal
    imagery.
4.  Ensemble and Multi-Model Approaches: Explore the use of ensemble methods
    that combine GPT Vision’s output with other models to see if accuracy at ﬁner
   taxonomic levels can be improved. Investigate multi-model approaches that inte-
    grate GPT Vision with traditional ecological and genetic data to create a more
    holistic species identiﬁcation system.
5.  Interactive AI for Taxonomy: Develop interactive AI tools that can work along-
    side taxonomists, allowing for a human-in-the-loop approach to reﬁne the
   model’s predictions based on expert feedback.
6.  Null Prediction Analysis: Analyze the circumstances and features associated
   with null predictions to better understand when and why the model chooses not
    to make a prediction, which could lead to more precise model tuning.
7.  Understanding Misclassiﬁcation: Undertake a thorough examination of misclas-
    siﬁcation patterns to identify any systematic biases or knowledge gaps in the
   model, which could inform targeted data augmentation and training strategies.

Nanostructured Sensors for Pesticide
Detection in Tea


Baharul Islam, Devabrata Sarmah, Rishu Jha, and Sunandan Baruah





Abstract Tea is a widely consumed beverage around the world. After China, India
is the world’s second-largest producer of tea. Assam in north east India contributes
around 52% of total output of India’s tea production. Pesticides are frequently used
in tea gardens to protect tea plants from different insects and mites and to increase
yield. Quinalphos, Fenazaquin, Thiamethoxam, and Emamectin Benzoate are some
insecticides often used in Assam tea gardens. To maintain the safety of human life,
the tea estates need to follow the maximum pesticide levels given by the Food Safety
and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI). Pesticide levels that exceed the permitted
range can cause different health issues. Detecting pesticide residue on tea leaves
before processing can help tea companies reduce losses. There are many methods for
detecting pesticides in processed tea. However, the application of nanotechnology-
based sensors offers a possibility for pre-processing detection. The goal of this review
is to provide insight into nanomaterial-based sensors and techniques for pesticide
determination from tea leaves.
