1  Introduction


Pesticides are harmful substances that are purposefully released into the environment
to eradicate living things, and they include herbicides, insecticides, fungicides, and
rodenticides [1]. Pesticide residue detection in agricultural goods is critical to guar-
anteeing food safety and consumer health [2]. Pesticides are commonly employed in
agricultural practices to protect crops from pests, illnesses, and weeds. However the
presence of pesticide residues above allowed levels might pose signiﬁcant dangers
to human health and the environment [3]. The demand for sensitive, dependable, and
quick pesticide detection systems has resulted in considerable advances in sensor
technology [3]. Owing to their unique qualities and characteristics at the nanoscale,
nanostructured sensors have emerged as a viable pesticide detection option [4]. These
nanomaterial-based sensors have signiﬁcant beneﬁts over standard detection methods
[5]. They have increased sensitivity, selectivity, and the ability to monitor in real time
making them ideal for detecting low quantities of pesticides in a variety of agricultural
goods including tea [3, 6, 7].
   Tea is produced from the Camellia sinensis plant and is one of the most widely
consumed beverages in world [8, 9]. Tea gardens use pesticides frequently to protect
tea plants from pests and diseases. As a result, the tea business has issues in assuring
the safety and quality of tea products [10, 11]. Excessive pesticide residues in tea
can harm human health and ruin the reputation of tea gardens. As a result, efﬁcient
pesticide detection procedures are critical for tea sector stakeholders such as growers,
regulators, and consumers [12].
   Traditional pesticide analysis methods in tea sometimes entail time-consuming
laboratory processes that need specialized equipment and expertise [13, 14]. These
approaches may not be viable for routine pesticide monitoring or detection prior to
processing tea leaves, posing hazards and economic losses to tea farmers. Nanos-
tructured sensors provide a promising alternative by providing sensitive and quick
detection capabilities, allowing for the identiﬁcation of pesticide residues in tea leaves
prior to processing [6, 15].
   This review paper focuses on the use of nanostructured sensors to detect pesticides
in the tea business. It intends to present an overview of the improvements, obsta-
cles, and possible beneﬁts of using nanostructured sensors in tea manufacturing
to ensure food safety and quality assurance. The article will go through the many
types of nanostructures utilized in pesticide detection, as well as the manufacturing
procedures and functionalization strategies used to improve detection sensitivity and
selectivity.
  The review will also dig into the particular uses of nanostructured sensors in the
tea sector, addressing the detection of regularly used pesticides as well as the issues
involved with detecting numerous residues at the same time. It will also emphasize
the potential beneﬁts of nanostructured sensors, such as improved food safety, greater
quality assurance, and higher customer trust in tea products.

  The tea industry can detect and reduce potential dangers connected with pesticide
residues at an early stage by using nanostructured sensors for pesticide detection [16].
This guarantees the security and excellence of tea goods while also enhancing the
longevity and standing of the tea business. The fusion of nanostructured sensors
with cutting-edge innovations like Internet of Things (IoT) platforms and data
analytics creates new opportunities for real-time monitoring and simpliﬁed detection
procedures.
   Using nanostructured sensors to detect pesticides in the tea sector is a huge step
forward in maintaining food safety and quality assurance [17]. With a focus on

and application of these sensors in tea manufacturing and quality control procedures.



2  Nanomaterials for Chemical Sensors


Due to their distinct characteristics and sensitivity, different kinds of nanomaterials
are utilized in chemical sensors. The following are some examples of frequently
used nanomaterials for chemical sensors: carbon nanotubes (CNTs), graphene,
metal oxide nanoparticles, quantum dots (QDs), metal–organic frameworks (MOFs),
nanowires, nanoporous materials. These are only a few illustrations of nanomate-
rials that are utilized in chemical sensors. The target analyte, intended sensitivity, and
sensor operating circumstances all have a role in the choice of a certain nanomaterial.
   Figure 1 shows the typical working of an electrochemical sensor. This system
consists of a nanotechnology-based pesticide sensor, one data acquisition system and
a data analyzing system. Using one micropipette, the pesticide samples are given to
the sensor. Depending on the type of the pesticide oxidation or reduction happens
with the sensing material and accordingly the conductivity of the sensor changes. As
a result, we get the resistance change at the output of the sensor. The output resistance
change is observed using one data acquisition system and displayed on LCD display.





Fig. 1  Typical working of electrochemical sensor

446                                                                      B. Islam et al.

2.1  Carbon Nanotubes


Chemical sensing is getting a new way because of a new class of nanomaterials
named carbon nanotubes (CNTs) [18]. Due to its unique properties, such as their
large surface area, superior electrical conductivity and chemical resistance, among
others, CNTs have demonstrated tremendous promise in the identiﬁcation and quan-
tiﬁcation of various analytes [19]. Carbon nanotubes in general are cylindrical struc-
tures comprised of carbon atoms organized in a hexagonal lattice [20]. They are
available in a range of diameters and lengths, and they can be single or multi-
walled [21]. These nanostructures have very good mechanical, electrical, and thermal
capabilities, making them excellent for chemical sensing applications. CNT-based
sensors have very good sensitivity and selectivity toward different gases. The large
surface area of CNTs allows for efﬁcient gas adsorption, enabling the detection of low
concentrations of analytes. CNT sensors have been employed to detect gases such
as ammonia, nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide, and volatile organic compounds
(VOCs) [22, 23].
   In addition to gas sensing, CNTs have been utilized in biosensors for the detection
of biomolecules and pathogens. Functionalizing CNT surfaces with speciﬁc receptors
or enzymes enables the selective capture and recognition of target analyzes leading
to highly sensitive biosensing platforms [23]. Applications range from healthcare
diagnostics to environmental monitoring. CNTs possess excellent electrical conduc-
tivity, making them suitable for electrochemical sensing. By integrating CNTs into
electrodes, electrochemical sensors can be developed to detect a wide range of chem-
ical species. CNT-based electrodes have shown enhanced electrocatalytic properties,
enabling efﬁcient electron transfer and improved sensor performance [24]. CNTs
have a lot of potential for chemical sensing to detect the pesticides [25]. However,
there are still some difﬁculties. These difﬁculties are extensive synthesis, regulation
of CNT characteristics, and incorporation into functional sensor systems. To address
these issues and to commercialize CNT-based sensors, efforts are still being made. To
further increase sensitivity and selectivity research is being done on functionalizing
CNTs with certain receptors and creating hybrid nanomaterials. As shown in Fig. 2,
carbon nanotubes are cylindrical in structures and can detect different analytes with
good selectivity.



2.2  Graphene


A very promising nanomaterial for sensing applications is graphene. It is an atomi-
cally thin sheet of carbon atoms. Graphene is the perfect choice for creating sensitive
and adaptable nanosensors due to its remarkable electrical, mechanical, and chemical
capabilities [27].
  Graphene is a two-dimensional honeycomb lattice of carbon atoms. It has emerged
as a potential material for sensing applications [28]. Its outstanding features which

--- Page 446 ---
Nanostructured Sensors for Pesticide Detection in Tea                                447

Fig. 2 Working of CNT as a
chemical sensor [26]





include high electrical conductivity, mechanical robustness, huge surface area, and
sensitivity to environmental changes make it an excellent choice for detecting a
variety of analytes. When the target analyte interacts with the graphene surface then
graphene-based sensors detect changes in electrical conductivity or other physical
characteristics [28]. This interaction may be done by functionalizing or modifying
the surface of graphene, which increases its selectivity and sensitivity to certain
analytes. Graphene has enormous surface area which used for adsorption and inter-
action with target molecules, resulting in increased sensitivity and detection limits
[29]. Further, graphene has strong electrical conductivity, and it enables quick and
real-time monitoring of analyte concentrations.
  Graphene sensors have great capabilities in detecting a wide range of analytes
including gases, chemicals, biomolecules, and environmental pollutants. They can
be used in areas such as environmental monitoring, healthcare, food safety like detec-
tion of pesticide and industrial quality control [30]. The development of graphene
sensors has some issues related to scalability, stability, and integration into existing
systems. Researchers are trying to overcome these problems by investigating inno-
vative production processes, enhancing the stability of graphene-based sensors and
combining them with complementary technologies.
  As a result, graphene-based sensors provide a very promising platform for sensi-
tive, selective, and quick detection of different pesticides. With continued improve-
ments and research, graphene sensors are set to revolutionize sensing technology
specially to detect pesticide, allowing breakthroughs in a wide range of sectors and
applications.



2.3  Metal Oxide Nanoparticles


Metal oxide nanoparticles have emerged as very good sensing materials for different
applications because of their unique characteristics and versatility. These nanopar-
ticles are made up of metal oxides including zinc oxide (ZnO), titanium dioxide
(TiO2), iron oxide (Fe2O3), and others. They have various beneﬁts for development

--- Page 447 ---
448                                                                      B. Islam et al.

of sensors to detect pesticides in agricultural ﬁelds. When target analytes interact
with metal oxide nanoparticles, these particles alter electrical, optical, or catalytic
characteristics [31]. Adsorption, chemical interactions, or changes in the surface
charge of the nanoparticles can all cause this interaction. The utilization of these
modiﬁcations as sensors is made possible by the measurement and correlation of
these changes to the presence or concentration of the analyte.
   Metal oxide nanoparticles have a high surface-to-volume ratio [32]. This results
in a sizable active surface area for analyte interactions. The increased sensitivity
provided by the large surface area of metal oxide nanoparticles, target analytes
at low concentrations can be detected [33]. Metal oxide nanoparticles like ZnO
nanoparticles can be synthesized in different sizes and morphologies offering ﬂexi-
bility in sensor design and optimization [34]. This versatility allows for tailoring the
sensor properties to speciﬁc applications and target analytes. The nanoparticles can
also be functionalized with speciﬁc ligands or receptors to enhance selectivity and
sensitivity. Metal oxide nanoparticles exhibit good stability, enabling their long-term
use as sensing materials. They are resistant to degradation and can withstand harsh
environmental conditions, ensuring reliable and repeatable sensor performance.
  While metal oxide nanoparticles offer tremendous potential in detection of pesti-
cides, challenges still exist in their implementation as sensors. These challenges
include optimizing synthesis techniques to control nanoparticle size and morphology,
improving sensor selectivity toward target analytes, enhancing sensor stability and
developing appropriate signal transduction mechanisms for accurate detection [35].



2.4  Nanowires


Nanoscale wires are used in nanowire sensors, a form of sensor technology to measure
and detect numerous physical and chemical characteristics. The tiny wires used to
make these sensors generally have nanometer scale widths and as a result of their
small size, display special electrical and optical characteristics. These nanowires
sensors’ can be created from a range of substances, including silicon, zinc oxide, or
carbon nanotubes [36]. Each substance has unique characteristics that make them
appropriate for various sensing applications. To improve their sensing abilities, the
nanowires are often organized in a particular pattern or structure.
  A broad variety of physical and chemical characteristics, including temperature,
pressure, strain, magnetic ﬁelds, gas concentrations, and biological molecules, may
be detected with nanowire sensors [37]. Typically, the sensing method depends on
how the target stimulus alters the electrical conductivity or optical characteristics
of the nanowires. The great sensitivity of nanowire sensors is one of its beneﬁts.
The wires’ nanoscale diameters allow them to sense incredibly minute changes in
their surroundings. The good selectivity of nanowire sensors also enables them to
discriminate between various analytes or target compounds.

--- Page 448 ---
Nanostructured Sensors for Pesticide Detection in Tea                                449

  Nanowire sensors have a wide range of uses in industries including electronics,
environmental monitoring, and health care. They may be used to detect the pesti-
cide of vegetables, contaminants in the air or water, monitor physiological indica-
tors in real time and enable new sorts of electronic devices with improved sensing
capabilities [38].

4  Conclusion


The utilization of nanostructured sensors for pesticide detection has great poten-
tial and can offer numerous advantages over traditional detection methods like Gas
Chromatography Mass Spectrometry (GC/MS). The special properties of nanoma-
terials like their high surface-to-volume ratio and enhanced sensitivity make them
highly effective for detecting pesticides at low concentrations. Detecting pesticides
at levels that were previously challenging to accomplish is now possible because
of the extraordinary sensitivity of nanomaterial-based sensors. This high sensitivity
enables early identiﬁcation of pesticide residues in diverse environmental samples,
maintaining the security of agricultural goods and reducing possible health hazards
related to pesticide exposure. In conclusion, we can say that nanostructured sensors
which have immense merits like high sensitivity, selectivity, quick response, mobility,
and cost-effectiveness offer a potential approach for pesticide detection. Progress in
this area might completely alter how pesticides are managed while also defending
the environment and human health at the same time.

Screening and Characterization
of Aroma and Flavor-Producing Bacteria
and Yeast from Traditional Fermented
Food and Beverages of Northeast, India



Debashree Borthakur    , Esha Barlaskar, Smriti Priya Medhi    ,
and Bipin Kumar Sharma



Abstract Fermented foods in India are diverse and play a signiﬁcant role in the
country’s culinary traditions. These foods are often categorized based on their base
material and include a variety of items with reported medicinal properties. Some
examples of these fermented foods are: Dahi, Gundruk, Sinki, Inziangsang, Iromba,
etc. While there were initially limited reports on the extraction of lactic acid bacteria
(LAB) from Indian fermented dishes, the growing awareness toward the health bene-
ﬁts associated with LAB has spurred increased research in this domain. LAB are
known for their probiotic properties, promoting gut health and overall well-being.
The increasing interest in the health beneﬁts attributed to lactic acid bacteria (LAB)
offers a valuable opportunity for food microbiologists to delve deeper into the study
and exploration of fermented foods. In the current study, bacteria and yeast were
isolated from the different traditional fermented foods of northeast, and their poten-
tial of ﬂavor production was studied. These isolated strains were used to check
the potential of undergoing fermentation and ﬂavor production by inoculating the
isolated strains in the raw milk for the development of novel probiotic products.

Keywords  Starter culture · Flavor production · Fermented foods · Lactic acid
bacteria

1  Introduction


Fermented foods have played a signiﬁcant role in human diets throughout history,
a fact supported by historical references. The passage emphasizes that fermented
foods have constituted a substantial portion of human diets for thousands of years, as
noted by scholars such as [1–3]. An example of ancient fermented food production is
provided, citing evidence of cheese-making dating back to the sixth millennium BC
in Northern Europe. This evidence is derived from the existence of lipids and fatty
acids in milk products in speciﬁc pottery sieves utilized for separating curd from
whey [4]. Originally, due to the presence of natural microbes, fermentation takes
place instinctively due to naturally occurring microorganisms. Individuals regulated
the fermentation methods for two primary reasons: preserving perishable products
like milk, meat, ﬁsh, cereals, and vegetables and enhancing the sensory properties
of food. Different communities developed their speciﬁc fermented foods over time,
which are now contemplate as legacy dishes [1, 5, 6]. Taste remains a crucial aspect
for consumers, and its generation is a tough process which requires the chemical
transformation of various constituents present in the food. LAB are found in nearly
all ethnic fermented dishes, either singly or in combination with other microbes
like yeast, fungi, and bacteria. LAB’s primary role is to swiftly lower the pH of the
food matrix by undergoing fermentation of sugar or carbohydrates into organic acids
like lactic acids. This also helps them in escalating their storage life and enhances
the well-being of the microbial cells. Additionally, most lactic acid bacteria exhibit
various ﬂavor-related activities. This chapter focuses on LAB’s role in generating
ﬂavor compounds in fermented foods, detailing the pathways involved and examining
factors affecting LAB’s contribution to ﬂavor formation [7–9].



2  Objective of the Study

•  Objective 1: Isolation of microbes from traditional fermented food and beverages
   of Northeast India.
•  Objective 2: Screening of potential aroma and ﬂavor-producing bacteria and yeast
  by biochemical characterization (proteolytic, lipolytic, carbohydrate fermentation
    test, and hemolytic test).
•  Objective 3: Preparation of curd from the isolated aroma and ﬂavor-producing
   strain and sensory evaluation of the curd.

4  Materials and Methods


4.1  Sample Collection


The samples from different traditional food sources like fermented beverages and
fermented food were collected from the eight states of Northeast India: Assam,
Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim, and Tripura.
The samples from the eight states which are collected for the study are shown in
Fig. 2 and listed in Table 1 along with their location [10–13].



4.2  Isolation and Characterization of the Flavor-Producing
   LAB


The isolation of microbes was carried out using the serial dilution technique in sterile
distilled water, reaching dilutions up to 10−6. Subsequently, 100 μl of the diluted
sample was spread plated on three types of agar media: De Man–Rogosa–Sharpe
agar (MRS), nutrient agar media plates, and yeast extract peptone dextrose agar
plates. This methodology was employed to cultivate and isolate microbial colonies
for further analysis and characterization [14].

  De Man–Rogosa–Sharpe agar, commonly abbreviated as MRS, is a selective
culture medium speciﬁcally formulated to encourage the robust growth of Lacto-
bacilli during laboratory studies. It provides an environment that favors the develop-
ment of Lactobacillus species. On the other hand, nutrient agar serves as a general-
purpose solid medium that supports the growth of a broad spectrum of non-fastidious
microorganisms [15]. It is widely used in microbiology for cultivating and isolating
various types of bacteria and fungi. YEPD, which stands for yeast extract peptone
dextrose and is often abbreviated as YPD, is a comprehensive medium designed for
the growth of yeast. This medium is composed of yeast extract, peptone, double-
distilled water, and glucose (dextrose). YEPD can be utilized as both a liquid and a
solid medium by incorporating agar, making it suitable for various applications in
yeast cultivation and experimentation [16].
  To get pure culture, the colonies obtained were streaked on nutrient agar media
plates, MRS plates, and yeast extract peptone dextrose agar plates and kept for
incubation at 37 and 28 °C. Colony morphology from the streaked plates is shown
in Fig. 3 [17–19].



4.3  Screening of Potential Aroma and Flavor-Producing
     Bacteria and Yeast by Biochemical Characterization
     (Proteolytic Test, Lipolytic Test, Carbohydrate
     Fermentation Test, and Hemolytic Test)


The intricate development of ﬂavor in dairy products hinges on three primary
processes: glycolysis, proteolysis, and lipolysis. Glycolysis, the metabolism of
sugars, particularly lactose, is orchestrated by lactic acid bacteria, converting lactose

--- Page 458 ---
460                                                              D. Borthakur et al.





Fig. 3  Isolated colonies on NAM and MRS media


into lactic acid and imparting a characteristic sour taste. Proteolysis involves the
degradation of proteins by enzymes like proteases and peptidases, leading to the
formation of peptides and amino acids. This breakdown of milk proteins contributes
to the savory and umami ﬂavors in dairy products. Lipolysis, the degradation of
lipids, releases fatty acids through the activity of lipolytic enzymes, contributing
to buttery and nutty notes. Microbial fermentation, involving various bacteria and
molds, further shapes the ﬂavor proﬁle, while aging and ripening processes, espe-
cially in cheeses, contribute to the ongoing evolution of taste. The interplay of these
processes, inﬂuenced by factors like microbial cultures and milk composition, results
in the rich diversity of ﬂavors observed in different dairy products [20]. In the realm
of dairy product development, the metabolisms of sugars, primarily lactose, stand
as signiﬁcant sources of numerous ﬂavor compounds. The exploration of these two
processes provides valuable insights into the intricate and multifaceted nature of
ﬂavor development in dairy products.
   Proteolysis emerges as a critical biochemical pathway, and the role of lactic acid
bacteria (LAB) is pivotal in unraveling its intricacies. LAB, encompassing various

--- Page 459 ---
Screening and Characterization of Aroma and Flavor-Producing …                      461

strains such as Lactococcus, Streptococcus, and Lactobacillus, are renowned for their
contribution to the sensorial qualities of dairy products. The enzymatic reactions
within LAB involve proteases and peptidases that meticulously dismantle complex
milk proteins. This breakdown leads to the formation of peptides and amino acids,
which serve as potent ﬂavor precursors. The diversity in LAB strains and their speciﬁc
enzymatic activities result in a wide array of ﬂavor compounds, contributing to the
unique taste proﬁles of different dairy items [21]. As proteolysis unfolds, it not only
generates savory and umami notes but also lays the foundation for the complex and
harmonious ﬂavor symphony characteristic of well-crafted dairy delights. Delving
deeper into the molecular intricacies of proteolysis in LAB offers valuable insights for
optimizing ﬂavor proﬁles in the dairy industry and elevating the sensory experience
for consumers [22]. Proteolysis, a fundamental biochemical pathway, takes center
stage in the complex choreography of ﬂavor development in dairy products, with the
indispensable participation of lactic acid bacteria (LAB). LAB, including diverse
strains like Lactococcus, Streptococcus, and Lactobacillus, are celebrated for their
pivotal role in shaping the sensory attributes of dairy delights. Within the intricate
molecular landscape of LAB, enzymatic reactions guided by proteases and peptidases
meticulously disassemble complex milk proteins. This enzymatic breakdown gives
rise to an array of peptides and amino acids, serving as potent precursors for the
diverse and nuanced ﬂavors that characterize different dairy items [15, 23].
  The rich tapestry of ﬂavor compounds produced by LAB is a testament to the
diversity in strains and their unique enzymatic activities. This diversity contributes
to the distinct taste proﬁles observed in various dairy products, showcasing the artistry
inherent in the microbial-driven ﬂavor development process. As proteolysis unfolds
within this microbial realm, it not only generates the savory and umami notes that
are hallmarks of quality dairy, but it also lays the foundation for a harmonious ﬂavor
symphony.
  The exploration of proteolysis in LAB extends beyond its role as a ﬂavor generator;
it provides a gateway to a deeper understanding of the molecular intricacies that
govern the sensory experiences of consumers. This knowledge becomes a valuable
tool in the hands of the dairy industry, offering insights for ﬁne-tuning ﬂavor proﬁles
and enhancing the overall sensory delight for discerning consumers. In essence, the
study of proteolysis in LAB unveils a fascinating journey into the heart of dairy ﬂavor
science, where microbes play the role of skilled artisans crafting the symphony of
tastes that elevate dairy products to culinary masterpieces [24]. The production of
free amino acids (FAA) through proteolysis in dairy products is a direct contributor
to ﬂavor. However, it is crucial to note that the fate of these free amino acids does not
end with their initial liberation. Instead, their subsequent metabolism is identiﬁed as
a key process in the broader context of ﬂavor formation [25].
  While free amino acids can individually impart speciﬁc taste qualities, their trans-
formation through metabolic pathways introduces additional layers of complexity to
the overall ﬂavor proﬁle. The metabolism of free amino acids involves various enzy-
matic reactions and microbial activities. These processes can lead to the generation of
new ﬂavor compounds, which contribute to the development of intricate and diverse
sensory characteristics in dairy products [26, 27].

--- Page 460 ---
462                                                              D. Borthakur et al.

  The speciﬁc pathways and transformations that free amino acids undergo depend
on factors such as the microbial composition, environmental conditions, and the
type of dairy product. This dynamic interplay between proteolysis, the liberation
of free amino acids, and their subsequent metabolism showcases the intricate and
multifaceted nature of ﬂavor development in the world of dairy. Understanding these
processes at a molecular level is essential for ﬁne-tuning and controlling the sensory
attributes of dairy products to meet consumer preferences and quality standards
[28–31].
   Screening of potential aroma and ﬂavor-producing bacteria and yeast were by
biochemical characterization of proteolytic, lipolytic, and carbohydrate fermentation
test.

Proteolytic Test

Proteolysis is the process of breaking down peptide bonds in proteins, resulting in the
production of smaller peptides and amino acids. The formation of amino acids and
their role in wide reactions like transamination, decarboxylation, desulfurization,
and deamination reactions help in shaping the taste or ﬂavor of food. Proteases,
enzymes responsible for protein hydrolysis, are particularly relevant in the generation
of the newly fermented output. The breakdown of proteins not only enhances ﬂavor
complexity but also introduces a nuanced interplay of textures and aromas, offering
consumers a distinctive and reﬁned gastronomic experience [32].

Media Used

Skim milk agar media is used. Skim milk agar serves as a differential medium
designed to assess the capability of an organism to produce an exoenzyme known as
casease. This enzyme functions to hydrolyze casein, and the medium is employed to
detect and evaluate this speciﬁc enzymatic activity in microbial organisms [33, 34].

Lipolytic Test

Lipolysis, a fundamental biochemical process, involves the hydrolysis of triglyc-
erides, the primary storage form of fats, resulting in the generation of free fatty acids,
glycerol, and intermediates like mono- and diglycerides. This intricate process is
orchestrated by enzymes known as lipases, which catalyze the breakdown of triglyc-
erides into their constituent parts. The liberated free fatty acids contribute signiﬁ-
cantly to the sensory characteristics of dairy products, imparting distinct ﬂavors and
aromas such as buttery and nutty notes. Glycerol, another byproduct of lipolysis, may
inﬂuence the mouthfeel and texture of the ﬁnal product. The complexity of lipolysis
is further accentuated by the potential formation of mono- and diglycerides, which
can participate in various reactions impacting both ﬂavor and texture. In the context
of dairy, lipolysis is particularly relevant in the development of cheeses and butter,
where the enzymatic activity of lipases contributes to the diverse and appealing
proﬁles that deﬁne these dairy delights. Understanding the dynamics of lipolysis is
essential for dairy producers seeking to craft products with desired ﬂavor nuances
and textures [35]. The extent of lipolysis conducted by LAB is a signiﬁcant factor in
selecting strains for use as starter cultures. This property holds particular relevance
in applications such as vegetable fermentation, baked foods, and the development of
ﬂavors in fermented milk products [36].

Media Used

Tributyrin agar media is used. Tributyrin agar is a specialized medium employed
for identifying and quantifying lipolytic bacteria and molds in various foodstuffs
and materials. This medium is speciﬁcally designed to support the detection and
enumeration of microorganisms capable of hydrolyzing tributyrin, a triglyceride,

Carbohydrate Fermentation Test

Carbohydrates, commonly referred to as sugars, are polyhydroxy aldehydes or
ketones composed of carbon (C), hydrogen (H), and oxygen (O) atoms in an empir-
ical formula of Cx(H2O)y. They exhibit diverse classiﬁcations based on various
criteria. However, in the context of microbiology and carbohydrate fermentation
tests, commonly utilized substrates include glucose, lactose, sucrose, arabinose, and
mannitol.
   During the fermentation process, these carbohydrate molecules undergo anaerobic
catabolism, resulting in the production of organic acids. This acid production leads to
a decrease in the pH of the media, resulting in the activation of the pH indicator which

4.4  Yogurt Preparation


For curd preparation, boiled milk was taken and transferred to the culture tubes in an
aseptic condition. The culture tubes were then inoculated with the strains and kept
inside an incubator at 37°C overnight [44, 45]



4.5  Sensory Evaluation


The sensory analysis or sensory testing of food has the mission of evaluating the
different characteristics of a product mainly color, texture, ﬂavor, appearance, body,
and overall acceptability.
   In the context of sensory evaluation, a panel of 8 people was invited for curd
tasting where appearance, odor, ﬂavor, and mouthfeel were considered and ratings
are given. And based on the ratings, the strains were considered to be the best among
the other strains for curd formation [46–48].



5  Results

5.1  Isolation and Characterization of the Flavor-Producing
   LAB


A sum of 82 lactic acid bacteria (LAB) strains was isolated using MRS and NAM
culture media, and 10 yeast strains were obtained on YEPD media from the fermented
foods. Based on the positive result of lipolytic, proteolytic, and carbohydrate tests,
9 strains were selected for the preparation of yoghurt. Among them, Akhuni/NA/
4, Khorisa/NA/3, TL3, B4, HTK5, NAP2, NGA-6, NGA-5, and Chuwan/YEPD/1
were selected for the preparation of curd.

A total of 46 strains were proteolytic positive out of 82 isolated strains. Both the

6  Discussion


The primary aim of this experiment was to isolate and recognize naturally occur-
ring LAB from fermented food samples in the northeast region of India. Collec-
tively, 82 LAB were successfully isolated from twelve different fermented food
samples. The ﬁndings of the study underscored the signiﬁcant diversity of lactic acid
bacteria present in these fermented foods. The existence of lactic acid bacteria in
these food dishes not only improves the accessibility of nutrients but also acts as
natural preservative agents.
  The experiment concluded that fermented foods are a rich source of LAB, demon-
strating both homofermentative and heterofermentative lactic acid bacteria. These
different types of LAB contribute to the generation of diverse ﬂavor compounds,
resulting in distinct ﬂavors and textures in the ﬁnal products, such as curd. The
identiﬁed fermented foods could potentially serve as valuable sources for beneﬁcial
lactic acid bacteria in the future research endeavors. Subsequent studies are planned
to delve into the characterization and identiﬁcation of these LAB at the species level,
as well as exploring their probiotic potential.



7  Conclusion


The aim of this experiment was to extract and recognize natural LAB from fermented
food samples in the northeastern region of India. A total of 82 bacteria and 10 yeast
samples were successfully identiﬁed from twelve different fermented food samples
as part of the investigation.
  Based on its aroma, ﬂavor, musty, acidity, astringment, and carbonation test,
9 strains namely Akhuni/NA/4, Khorisa/NA/3, TL2, B4, HTK5, NAP2, Chuwak/
YEPD/1, NGA-6, and NGA-5 were selected for curd production. Curd produced
by the inoculation of strains Akhuni/NA/4, B4, HTK5, and NAP2 is found to be
most palatable and was best reviewed. Hence, these four strains were selected for its
further study.



8  Future Work


Ethnic fermented dishes are experiencing a resurgence of attention among users and
food industry, presenting an opportunity to bolster sustainable food systems amid
growing pressures on food resources. To guide ﬂavor enhancement or diversiﬁca-
tion, more research is needed to pinpoint the key ﬂavor components in the terminal
products and unravel the primary living entities that contribute in the production of
ﬂavors. The ultimate role of lactic acid bacteria in shaping the ﬂavor of traditional
fermented foods hinges their inherent ability to generate aroma compounds at the

--- Page 472 ---
474                                                              D. Borthakur et al.

time of fermentation. Investigating the possible lactic acid bacterial species can be
approached through a spectrum of techniques.
  The upcoming phases of this study will involve the morphological, physiolog-
ical, and biochemical characterization of the chosen ﬂavor-producing bacteria and
yeasts. Additionally, the identiﬁcation and characterization of ﬂavor compounds will
be conducted through chromatography techniques, speciﬁcally gas chromatography
coupled to mass spectrometry (GC–MS). This comprehensive approach will provide
a detailed understanding of the selected microorganisms’ characteristics and their
contributions to ﬂavor proﬁles, enhancing our knowledge of the complex interactions
within this system.

MindWell: A Dataset Related to Mental
Health


Pushpendra Kumar, Aanchal Punia, Anjali Dagar, and Satyavrat Gaur





Abstract Mental  health research plays a  pivotal  role  in understanding and
addressing the complex challenges faced by individuals worldwide. However,
existing datasets in this ﬁeld often lack comprehensive and diverse information,
limiting the scope of analysis and the development of effective interventions. In
response, this study aims to bridge this gap by creating a new dataset on mental health.
Through a rigorous data collection process, we gathered data from multiple sources,
including surveys, available online documents, etc. The introduced MindWell dataset
comprises a diverse sample of participants across different demographic groups,
capturing a wide range of mental health dimensions, such as symptoms, diagnostic
information, treatment history, lifestyle factors, and socio-economic variables.

Keywords Clinical records · Dataset · Data quality · Mental health



1  Introduction


Impact of datasets used for data-driven methods are signiﬁcantly very huge for the
better performance of decision-making methods [1]. It is a collection of data that
could be used in machine learning. There are various datasets present (e.g., LoST
dataset [2]) related to mental health, but the existing datasets often lack the breadth
and depth necessary to comprehensively investigate the complex interplay of factors

inﬂuencing mental health outcomes. To address this critical gap, the present study
aims to create a novel and comprehensive dataset on mental health, encompassing
various dimensions of mental well-being and related factors. In this work, a new
dataset named “MindWell” has been created. By capturing diverse data sources and
incorporating a wide range of variables, this dataset aims to facilitate in-depth inves-
tigations into the etiology, manifestation, and treatment of mental health conditions.
Moreover, the presence of such a dataset has the potential to encourage cooperation
and the exchange of knowledge among researchers. This, in turn, could facilitate the
creation of strategies rooted in evidence to enhance mental well-being and enhance
mental health results worldwide. In essence, the objective of this dataset is to augment
the expanding repository of information in the realm of mental health and bolster
endeavors aimed at tackling the intricate issues encountered by individuals grappling
with mental health concerns.
   This paper has been divided into different sections; in Sect. 2, datasets available
on mental health have been discussed. Section 3 discusses the proposed dataset
“MindWell.” Further sections discuss the conclusion, future scope, and references.



2  Background


Mental health research has greatly beneﬁted from the availability of various datasets
that capture different aspects of mental well-being. Numerous studies have utilized
these datasets to investigate the prevalence, risk factors, treatment outcomes, and
public health implications of mental health conditions. Some available datasets are
discussed below. National Comorbidity Survey-Replication (NCS-R) [3], this dataset
offers extensive data regarding the occurrence and co-occurrence of psychological
ailments within the USA. It covers details concerning a variety of mental health condi-
tions, encompassing anxiety disorders, mood disorders, and substance use disorders.
For instance, the UK Biobank [4] dataset, while not exclusively dedicated to mental
health, offers a substantial amount of information regarding mental health outcomes,
genetic data, and diverse cognitive measurements. This dataset facilitates exten-
sive analyses to investigate the interplay between genetics, the environment, and
mental health conditions. Similarly, the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development
(ABCD) [5] Study, a longitudinal research initiative, gathers comprehensive data on
brain development, cognitive performance, mental health, and substance use within a
large cohort of American adolescents. It aims to understand how these factors impact
each other over time. The World Mental Health Surveys dataset is a collection of
nationally representative surveys conducted across different countries. The World
Mental Health Surveys dataset is a collection of nationally representative surveys
conducted across different countries [6]. It provides valuable cross-cultural insights
into the prevalence, treatment, and impact of mental disorders worldwide. National
Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions (NESARC). Focusing on
alcohol and substance use disorders, the NESARC dataset includes detailed infor-
mation on mental health, substance use, and associated risk factors. It provides

--- Page 477 ---
MindWell: A Dataset Related to Mental Health                                      479

important insights into the epidemiology and comorbidity of these conditions. Fram-
ingham Heart Study [7], although primarily a cardiovascular study, the Framingham
Heart Study dataset includes measures related to mental health, such as depression,
anxiety, and cognitive function. It enables researchers to investigate the relationship
between mental health and cardiovascular well-being. The MuDoCo dataset [8],
consisting of a total of 8,429 conversations with an average of 5.36 exchanges per
conversation, provides a collection of scripted dialogues between an imaginary user
and a system. Within these dialogues, users instruct the system to carry out a wide
array of tasks across six distinct domains: initiating phone calls, sending messages,
scheduling reminders, checking the weather, delivering news updates, and playing
music. Furthermore, a dataset was assembled to evaluate the psychological ramiﬁca-
tions of e-learning digital tools in response to COVID-19 [9] on the overall well-being
of university students in Jordan. A new Early Mental Health Uncovering (EMU) [10]
framework aims to improve mental illness screening, using both active and passive
data collection methods, including scripted audio recordings. While the mentioned
datasets in [11] have contributed signiﬁcantly to mental health research, they do have
some limitations and shortcomings. Here are a few potential shortcomings of these
datasets:

•  Limited generalizability: Some datasets may lack diversity in terms of demo-
   graphic representation, which can limit the generalizability of ﬁndings to different
   populations or cultural contexts. This could lead to potential biases and challenges
   in understanding the broader mental health landscape.
• Focus on speciﬁc disorders or conditions: Certain datasets may focus primarily on
   speciﬁc mental health disorders or conditions, which might limit their utility for
   studying a wide range of mental health dimensions. This can restrict the ability
   to explore comorbidity patterns or broader mental health trends.
•  Reliance on self-reported measures: Many datasets heavily rely on self-reported
   measures, which may introduce biases and measurement errors. Participants’
   subjective interpretations, recall biases, and social desirability biases can impact
   the accuracy and reliability of self-reported mental health information.
• Lack of longitudinal data: While some datasets do capture longitudinal informa-
   tion, others may be cross-sectional or have limited follow-up periods. The absence
   of long-term data can hinder the ability to study mental health trajectories, changes
   over time, or the impact of interventions and treatments.
•  Potential under-representation of certain populations: Some datasets may not
   adequately capture the experiences and perspectives of marginalized or underrep-
   resented populations. This can limit the understanding of mental health disparities
  and hinder efforts to address the speciﬁc needs of these populations.
•  Challenges in accessing and analyzing the data: Depending on the dataset, there
  may be restrictions or complexities associated with accessing and analyzing
   the data. Data access protocols, data sharing agreements, or limitations in data
   documentation can pose challenges for researchers.

   Proposed dataset MindWell takes care of above shortcomings (with help of infor-
mation available at internet and Chat-GPT3.5) as this is designed to have a more

--- Page 478 ---
480                                                                                           P. Kumar et al.

diverse representation of demographic groups; it aims to collect data on a wide range
of mental health dimensions, not just speciﬁc disorders or conditions; it is designed
to capture longitudinal data over extended periods; it can actively seek to include and
amplify the voices and experiences of marginalized and underrepresented popula-
tions. Researchers can work with community organizations and engage in outreach
efforts to ensure that these populations are adequately represented. This will help
address mental health disparities and better serve the speciﬁc needs of these groups.
For accessing the dataset researcher can use the GitHub link https://github.com/pus
hpendra1bel/MindWell 1.0. In case of any issue in accessing this link, researcher can
request through mail to any author of this paper.



3  Methodology


Highly common conditions like depression, categorized as mental illnesses, have
demonstrated their capacity to affect an individual’s physical well-being. In recent
times, the ﬁeld of artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) has introduced various methods aimed
at supporting mental health professionals, including psychiatrists and psychologists.
These methods leverage patients’ historical data to aid in decision-making processes
[12]. The compilation of this dataset involved referencing multiple data sources,
including but not limited to medical records, behavioral data, and social media usage,
as well as incorporating insights from ChatGPT 3.5 [13] were also used for gener-
ating questions and answers from the documents, some algorithm has been used for
creating the answer span in the context. Dataset evaluation has been done in many
way, i.e., manually, discussion with NLP scholars, using ChatGPT, Google Search,
etc.

A.  Ethical Mental Health QA Dataset

This dataset was meticulously curated with a strong ethical foundation, emphasizing
the importance of responsible and sensitive handling of question-answering tasks
related to mental health.

B. Corpus for the Dataset

In the context of data analysis and natural language processing, a “corpus” refers to
a large collection of text documents or spoken language recordings that are used for
linguistic analysis, language modeling, and various computational linguistics tasks.
Essentially, a corpus is a structured and organized dataset speciﬁcally designed for
studying language patterns and linguistic phenomena.
  The task of corpus construction for MindWell dataset has been discussed by
an expert team working on NLP models. After discussion and suggestion from
this expert team, Corpus for the dataset has been derived from various sources,
some of them are online resources, e.g., WHO website, AIIMS website, Wikipedia,
etc., whereas some sources are literature surveys on mental health. ChatGPT 3.5 is
also used for different question-answer set generation. Before adding the outputs

--- Page 479 ---
MindWell: A Dataset Related to Mental Health                                      481

of ChatGPT into the dataset, they were veriﬁed and, if required, corrections were
applied. Questions in the dataset are in such a way that the user can get information
that covers the following area:

•  General Information on mental health.
• Beneﬁts of being mentally healthy.
• Symptoms of mental health.
• Reason of mental health.
•  Solution of mental health.

C. Key characteristics for MindWell dataset

•  Structured Format: MindWell dataset is organized in a structured format, often
   resembling a table, this dataset would be used particularly in supervised learning,
   datasets are typically divided into three main subsets: the training dataset, the
   validation dataset, and the testing dataset.
•  Dataset Splitting: The process of dividing the original dataset into these subsets
    is called dataset splitting. The ratios for splitting the data are 70-15-15 (70% for
   training, 15% for validation, and 15% for testing) or 80-10-10. However, the split
   ratios can vary based on the size of the dataset and the problem’s complexity.
•  Instances: Each row represents a single instance of a set of particular question–
   answer and its context.
• Data Types: Every attribute within this dataset is associated with a particular data
   type, which speciﬁes the nature of values it can contain. Common data types
  encompass numerical values (integers, ﬂoating-point numbers), text strings, date
   formats, and various others.
• Data Points: A speciﬁc value in the dataset at the intersection of a row and a
  column is referred to as a data point. Each data point provides information about
   a particular attribute for a speciﬁc instance. For training a NLP model number of
   data point should be more. MindWell is expandable in terms of data points, size
   of this dataset would keep on increasing in the future.
• Domains and Applications: Its particular domain is related to mental health.
• Data Quality: The features of this dataset are similar to the SQuAD Dataset
   [14]. The SQuAD (Stanford Question Answering Dataset) is a widely recognized
  benchmark dataset in natural language processing (NLP) and machine reading
   comprehension. It was created by Stanford University researchers to advance
   question-answering model development. SQuAD consists of context paragraphs
  and corresponding questions with answers, serving as a critical resource for
   evaluating and training NLP models.
• Machine Learning: Different NLP models would be trained using this dataset,
  and the best one would be chosen.
•  Cross-Validation: Cross-validation is a method used to optimize data utilization
  when evaluating a model. In kfold cross-validation, the dataset is divided into k
   subsets, or folds. The model undergoes training k times, with each fold serving
   as the test set once, while the remaining k-1 folds are used for training in each

--- Page 480 ---
482                                                                                           P. Kumar et al.

   iteration. This strategy enhances the reliability of performance estimation for a
   model, as it ensures that all data points are employed for both training and testing
   throughout the cross-validation procedure.
•  Features of Dataset

D.  Features of Dataset

With discussion from NLP domain experts, the features for the “MindWell” dataset
have been advised to take the SQuAD dataset which is publicly available on
huggingface.co. The dataset is designed for question-answering tasks.
  Data Fields of Dataset: The data ﬁelds are the same among all splits.
   Various features of this dataset are as below:

•  Title: a textual attribute.
•  ID: a textual attribute.
•  Context: a textual attribute.
•  Question: a textual attribute.
• Answers: a dictionary attribute comprising:

   Text: a textual attribute.
   Answer-start: an integer feature.
  The dataset consists of two main components. The ﬁrst part is referred to as
“Context,” which comprises a brief paragraph containing relevant information related
to mental health. These context paragraphs are limited to a maximum of 480 words
each.

•  Title: This ﬁeld denotes the title or topic associated with the context.
•  ID: An identiﬁer for the speciﬁc question–answer set.
•  Question: This ﬁeld contains a question that pertains to the information presented
   in the context.
• Answer: The answer ﬁeld contains the response to the question, and this answer
    is located within the context paragraph.
•  Answer-Start: An integer value indicating the character position within the
   context paragraph where the answer can be found.

   This dataset is designed to be expandable, allowing for the addition of more
question–answer sets in the future as new data becomes available or for updates to
existing data. A snap of dataset content is shown in Fig. 1.

E.  Data Validation and Quality Assurance

Data validation has been done on small chunks of the dataset, e.g., when a dataset
for 200 question gets ready, then an NLP model has been trained on this dataset and
different answer related to mental health been asked, the answer given by the model
has been checked and veriﬁed if the answers generated by the model are correct
then dataset has been expanded by adding with more question-answers sets if the
answers are not generated correctly then recheck the dataset and modify accordingly
and again feed it to NLP model and then check the regenerated answers, repeat this

5  Conclusion and Future Work


The development and release of the question-answering task-based dataset have
provided a valuable resource for advancing research in the ﬁeld of question-
answering. The dataset encompasses a diverse range of questions and corresponding
answers, representing various domains, topics, and levels of complexity. It has been
meticulously annotated and curated to ensure high-quality data for training and evalu-
ating question-answering models. Through the utilization of this dataset, researchers
and practitioners have gained insights into the challenges and intricacies of the
question-answering task. The dataset has enabled the creation and assessment of
innovative machine learning algorithms and natural language processing methods,
resulting in enhanced question-answering systems and pushing the boundaries of
what is achievable in the ﬁeld.
  While the question-answering task-based dataset has provided a strong foundation
for research, several avenues for future work can further enhance its utility and impact.
These include

•  Fine-Grained Annotations: Future iterations of the dataset could incorporate
   ﬁner-grained annotations, such as entity-level or relation-level annotations. This
  would enable researchers to explore more complex question-answering scenarios
   involving entity relationships, knowledge graphs, or multi-hop reasoning.
•  Evaluation Metrics and Bench marking: The development of robust evaluation
   metrics and bench marking procedures can provide standardized and objective
   measures for assessing the performance of question-answering models. This
  would facilitate fair comparisons between different approaches and foster healthy
   competition in the ﬁeld.
• User feedback and human evaluation play pivotal roles in enhancing question-
   answering systems. These processes offer valuable insights into the quality, utility,
  and constraints of such systems. By incorporating user feedback and conducting
  human evaluations, we can achieve the following:

  –  Quality Improvement: User feedback helps identify and rectify issues in the
      system’s responses, ensuring that answers are accurate, relevant, and up-to-
      date.
  –  Usefulness Assessment: Feedback and evaluations gauge how well the system
     meets user needs and whether it provides genuinely helpful information.
  –  Limitation Discovery: User comments and human evaluations shed light on the
      system’s limitations, such as its inability to answer certain types of questions
      or understand context fully.
  –  Dataset Reﬁnement: Insights from user feedback can guide updates to the
      dataset, ensuring it remains relevant and comprehensive.
  –  User-Centric Development: Feedback guides the development of more user-
      centric question-answering models, aligning the system with user expectations
     and preferences.

--- Page 484 ---
486                                                                                           P. Kumar et al.

   In summary, user feedback and human evaluations are essential tools for contin-
uous improvement in question-answering systems, fostering systems that are more
accurate user-friendly, and adaptable to evolving user needs.

• Real-Time and Interactive Question-Answering: Exploring the challenges of real-
   time and interactive question-answering can be an interesting direction for future
   work. This would involve handling dynamic contexts, live updates, and inter-
   active dialogues, allowing question-answering systems to effectively respond to
   changing information and user interactions.
• Expansion of the Dataset: Although this dataset is related to “mental health,” there
    is potential for expansion to include additional domains, languages, or specialized
   ﬁelds.

   This would allow for more diverse training and evaluation scenarios, making the
dataset more representative of real-world question-answering challenges.

•  Fine-Tuning [15] of the Dataset: “Fine-Tuning” of different NLP models (related
   to question-answering tasks) could be done using this dataset, the output can be
   used for the analysis of performance comparison of these models.

Gadolinium Dilemma: Navigate Water
Contamination in the Face
of Indispensable Medical Advancements


Subhrata Dutta    , Sunandan Baruah    , and Papia Dutta





Abstract The rare earth element, Gadolinium Gd(+3) has strong paramagnetic
nature, due to which it is being extensively explored in Magnetic Resonance Imaging
(MRI). The Gd (+3) ions are converted into different chelate forms by using different
derivatives of ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) and administered as contrast
agents. However, repetitive doses of Gd (+3) ion cause harmful effects toward phys-
iological processes of human health; and when these metal complexes are released
into the surface water as medical sewages, they disrupt even the aquatic balance.
This review article aims to raise awareness about the health issues caused due to the
elevated use of the metal ion in medical ﬁeld and its related toxicity. It also high-
lights about the development of some cost effective, innocuous, natural plant-based
as well as synthetic metal-based nanomaterials, which may help in the breakdown
or removal of the Gd (+3) metal ion from the waste water making it less toxic.

Keywords Contrast agent · Gadolinium · MRI · Nanomaterials · Toxicity



1  Introduction


With the discovery of the ﬁrst rare earth element (REE), i.e., yttrium by Johan Gadolin
in the late 1700s, these metals were mostly employed in electronic components like
electric motors, speakers, and hard drive magnets [1]. They were also essential parts
of various lasers, ﬂuorescent lighting, and industrial process catalysts. Gradually,
they have been found to have several applications in the medical ﬁeld during the
preliminary period of twentieth century. However, the lanthanide (III) ion complexes
were later found to exhibit several biological properties such as anti-inﬂammatory,
anti-coagulation, anti-bacterial and anti-cancer [2]. These metal complexes were
also found to be effective in burn related cases [3]. Because of their emission in the

--- Page 487 ---
490                                                                                S. Dutta et al.

near-infrared (NIR) region, that can be detected through animal tissue of signiﬁcant
thickness, the lanthanide ions were useful components for luminescence imaging.
Different other lanthanide ions were applied in the early stages as contrast agents
in X-ray imaging. Lanthanide ions like lanthanum chloride was utilized for its anti-
atherosclerotic actions; lanthanum carbonate for the treatment of hyperphosphatemia
and salts of rare earth metal ions to cure tuberculosis. Unfortunately, because of their
side effects, their applications were restricted in their respective ﬁelds. However,
their signiﬁcance cannot be still ignored. Their versatile potentiality in medical tech-
nology and research has attracted increased attention in recent years, resulting in
improvements in a range of medical procedures and therapies [4, 5].
   Gadolinium (Gd) is one such rare earth metal, which has been used as a contrast
agent in its complexed form in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), a technique used
to scan organs in the diagnostic area for the detection of any ailment [6]. It has an
atomic mass of 157.25u and an atomic number of 64. This delicate silvery white
metal from the lanthanide class is normally found in the +3 oxidation state. Natural
Gadolinium is a mixture of 7 isotopes namely 154Gd, 155Gd, 156Gd, 157Gd, 158Gd,
159Gd and 160Gd [7]. Artiﬁcially, it can be prepared by reduction of the anhydrous
ﬂuoride with metallic calcium, and in solutions, it exists as the Gd3+ ion surrounded
by 9 water molecules [8]. The neutral gadolinium atom’s electronic structure is
denoted by [Xe]4f75d16s2, and it utilizes the 6s2 and 5d1 electrons for bonding. It
has a unique property of paramagnetic effect due to the presence of seven unpaired
electrons in the 4f spherically symmetric orbital. Owing to this quality, Gd (3+) is
intravenously administered in MRI diagnostics in the form of certain chelates but
as soon as they are discharged from the human body in the form of urine, they are
released into the environment, and in the due course of time, these complexes break
down and release the free metal ion into the aquatic ecosystem.
   This contaminant pollutes the surface water making it impure and unﬁt for use.
Gadolinium pollution in water is a concern because it can accumulate in aquatic
ecosystems and potentially impact the health of aquatic organisms and even human
populations that rely on these water sources for drinking and other household
purposes. As a result, millions of people globally suffer from the shortage of water.
Moreover, free Gd3+ ions can disturb the physiological processes like contraction of
smooth, skeletal, and cardiac muscle; blood coagulation, etc. [9]. Gd3+ ion inhibit
Ca2+ regulated signaling in the cells. These lead to several illness caused by the
contaminated and degraded water. Repeated usage of Gd-based contrast agents affect
even patient with normal kidney function. Gadolinium deposition diseases are more
commonly seen in individuals with pre-existing kidney problems, as the kidneys
play a role in excreting gadolinium from the body. In response to these concerns,
regulatory agencies, and medical professionals have taken steps to minimize the risks
associated with gadolinium-based contrast agents. They have recommended the use
of the lowest possible dose and the use of agents with a lower likelihood of deposi-
tion. Gadolinium was proved to affect hazardously skin, bone, tissues and brain too
[6]. Moreover, Gd-based MRI used on pregnant ladies showed some toxic effects on
fetuses [10].

--- Page 488 ---
Gadolinium Dilemma: Navigate Water Contamination in the Face …                    491

   This review paper aims toward the compilation of the extensive study of the
applications and toxicity level of Gd(+3) ion in the medical ﬁeld and to observe
its physiological and chemical behavior when involved in reactions for any kind of
synthesis.



2  Gadolinium Ion and Its Derivatives

Gadolinium ions (Gd3+) can interact with other molecules or ligands in water to
generate gadolinium complexes. The gadolinium ion is encircled and stabilized by
ligands during a procedure known as chelation, which results in the formation of coor-
dination compounds. Gadolinium complexes are used in medical imaging to make
certain tissues or structures more visible during magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
The relaxation times of adjacent water protons are impacted by the magnetic char-
acteristics of the gadolinium ion, which alters the MRI signal intensity. By using
different derivatives of ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) [6], Gadolinium
(Gd) is converted into various chelate forms [11], which are used as contrasting
agents in MRI. The gadolinium complexes are diffused into the interstitial space
after intravenous injection and a short intravascular phase in human body due to
their relatively low molecular weight and high hydrophilicity [10].
  The ﬁrst approved and widely used complex of Gd3+ and diethylenetriamine-N,
N, N., N.., N..-pentaacetic acid is Gd-DTPA (Fig. 1), which was the agent for MRI
diagnostics. Two other Gd-chelates that are particularly used in liver imaging are
Gadoxetic acid and Gd-BOPTA (Gadobenate dimeglumine). Through transmetalla-
tion, Gd3+ ions in chelates can be exchanged with body cations such as copper, zinc,
calcium, or iron [11].
  Upon excretion of urine from human body, these complexes are released in much
higher quantity into the medical sewages. Waste water treatment plant (WWTP)
breaks down these complexes and release the free metal Gd(+3) ions into aquatic
ecosystems [12].



2.1  Application of Gadolinium Ion in Various Fields


Gadolinium has several industrial uses. In the magnetic bubble memory device,
which converts a vertically structured magnetic ﬁeld into a cylindrical one of a
substance, the gadolinium–potassium–garnet media material is used. This magnetic
bubble memory device is typically used to gather data. The Gd-garnet is used to create
diamond imitations [13]. Like how terbium and dysprosium are used in optical disks
and ﬁbers, gadolinium is also used in these materials. Anthropogenic Gd is used
in microwaves, compact disk players, radar technologies, and other magnetic and
electronic equipment. To create the phosphorous for color television, it uses sulfur
dioxide [14]. It can also be used to make a solid magnetic refrigeration medium.

--- Page 489 ---
492                                                                                S. Dutta et al.





Fig. 1 Chemical structures of marketed Gadolinium Chelates (Caravan et al. 1999)


The glass’s thermal stability is improved when gadolinium oxide and lanthanum are
mixed. The Gd isotopes are utilized as control rods and neutron absorbers in light
water reactors and fast breeder reactors in the atomic energy sector because they
have a large neutron absorption cross section [15]. Gd can absorb invisible neutrons
that emit light; hence, it is also employed as a ﬂuorescent agent for photosensitive
X-ray ﬁlm. In addition to its industrial use, it is more signiﬁcant in the medical ﬁeld
as a contrast agent and for the other uses listed below.



2.2  Medical Use of Gadolinium Ion:

Among all the inner-transition metal ions, the lanthanide series metal ion Gd3+ has
the largest number of unpaired electrons, and thus, it forms a strong paramagnetic
ﬁeld [16]. This magnetic ﬁeld provides the intermolecular interaction by making it
NMR (nuclear magnetic resonance) active. This effect is used in medical purpose
like magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to get clear vision of the organs using Gd3+
ion as a contrast agent [17].
   Gadolinium contrast agents can also be applied to musculoskeletal imaging for
highlighting cartilage, ligaments, and joints. This is especially helpful in the diag-
nosis of injuries to ligaments and diseases like tendinitis and arthritis. Gadolinium-
enhanced MRI is useful for visualizing blood vessels, which can help in the diagnosis
of diseases such aneurysms, stenosis, and vascular malformations [18].

--- Page 490 ---
Gadolinium Dilemma: Navigate Water Contamination in the Face …                    493

   Gadopentetate dimeglumine was the ﬁrst contrast agent that was used for MRI in
1988 and from 1995 to 2008, six more contrast agents were authorized by FDA for
clinical use [19]. Those are mentioned below:


 Common name                                         Formula

 1. Gadopentetate dimeglumine                       Gd-DTPA

 2. Gadodiamide                                Gd-DTPA-BMA

 3. Gadoteridol                                 Gd-HPDO3A

 4. Gadoterate meglumine                          Gd-DOTA

 5. Gadobutrol                                       [Gd (DO3A-butrol)]

 6. Gadobenate dimeglumine                            [Gd (BOPTA)]


  The macrocyclic gadolinium-based contrast agents are highly stable in compar-
ison to the linear one, and it has been proven to be safe for humans as it is excreted
through urine [20]. On the other hand, the non-chelated Gd complexes are not used
in medical ﬁeld due to the toxicity of Gd3+ ion.



2.3  Use of Gadolinium Complexes in Nano Related Field


Gadolinium oxide (Gd2O3) nanoparticles have been used by Kumar et al. in 2022 to
create an immunosensor which was found to be effective in detecting Vibrio cholerae
toxin (CT) [21]. It was utilized to functionalize 3-(Aminopropyl) triethoxysaline
(APTES) that produced a -NH2 group on the surface, after creating Gd2O3 NPs
using a microwave approach. A ﬁlm made of APTES, Gd2O3, and indium–tin oxide
(ITO) was created. This newly created biosensor performed superbly in detecting
germs.
   In order to accelerate the breakdown of the dyes, methylene blue (MB) and
methyl orange (MO), Panwar et al. synthesized ZnO:TiO2 nanocomposites by doping
various amounts of gadolinium [22]. Increasing the doping concentrations caused
the surface shape to change from nanorod to nanocauliﬂower covered in Gd (3+) ion.
With a loading dose of 1 gm/L, the gadolinium-based nanocomposites assist in the
degradation of MB and MO by 93% and 94.4%, respectively.
  A brand-new nanohybrid material called Mag@Gd(OH)3 consisting of magnetite
and gadolinium hydroxide was created in 2023 by Schneider et al. [23]. This newly
created system keeps its superparamagnetic property after being modiﬁed by the
paramagnetic chemical. The stability of the coated system is higher than the uncoated
one when additional mannose coating is present. It was also claimed that fetal bovine
serum (FBS) treatment could stabilize the hybrid nanoparticles.
   Since the biological function of human mesenchymal stem cells (hMSc) after
transplantation is still unknown, Papov et al., in 2023, created highly gadolinium-
doped cerium oxide nanoparticles (Ce0.8Gd0.2O2-x) using two synthetic methods to
examine the stem cells’ distribution in tissues and organs using magnetic resonance

--- Page 491 ---
494                                                                                S. Dutta et al.

imaging (MRI), a non-invasive method [24]. These nanoparticles have demonstrated
outstanding MRI contrast qualities due to their low toxicity to hMSc, making them
suitable as a theranostic tool. The results revealed that the relaxivity values were
much higher than those of the commercial Omniscan MRI contrast agent.
   In order to overcome the drawbacks of low selectivity, poor adsorption capacity,
and challenging preparation in conventional adsorbents, in 2022, Liu et al. developed
a new ionic imprinted carboxymethyl chitosan (CMC) sponge functionalized by
hyperbranched polyethyleneimine (PEI) with a 3D network structure (PEI-CMC-
IIS) and used it in the selective adsorption of Gd(III) [25]. The PEI-CMC-IIS is
provided with considerable number of amino groups, which is advantageous for the
adsorption of Gd (III), due to the combination of biomass CMC and highly branched
PEI. It was found that in PEI-CMC-IIS, imprinting sites are positioned at the channel
surfaces in order to boost the Gd (III)-speciﬁc adsorption capacity to a considerable
extent.
   In 2017, Pylypchuk et al. described how chitosan (CS) can be covalently immobi-
lized onto the surface of NH2-functionalized magnetite nanoparticles [26]. Covalent
bonding of CS to the surface of magnetite was achieved by using a cross between
a free -CH2OH group of CS and an NH2-group of magnetite using epichlorohydrin
(ECH) as a binding agent. The produced nanocomposites were functionalized using
DTPA-groups. Composites were described using FT-IR, XPS, ASAP, and elemental
analyses. According to TGA results, 3.7% of the hybrid material’s total organic phase
(CS-DTPA) was present. The proposed chemical structure of the hybrid material takes
into account the atomic ratio of oxygen in the ECH residue and chitosan. The study
examined the adsorption of Gd-DTPA and Gd3+ onto the resulting nanocomposite.



3  Toxicity of Gd


See Fig. 2.



3.1  Effect of Gd-Based Compounds in Environment


A Gd anomaly was reported in river water for the ﬁrst time in 1996 [27]. In 1999,
more than 1000 kg of Gd were discharged into the surface waters nearby the areas
of Germany, which is approximately 5% of the total amount of Gd used globally for
medical purpose [28]. The non-complexed free Gd3+ ion degraded from the chelated
form of Gd is highly toxic. It has long been reported that deposition of the Gd3+ ion in
skin, bone, kidney, liver, and brain tissues after repetitive use of doses is a source of
toxicity in animals and humans [29–36]. As generating harmful effects in the brain
cell was the major problem in last few years, it was mentioned that the European
Medical Agency (EMA) restricted the use of linear gadolinium-based contrast agent
[35]. The macrocyclic Gd-based contrast agents are allowed to use in lowest doses.

  An experiment was done on pregnant mice injecting 2 mg/kg body weight of
macrocyclic gadoterate meglumine or linear gadodiamide and some behavioral
changes like anxiety, impaired memory function, decreased muscle strength, etc.
have been noticed [36, 37]. Another research team also discussed their utilization of a
gadolinium-based contrast agent in pregnant non-human primates, revealing an asso-
ciation between lower fetal tissue concentrations and higher placental gadolinium
storage, indicating elevated risks [38, 39].

3.2  Effect of Gd-Based Compounds on Human Health


In 1998, Gd-based contrast agent was used in clinical practice [40]. However, it was
in the year 2004, that the ﬁrst report of Gd deposition in patients with normal renal
function was documented by Gibby et al. after the administration of gadodiamide
and gadoteridol [41]. The ﬁrst serious side effect was observed after the approval of
GBCA by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) [42]. The severe side effect
observed following the administration of gadolinium (Gd) was reported 18 years
after the approval of Gadolinium-Based Contrast Agents (GBCAs) by the U.S. Food
and Drug Administration (FDA). Ray et al. reported that patients suffering from
renal failure had continued elevated amounts of Gd excreted by their urine thereby
conﬁrming the harmful effect of persistent presence of Gd metal [43]. All GBCAs
approved for clinical use were considered safe in their low doses, i.e., 0.1–0.3 mmol/
kg with normal renal function and the safety records were found excellent at 0.03%
doses [44, 45]. In 2004, Gibby et al. recognized the presence of Gd in the part of a
femoral head specimen after using both complexes, i.e., gadodiamide and gadoteridol
in greater amount [46].
   Scheida et al. reported that within 24 h of injecting GBCA, allergic like reactions
were observed in some of the patients. Furthermore, after receiving high doses of
GBCA intravenously, most of the patients suffered from nephrogenic systematic
ﬁbrosis within days to months [47].



3.3  Detection of Gd and Its Complex Forms in Different
     Sources of Water in the Environment


A variety of medical disorders can be diagnosed with gadolinium-based contrast
agents (GBCAs) because they can be adjusted to induce contrast effects that empha-
size certain body regions by attaching gadolinium ions to ligands. Gadolinium
complexes used in GBCAs are carefully designed to be stable in the body and to
minimize potential toxicity. The stability of these complexes is crucial to ensure that
the gadolinium remains bound to the ligands during the imaging process and do not
release free gadolinium ions into the body [11], which could lead to potential health
concerns. However, the stability of some gadolinium complexes has come under
scrutiny in recent years due to the discovery of gadolinium deposition in certain
tissues and in water bodies too.

  Above studies revealed that surface water samples had a higher detection rate of

toxicity level of Gd-based contrast agents in surface water is a novel ﬁeld of research,
it has been successful in attracting the researchers, and thus, some preliminary work
has been reported till now.
  The Predicted No-Effect Concentration (PNEC) value is less than 1 for Gd-DTPA
chelate and even lower for other chelates such as Gd-DOTA and Gd-BT-DO3A,
indicating minimal impact on aquatic organisms [6].

3.4  Removal of Toxicity Using Nanomaterials


Now-a-days, one of the primary concerns raised by the public is the need to elimi-
nate toxicity from wastewater and to recover the precious rare earth elements from
the water. The most widely used methods for removing toxicity from wastewater
include the applications of nanomaterials. In order to extract rare earth elements
(REEs) like Eu(III) from mining wastewater, bio-nanoparticles (BC@FeNPs-EPS)
were utilized. These nanoparticles were created by coupling extracellular polymeric
substances (EPS) with iron nanoparticles (FeNPs) using Bacillus cereus [60]. The
result revealed that the removal efﬁciencies of the three constituent components sepa-
rately, FeNPs (85%), Free cell (67%), and EPS (10%) were lower than the newly
formed nanoparticles, i.e., BC@FeNPs-EPS (90.2%) [60]. In another succeeding
work, after the recovery of rare earth elements, the microbially synthesized iron
nanoparticles had been utilized as an eco-friendly substance to further eliminate
arsenic from groundwater. The removal efﬁciencies of As(III) and As(V) were 94.5%
and 96.0%, respectively; which was observed more effective than the individual Fe
NPs [61].



4  Conclusion


This research will provide new opportunities for using gadolinium metal ions in less
hazardous ways. Gd (+3) ion is used as a contrast agent in MRI because there is
currently a dearth of suitable alternative for it. Therefore, the goal of our research
is to discover a way of removing the metal ion from contaminated water using
nanotechnology so that the resultant treated water is made less harmful.
