Blockchain-Based Certiﬁcate Veriﬁcation
System: A Decentralized Approach


Lovnish Verma, Anita Budhiraja, and Sarwan Singh





Abstract As technology continues to shape aspects of society, there is an increasing
demand, for secure methods to verify academic certiﬁcates. This research paper
introduces an approach that utilizes technology to address this crucial challenge.
The goal of the research is to create, implement, and assess a system powered
by Blockchain that enhances the security and trustworthiness of verifying certiﬁ-
cates. Using techniques smart contract development and leveraging technology our
methodology ensures that academic certiﬁcates are securely stored and validated. By
decentralizing the veriﬁcation process and utilizing trustless contracts, this approach
reduces the risk of claims while also providing scalability and cost effectiveness.
This paper contributes to the ﬁeld of education technology by offering a solution
for verifying certiﬁcates taking advantage of the transparency and security features
inherent in Blockchain technology.

Keywords Academic certiﬁcates · Blockchain technology · Certiﬁcate
veriﬁcation · Cost effectiveness · Decentralized veriﬁcation · Education
technology · Security · Smart contract development · System implementation ·
Technology trustworthiness · Transparency



1  Introduction


In the present era, Blockchain technology has gained signiﬁcant attention within both
industry and academic domains. It can be described as an openly accessible ledger
where all conﬁrmed transactions are systematically recorded within a network of
interconnected blocks. This chain continuously extends as new blocks are incorpo-
rated. To uphold user security and ensure ledger consistency, Blockchain relies on the

utilization of asymmetric cryptography and distributed consensus algorithms which
is presented in [1].
   Blockchain technology  is  characterized by  several fundamental  attributes,
including decentralization, immutability, transparency, and security. These distinc-
tive features empower Blockchain to achieve considerable cost savings while
simultaneously enhancing operational efﬁciency.
   Tamper-proof and decentralized system for certiﬁcate veriﬁcation has never been
more critical. This paper presents a comprehensive exploration of a Blockchain-based
certiﬁcate veriﬁcation system, which offers a decentralized and secure approach to
validate academic credentials. The introduction section sets the stage for the research
by highlighting the growing signiﬁcance of academic certiﬁcates and the challenges
associated with their veriﬁcation in the digital age. It outlines the objectives of the
study, emphasizing the creation of a system that leverages Blockchain technology to
provide an immutable and transparent ledger for academic certiﬁcates. This research
paper comprehensively explores the Blockchain-based certiﬁcate veriﬁcation system
and proposes an innovative decentralized academic qualiﬁcation veriﬁcation method.
This is a response to the urgent needs of a world increasingly reliant on digital
documents. By leveraging the security and transparency inherent in Blockchain
technology, this research aims to transform the ﬁeld of academic certiﬁcate veri-
ﬁcation. Our approach focuses on the design, implementation, and evaluation of
Blockchain-based systems to improve the security and trustworthiness of academic
credentials.
  The importance of this research extends beyond academia and is reﬂected in
the broader ﬁeld of educational technology. It leverages the core functionality of
Blockchain technology to provide practical and innovative solutions for academic
certiﬁcate veriﬁcation. The journey that unfolds in the following sections of this
article demonstrates the transformative potential of Blockchain and how it can ensure
the foundation for academic and professional success in the digital age.
  Our approach draws signiﬁcant inspiration from the principles outlined by Lee
et al. in their research [2]. Expanding upon the groundwork they laid, our study delves
deeper into these concepts, concentrating on the creation, execution, and assessment
of Blockchain-based systems. These systems are intricately crafted with the primary
aim of bolstering the security and reliability of academic credentials. It provides
valuable insights into how smart contracts can be formalized and veriﬁed using
ontology and XML-based methods. It offers a glimpse into the evolving landscape
of smart contract technology and its potential for formalization and validation.
   In the contemporary digital landscape, the secure preservation and authentication
of educational degree certiﬁcates hold signiﬁcant importance. In response to this
pressing concern, our investigation builds upon the pioneering Blockchain-based
framework introduced in [3]. Harnessing the functionalities of Hyperledger Fabric,
this hierarchical system is meticulously engineered to establish robust safeguards
against tampering, streamline transaction processing efﬁciency, and attain note-
worthy levels of superior throughput. In a time when the credibility of academic qual-
iﬁcations carries substantial weight, this system lays the foundation for an elevated
standard of educational record administration and validation.

2  Literature Review


In this section, we provide a more in-depth review of the literature related to
the Blockchain-based certiﬁcate veriﬁcation system. The literature review aims
to contextualize the research within the broader academic discourse and highlight
speciﬁc studies that contribute to the understanding and development of secure and
reliable certiﬁcate veriﬁcation systems.



2.1  Blockchain Technology in Certiﬁcate Veriﬁcation


Zheng et al. present a comprehensive overview of Blockchain technology, discussing
its architectural intricacies, consensus mechanisms, and future trends [1]. This foun-
dational work forms the basis for understanding the fundamental principles of
Blockchain and its application in academic certiﬁcate veriﬁcation.
  Hammoudeh et al. delve into the role of Blockchain in digital certiﬁcate validation,
providing insights into recent advances and emphasizing the technology’s potential
in enhancing security and trustworthiness [4]. This study serves as a guide to the
broader implications of Blockchain in the context of certiﬁcate veriﬁcation.



2.2  Blockchain for Certiﬁcate Distribution and Security


Seng and Rana offer recommendations for implementing a Blockchain-based educa-
tional certiﬁcate distribution system, focusing on combating counterfeit certiﬁ-
cates [5]. Their hierarchical system, built on Hyperledger Fabric, provides insights
into establishing robust safeguards against tampering and improving transaction
processing efﬁciency.
  Chowdhary et al. contribute a Blockchain-based framework for student identity
and educational certiﬁcate veriﬁcation [6]. Their framework, covering enrollment,
certiﬁcate issuance, and veriﬁcation phases, presents a holistic approach to fortifying
the veriﬁcation process.



2.3  Addressing Vulnerabilities with Blockchain


Huynh et  al. explore the issuance and veriﬁcation of digital certiﬁcates with
Blockchain, highlighting the technology’s role in enhancing the integrity and secu-
rity of digital certiﬁcates [7]. The study emphasizes the immutability property of
Blockchain in safeguarding the authenticity of certiﬁcates.

--- Page 503 ---
508                                                                          L. Verma et al.

   Liu and Guo propose a Blockchain-based storage and veriﬁcation scheme for
credible degree certiﬁcates, leveraging Hyperledger Fabric for creating a secure
and tamper-proof system [3]. This study addresses vulnerabilities in traditional
veriﬁcation methods.



2.4  Emerging Trends and Future Prospects


Makridakis and Christodoulou discuss the current challenges and future prospects of
Blockchain applications, emphasizing the technology’s potential in reshaping digital
interactions and processes [8]. Their insights underscore the transformative potential
of Blockchain technology in securing and validating academic certiﬁcates.



3  Related Work


In the ﬁeld of digital certiﬁcates and Blockchain technology, several notable studies
and projects have made signiﬁcant contributions to the ﬁeld. This section provides
an overview of some of these key initiatives.
  A cryptographic key plays a crucial role in the veriﬁcation process. Using this
key gives the veriﬁer the ability to determine both the issuer of the certiﬁcate and
the entity to which it was issued. In addition, the key enables the validation of the
certiﬁcate contents [9].
  Land Records on Blockchain for Implementation of Land Titling in India [10],
this study focuses on designing a Blockchain-based system for land title registration
in India. The system includes various government institutions, banks, courts, and
tehsil ofﬁces. Unlike some previous systems, this system integrates the role of the
government and is therefore suitable for practical implementation.
   In the domain of combatting counterfeit educational certiﬁcates, notable progress
has been achieved by scholars A. Chowdhary, S. Agrawal, and B. Rudra, as evidenced
in their scholarly work [6]. Their innovative security approach revolves around
the integration of certiﬁcates with unique user identities, thereby fortifying the
veriﬁcation process with an additional layer of protection.
   Their proposed framework comprises two pivotal phases: the enrollment and
certiﬁcate issuance phase, along with the user and certiﬁcate veriﬁcation phase. This
strategic approach not only assures the authenticity of certiﬁcates issued by accredited
educational institutions but also establishes a robust veriﬁcation mechanism that
operates autonomously, eliminating the need for reliance on external third-party
intermediaries.
   These pioneering contributions, as expounded in [6], serve as a signiﬁcant
benchmark in the ﬁeld of Blockchain-based educational certiﬁcate veriﬁcation and
constitute a crucial aspect of the related work in this research area.

   In the context of addressing the issue of counterfeit educational certiﬁcates within
the ﬁeld of education, the work presented by Huynh et al. in their paper [7] attempts
to illustrate the diverse approaches to leveraging Blockchain for solving the problem
of counterfeit certiﬁcation in education. Each application has its unique features and
advantages, and they all contribute to the broader effort of enhancing the integrity
and security of digital certiﬁcates.



4  Objective of the Proposed System


The proposed Blockchain-based certiﬁcate veriﬁcation system aims to improve the
security and reliability of education certiﬁcate veriﬁcation. Its core purpose involves
using Blockchain technology and encryption to create a fair, transparent, and proof-
free educational platform. The system ensures the reliability of the veriﬁcation
process by using trustless contracts, thus reducing the risk of fraud. Additionally,
its focus on efﬁciency, effectiveness, user friendliness and compliance with data
protection laws makes it useful for training certiﬁcation auditing.



5  Architecture Design


The architecture of our proposed system is meticulously crafted to offer a seamless
and secure experience for all stakeholders. At its core, we employ a Blockchain
network, with Ethereum serving as the preferred platform due to its smart contract
capabilities. Smart contracts, the system’s workhorses, store certiﬁcate details
and enable automated veriﬁcation processes. Academic institutions, the certiﬁ-
cate issuers, play a pivotal role in this ecosystem, digitally signing and uploading
certiﬁcates onto Blockchain (Fig. 1).
   Users, including employers and educational  institutions,  interact with the
system through an intuitive user interface, initiating certiﬁcate veriﬁcation requests.
Blockchain explorer enhances transparency by allowing users  to inspect the
transaction history and certiﬁcate information stored on the Blockchain.



6  Proposed System


The proposed system introduces a groundbreaking Blockchain-based certiﬁcate veri-
ﬁcation solution poised to revolutionize the realm of academic credential validation.
This innovative approach combines the transparency, security, and decentraliza-
tion inherent in Blockchain technology to create a robust and efﬁcient certiﬁcate
veriﬁcation ecosystem.

6.1  User Interface


The architecture of the proposed system is meticulously crafted to offer a seamless
and secure experience for all users. At its core, we employ a Blockchain network,
with Ethereum serving as the preferred platform due to its smart contract capabil-
ities. Smart contracts, the system’s workhorses, store certiﬁcate details and enable
automated veriﬁcation processes. Academic institutions, the certiﬁcate issuers, play
a pivotal role in this ecosystem, digitally signing and uploading certiﬁcates onto
Blockchain. Users register on the portal with their registered email ids to interact
with the system through an intuitive user interface, initiating certiﬁcate veriﬁcation
requests. A Blockchain explorer enhances transparency by allowing users to inspect
the transaction history and certiﬁcate information stored on the Blockchain through
the certiﬁcate’s unique transaction id (Fig. 2).



6.2  Admin Interface


In addition to the user interface, the system has a robust admin interface that
allows administrators comprehensive control over certiﬁcate management. Within
this admin panel, administrators can perform a variety of important tasks that improve
the efﬁciency, security, and overall functionality of the system (Figs. 3, 4, and 5).

7  Conclusion


In a rapidly evolving technological landscape, the establishment of a robust and
dependable certiﬁcate veriﬁcation system has become increasingly imperative. This
research paper introduces an innovative Blockchain-based methodology tailored
to address the pressing challenges associated with certiﬁcate authentication. After
conducting an exhaustive examination of this decentralized solution, it becomes
unmistakably clear that the strategic application of Blockchain technology provides a
compelling response to the need for a decentralized, secure, and transparent certiﬁcate
veriﬁcation framework.
  The signiﬁcance of this research extends well beyond its immediate applications,
reaching into the broader realm of educational technology. By harnessing the capa-
bilities of Blockchain, we have developed a solution that not only enhances the
security and trustworthiness of academic certiﬁcates but also sets a new standard for
certiﬁcate validation in the digital age. This technology has the potential to revolu-
tionize not only the education sector but also various industries that rely on veriﬁed
credentials.
  Our approach draws inspiration from the foundational principles outlined by Lee
et al. [3], and it advances their work by delving deeper into the creation, execu-
tion, and evaluation of Blockchain-based systems. We have effectively demonstrated
how smart contracts can be formalized and veriﬁed using ontology and XML-
based methods, providing a glimpse into the evolving landscape of smart contract
technology and its potential for formalization and validation.
   Furthermore, our research aligns seamlessly with the pioneering efforts of scholars
such as Seng and Rana [5], Chowdhary et al. [6], and Huynh et al. [7], who have
explored various facets of Blockchain’s role in combatting counterfeit educational
certiﬁcates.
  As we conclude  this  insightful examination of the innovative domain of
Blockchain-powered certiﬁcate veriﬁcation, we assert that this technology lays the
foundation for a promising future characterized by heightened security, improved
efﬁciency, and enhanced transparency in the domain of academic credentials. The
impact of this research extends far and wide, touching not only the realm of education
but also the broader landscape of credential veriﬁcation in a digitally interconnected
world.
   In closing, we underscore that this research represents a signiﬁcant milestone in
the ongoing quest for secure and trustworthy certiﬁcate validation. The future holds

boundless opportunities for further exploration, reﬁnement, and implementation of
Blockchain technology across various domains. As technology continues to advance,
so will the methodologies through which we secure and validate academic certiﬁ-
cates, ensuring that the foundation for academic and professional success remains
robust and unassailable in the digital age.

Examination of Broken
or Non-responsive Touch Screen Display
Mobile Phones


Locktongbam Nato





Abstract Non-responsive touch screen or broken touch screen display panels in
mobile phones which may be caused deliberately or accidentally are encountered by
the Mobile Forensic Examiner. In such cases, extraction of data from mobile phones is
extremely difﬁcult as the mobile phones require a debugging process to synchronize
with the tools for extraction. In routine practice, debugging settings are carried out
on the touchscreen display panel of mobile phones. As such, extraction of data from
mobile phones with non-responsive or broken touchscreen display panels is usually
unsuccessful. An approach has been made to extract data from these types of mobile
phones using the bootloader method in Cellebrite UFED Touch2. The methodology
and results are presented in this paper. The objective of this study is to explore the
possibility and probability of extraction of data from an aberrant environment of
mobile phones in Digital Forensics.

Keywords Bootloader · Broken display · MediaTek chipset · Mobile Forensics ·
Non-responsive display · UFED Touch2



1  Introduction


Extraction of data from a mobile phone is one of the major aspects of Mobile Forensic
Examination. Successful extraction of data from a mobile phone depends on two
major factors: the compatibility of the mobile phone with the analytical tool and
the physical or technical condition of the mobile phone. Generally, a mobile phone
needs to be conﬁgured for debugging the system program and allows extraction of
data from the mobile phone using an extraction device. Debugging processes are
usually carried out on the display touch screen of mobile phones using the menu
in the Settings icon. When a mobile phone touchscreen display is not responsive

   Chipset details of the mobile phone and the application of bootloader options avail-

   Using a commercially available signed bootloader, one can attend maximum
extraction by ﬂashing those bootloaders with known vulnerabilities into the suspected
mobile phone, which can lead to full control of the device, allowing successful acqui-
sition of the memory data [1]. Physical extraction using the boot loader method
is considered one of the prime concerns in recovering data from Android devices
including deleted data. When the device is in bootloader mode during extraction,
the operating system does not run, and therefore, the device cannot connect to the
mobile network. It bypasses any user security lock and is forensically sound [2]. The
bootloader methods of physical extraction are speciﬁc to a particular chipset and are
supported by the Android OS version. Android phones having MTK chipsets are
commonly found with unlocked bootloaders. These phones can easily be synchro-
nized to establish a connection to the suspected phone with any storage media. Simi-
larly, in computer forensics where a forensic boot disk is used to operate the cloning
process for acquiring data from the target computer without affecting the original
hard disk. This method provides the advantages of bypassing rooting the devices or
enabling the USB debugging mode before extraction resulting in the accessibility of
a password-protected phone. The entire process is forensically sound as it will not
interfere with the internal storage of the device [3].
   In a similar situation, two numbers of mobile phones were received in our labo-
ratory for the extraction of data. An attempt has been made to extract the data from
these mobile phones using the bootloader options available in the UFED Touch2.

3  Methodology 1


   (i) The touchscreen display panel was broken; as a result, it was not possible to
      enable Flight Mode on the phone as per the Standard Operating Procedure. To
      overcome this situation, the SIM card and MicroSD card were removed from
        their slot for extraction of the data separately and the phone was switched
     ON.
   (ii)  The phone was charged for about two hours, assuming that during this period
       the phone may get fully charged.
  (iii) An attempt was made to enable USB debugging for physical/logical extrac-
       tion using the Android Debug Bridge (ADB) method [5]. The phone was
      connected to a working monitor for the mirror-casting process using a USB-
    HDMI converter. The OGT mode could not be activated, which may be due
       to damage to the display panel. The attempt for mirror casting was ruled out
       as USB debugging could not be carried out. Physical/logical extraction by the
    ADB method remained unsuccessful.
  (iv)  The phone was switched off and the battery was removed.
  (v)  Another attempt was made for chipset level analysis and identiﬁcation of the
       chipset for the concerned mobile phone was carried out using the Google
       search engine. MediaTek MT6735 of Android MTK chipset was found to be
       the processor for said mobile phone.
  (vi)  The phone was connected to Cellebrite UFED Touch2 and switched ON.
 (vii) From the list of phones, ‘Chinese phones Android MTK’ was selected. Phys-
        ical extraction with lock bypass was selected from the menu of Chinese phones
      Android MTK. Out of the four different ‘Boot loader’ methods available
       in UFED Touch2 for lock bypass, ‘Bootloader Method-1’ was selected but
      remained unsuccessful and the extraction process was aborted.
(viii)  ‘Bootloader Method-2’ was selected from the menu, run for extraction, and
       physical extraction was completed successfully.
  (ix)  The physical dump ﬁle was loaded in UFED Physical Analyzer, and the
       report was generated. Deleted data were also recovered along with active
       data (Figs. 3, 4, and 5).

6  Conclusion


The chipsets MediaTek MT6735 and MediaTek MT6737 were used in mobile phones
in Case-1 and Case-2, respectively. There are roughly 97 different models of mobile
handsets in the market that use the MediaTek MT6735 chipset processor [6]. Simi-
larly, about 230 different mobile handsets are available in the market that have
MediaTek MT6737 chipset processors in the mobile phone [7]. If the OS compati-
bility is compromised, the same procedure can be applied for the extraction of data
from other models of mobile phones having similar chipset processors using UFED
Touch2. Similar approaches can be made in other series of chipsets, particularly in
the case of broken and non-responsive touchscreen display panels of smartphones.
Chipset-based extraction of data using a compatible bootloader can be applied in
the upcoming models of smartphones. Understanding and applying the concept of
bootloader has become one of the dependable approaches in the case of the broken
and non-responsive touchscreen display panels of smartphones. In both cases, the
compatible mode of extraction was found to be physical extraction and the chances
of retrieving the deleted data were considerably very high.

A Review in Assamese Handwritten
Character Recognition


Bidur Bhushan Handique and Pranab Das





Abstract Detection and recognition of handwritten characters has been an existing
ﬁeld since the early age of computing. The main purpose of character recognition
is to detect characters from the digitized form of a printed or handwritten docu-
ment. Though much work remains, two relevant factors are preventing OCR systems
from recognizing handwriting at its best: the variance in handwriting and the large
number of scripts in use worldwide. As a result, a speciﬁc solution to the handwriting
recognition problem is not achieved. Assamese script, the ofﬁcial writing system for
the Assamese language, is spoken in the Indian state of Assam. Its characters are
distinct and intricate, making it difﬁcult to recognize. This study assesses how well
the current recognition systems function when used with the Assamese script and
numerous other Indian scripts. Though the paper is meant for Assamese script an
abundance of discussions is briefed according to the research meant on scripts around
the world and in India. The paper also shares a comparison among various recognition
techniques.

Keywords OCR · Optical character recognition · Ofﬂine · Ofﬂine character
recognition



1  Introduction


Optical Character Recognition (OCR), or Character Recognition, is a conventional
technique implemented for printed and handwritten character recognition [1]. It
is made up of a set of processes implemented together to recognize characters
based on a predeﬁned class of characters [2]. OCR is an area of research in

Pattern Recognition, Artiﬁcial Intelligence, Machine Vision, and Natural Language
Processing [3–5]. It has an extensive array of implementations from invoice imaging,

  OCR creates a digital representation from an image of handwritten or printed
characters [3, 7]. Then the new form can be amended, stored, and searched more
efﬁciently and effectively [1].
   Although the human eye’s capabilities are far more advanced than OCR’s, the
two have similar functioning in terms of character recognition [2]. OCR is further
separated into two groups based on the inputs, i.e., Online Character Recognition and
Ofﬂine Character Recognition [8]. Online Character Recognition system performs
in real-time while the user is writing the character or when the characters are under
creation [7, 9]. Ofﬂine Character Recognition systems operate on static data i.e., the
data is fed as images [7]. The images are either captured or scanned form of the

history of OCR, the next section discusses the various phases of OCR, and then comes
the dataset section highlighting the various handwritten datasets available in India.

the script. In the literature review section, discussion about OCR research on various
scripts around the world and in India is done. The optimum method for character
recognition is asserted in the ﬁnal part, which also serves as the paper’s conclusion.



2  History of OCR


OCR is comparatively an old ﬁeld of pattern recognition, and almost everyone consid-
ered it in the early days of pattern recognition [10]. Many considered this ﬁeld with
an expectation to get a solution but had to diversify their interest after difﬁculties
surfaced gradually [10].
  The origins of OCR dates to 1870 when an American inventor, Charles R Carey,
invented the retina scanner that transmitted image using a mosaic of photocells [11,
12]. In 1884 a German engineering student, Paul Nipkow invented a mechanical
device, using his patented Nipkow disks, that could generate a given image at the
receiver’s end [11, 13, 14]. Nipkow’s device faced numerous improvements resulting
in a new development of modern television [11, 13].

--- Page 523 ---
A Review in Assamese Handwritten Character Recognition                            529

   Character recognition was used to aid the visually impaired, Russian scientist,
Tyurin made the ﬁrst successful attempts in 1900 [11, 15]. Optophone, by Dr. Fournier
d’Albe, this device in 1912 could produce musical chords of characters in sequence
in a telephone [11, 16].
  OCR was gradually acknowledged as a data processing technique with a wide
range of uses [11]. Regarding the invention of commercial OCR machines, David
Shepard is regarded as a pioneer [11]. D. Shepard’s Gismo in 1951 could convert
printed messages into machine language for a computer to process [17].
  With the development of digital computing in the middle of the 1940s, advanced
OCR emerged [11, 18]. The systems built were more efﬁcient in dealing with both
printed and handwritten characters, and this led to the availability of such devices
commercially [18].
   Early contributions to character recognition were more concentrated on machine
printed and upon a little set of handwritten texts or symbols. Systems meant for
machine printed characters used template matching as an image was compared
with images in a library. Low-level methods of image processing were applied by
systems meant for handwritten text [19]. Algorithms implemented successfully were
constrained [19]. Studies on printed and handwritten characters and numerals of
Japanese, Chinese, Hebrew, Indian, Cyrillic, Greek, and Arabic were initiated [19].
   In the 1960s OCR systems could only read a limited number of fonts and shapes of
characters [20]. Some commonly available systems are NCR 420, Farrington 3010,
IBM 1418, IBM 1428, and IBM 1285; machines by IBM were mainly designed to
implement logical template matching [20]. Japanese companies also contributed to
the ﬁeld by bringing out 6300A by Fujitsu, H-852 by Hitachi, and N240D-1 by NEC
[20]. The ﬁrst ever machine, introduced in 1965 at the World Fair in New York, built
to read handwritten characters was IBM 1287 [18]. Researchers in the 1970s were
more focused on bringing improvements to the OCR system’s response time and
performance [18]. Thus, Toshiba introduced the Letter Sorting Machine, and it used
the structural analysis method [20].
  The systems introduced from 1975 through 1985 could comparatively operate
on large character sets and could also read poor quality characters [20]. After that
from 1985–1995, software packages of OCR were introduced to address the issue
of recognition instead [20]. The packages could read intermixed text, mathemat-
ical symbols, noisy documents, unconstrained handwritten characters, and coloured
documents [20]. It should also be brought to notice that real progress in OCR can be
noticed from the 1990s as the computation methods of the machines have increased
[19]. Since the initial days of the 1990s image processing and pattern recognition
were paired with artiﬁcial intelligence methods [19]. New methodologies such as
Hidden Markov models, Neural Networks, and fuzzy set reasoning came up along
with powerful machines [19].

530                                                           B. B. Handique and P. Das

3  Phases of OCR


The diagram below shows the phases of OCR:


       Image Acquisition      Preprocessing        Segmentation


         Post Processing          Classification        Feature Extraction




3.1  Image Acquisition


Initially, images of digitized handwritten documents are acquired by a computer
either by scanning or capturing a handwritten document [7, 21, 22]. This phase is
also known as digitization [21]. The image acquired must be of a speciﬁc image
format such as jpeg, bmp, png, etc. [23, 24].



3.2  Preprocessing


The image acquired must go through preprocessing operations to improve its quality
[7]. The image’s quality is improved by controlling the suitability for the successive
phases [23, 24]. Following is the list of operations [23, 24]:
   Noise Reduction. Document at the time of scanning, to acquire, might get contam-
inated with noise [23, 25]. And so, this operation is necessary to remove such noise
prior to sending an image to the next stage [23, 24].
  Image noise is categorized as: salt and pepper noise is common, with sprinkles
of black and white points on documents [23]. Ruled line noise occurs often in hand-
written documents as characters are written on pre-printed lined paper. Leading to
incapable detection of a letter, ‘z’ for example, on a ruled line [26]. Stroke like pattern
noise, is independent of the text’s properties in a document. Its presence near text may
alter a word’s meaning, and background noise is often found in historical manuscripts
or handwritten documents [26]. The noise degrades the image caused by humidity
absorbed by the paper, uneven contrast, background spots, and interfering strokes
[26].
   Binarization. Binarization or thresholding plays a decisive role in OCR, computer
vision, and machine vision applications [27–29]. Its result helps with character recog-
nition and segmentation [23]. The procedure of binarization converts colored or
grayscale images to binary images with values of either black or white [27]. White
pixels are referred to as background and black pixels are referred to as text [30].

--- Page 525 ---
A Review in Assamese Handwritten Character Recognition                            531

  Image conversion to binary involves determining a thresholding value [30]. Bina-
rization affects the ﬁle size by reducing it to be stored by beneﬁtting the computational
process ahead [28]. Images can be categorized into two types of thresholding: global
and local [30, 31]. If a thresholding value is accustomed to binarize every pixel within
a document, then global thresholding is performed [30, 31]. Local thresholding is
adaptive and does not produce positive outcomes as a new thresholding value is
decided for a local window or every single pixel in an image [30, 31].
  Edge Detection. An edge in a picture is deﬁned by the bounds of an object and its
background [29, 32]. The goal of edge detection is to retrieve the image’s boundary
information. [33].
   Performance of edge detection in noisy images is difﬁcult as both the edges and the
noise contain high-frequency content [32, 34]. So, operators used on a noisy image
have a larger scope that averages enough data to decrease noisy pixels [32, 34].
  Skew Detection. A document image is skewed when the document on a ﬂatbed
scanner is rotated at an angle [35]. Skewness on an image degrades its quality leading
to problems in analysing the image, extracting content, and reducing the performance
of OCR [35].
  The skew angle of a page is determined by the dominant orientation of its text
lines [36]. A group of characters, symbols, and words is a text line [36]. Zero skew is
a term used on documents with text lines, either horizontal or vertical, parallel to the
document boundaries [36]. And non-zero skew is introduced on a scanned document
[36].
   Categories of Skewness are: global skew occurs in scanned documents, it happens
when a document has a common angle of orientation, multiple skew can also be
termed as numerous skew. Documents with this skew have different skew angles,
and non-uniform text line skew is noticed on documents with different angles of
orientation in every single text line in the document [35, 37].
   Slant Estimation and Normalization. Slant is inevitably introduced to hand-
written text depending on varying factors, such as writing speed, style, and mood
of the writer [38]. It is the angle that forms between a handwritten text’s dominant
stroke direction and vertical direction [38]. Slanting of text can also be introduced
at the time of scanning due to misalignment of documents on the scanner’s ﬂatbed
[38].
   There are two primary challenges faced by OCR systems in the presence of slanted
characters: vertical segmentation of characters could result in defective segmented
characters with accompanying noisy segments and computational cost of the training
procedure and accuracy of recognition will be affected in a negative way [39].
   Slant normalization normalizes the characters into a standard form [23]. Hough
transformation, projection proﬁles, and determining the core regions of a word are
the three techniques most frequently employed for slant normalization [38].
  Thinning or skeletonization. Thinning, or skeletonization, is a morphological
analysis process to represent the ‘medial axis’ or ‘skeleton’ of a given image object
[40–42]. Thinning is an iterative process of peeling off a given object layer by layer
until the skeleton of the object is achieved [43]. The skeleton achieved is a one-pixel

--- Page 526 ---
532                                                           B. B. Handique and P. Das

width representation of the image object, it preserves the topological as well as the
geometric properties of the object [40, 41, 44].



3.3  Segmentation


The process of dividing a digital image into several signiﬁcant parts to facilitate
examination is called segmentation [45, 46]. Segmentation has never been satisfac-
tory on unconstrained handwriting styles having cursive and touching characters
[23, 47]. Sometimes the characters, be it printed or handwritten, may overlap too;
overlapping and touching of characters is common among many Indian languages
[23]. Recognition of text region in a given document is the ﬁrst activity to initiate
segmentation [47]. Additionally, labeling a collection of pixels is a part of it i.e.,
of segments sharing similar visual features [47]. A preset set of semantics is then
represented by grouping these labels into various logical areas [47].
   Character segmentation techniques have three different categories: Explicit
segmentation or dissection, employs a vertical segmentation technique to split
word pictures made up of a string of characters into sub-images that represent the
constituent characters that need to be classiﬁed [48]. Implicit segmentation, char-
acter recognition and segmentation are done simultaneously. The segments of word
images, are tentative and are sent to a classiﬁer iteratively with the feedback informa-
tion until satisfaction is achieved [48]. Holistic segmentation is a segmentation free
approach, a word or unit is extracted from a string. It is focused on word extraction
instead of letters [48].



3.4  Feature Extraction


Every character has a different feature making them different from the others [49].
Feature extraction is a process of extracting such features as important data from raw
data [23, 50]. The data extracted will help the characters to be represented accurately
[23]. Feature extraction of handwritten text is a difﬁcult task, as the degree of vari-
ability and imprecision is very high [51]. Relevant features are extracted during the
feature extraction process to form feature vectors, and each feature vector becomes
an identity of a particular character [23, 50].
  A good set of features must contain enough information so that it discriminates
an object from another object [50]. The set of features formed should be small and
similar to patterns within the class [50].
  Two  categories  can be  used  to  categorize  feature  extraction  techniques
[23, 50, 51].
   Statistical features. The statistical distribution of an object’s points yields its
statistical characteristics [23, 50]. These features may reduce the dimension of the
feature set [50]. They take care of style variances to some extent and provide high

--- Page 527 ---
A Review in Assamese Handwritten Character Recognition                            533

speed and low complexity [23, 50]. Zoning, projection and proﬁles, and crossings and
distances are few of the various statistical features. In zoning the character’s image is
placed in a N × M frame containing several overlapping or non-overlapping zones
[23, 50]. From each of such zones features of the character are extracted to form the
feature vector [23]. Projections and proﬁles: projections represent a 2-D character
image as a 1-D character and proﬁle describes the external shapes of the characters
and distinguishes a great number of characters, such as ‘p’ and ‘q’ [51]. Crossings and
distances: the transitions from background to foreground pixels along the character
image’s horizontal and vertical lines are counted and the count is referred to as
crossings and the calculation of distance between the ﬁrst detected pixel from the
upper and lower boundaries along the horizontal threshold gives the distance [50, 51].
   Structural features. Structural features are based on geometrical and topological
features of characters [51]. These features may encode knowledge of the character’s
contour or may require knowledge about the kind of components that make up the
character [50]. Strokes, complex curves, and chain codes are a few structural features
[50]. A stroke is a primitive element that builds a character [50]. It can be as simple
as a line or an arc, and can also be a complex curve, stroke directions and bays are the
sequence of direction of pen motion that can be applied as features, and chain codes
are dimensional parameter space composed of codes is used to map the strokes of a
character to attain its features [50].



3.5  Classiﬁcation and Recognition


Classiﬁcation is a process of training models using methodologies or algorithms
of pattern recognition to assign an unknown sample to a predeﬁned class or cate-
gory [18, 19]. It is the recognition system’s decision-making stage, which uses the
feature vectors extracted in the previous phase of character recognition [23, 49]. There
are several techniques of pattern recognition but are categorized into the following
approaches:
  Template matching. As the name suggests small parts of an image are matched
with a predeﬁned template [18, 49]. Template matching is performed by using a
sliding window approach in which the template or feature image is slid above an
image that is to be recognised [18]. The degree of similarity between two images
is found while matching them [19]. It is a process for locating sub-images within
an image [23]. Direct matching, deformable templates and elastic matching, and
relaxation matching are the classes of template matching techniques [19, 49].
   Statistical techniques. Statistical techniques determine the category of a given
pattern [49]. Parametric recognition, non-parametric recognition and clustering
analysis are three statistical techniques [18, 19].
   Structural techniques. Structural techniques classify objects based on a rela-
tionship between their pattern structure [18]. These structures are pattern primitives,
i.e., edge, contour, geometry of connected components, etc. [18]. Graphical and
grammatical are two methods meant for structural techniques [18, 19].

--- Page 528 ---
534                                                           B. B. Handique and P. Das

  Neural networks. Several processing units known as neurons make up a neural
network, its architecture is inspired by biological neurons [18, 19]. The network has
emerged to be a fast and reliable tool in the process of classiﬁcation to achieve a
higher rate of recognition [23]. Due to its adaptive nature, the network can adjust to
changes in the input and learn the characteristics of the input [19]. Nodes, or neurons,
are the main unit of any neural network [18]. The ﬁnal decision made by any network
depends on the complex interaction among the nodes, as an output of one node is
fed to another node [19]. Each such node is assigned a weight, which is adjusted in
a supervised environment to reduce squared error on training samples [18].
  Two main groups of neural networks can be distinguished: feedforward and feed-
back (recurrent) network [19, 23]. Single layer perceptron (SLP), multilayer percep-
tron (MLP), radial basis function (RBF), higher order neural networks (HONNs),
are some of the widely used feed-forward neural network [52].
   Recurrent neural network (RNN) and Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) have
established themselves as prominent in the ﬁeld of recognition with the advent of
deep neural architectures [18].



3.6  Post Processing


Post processing is last among all the phases of OCR. This phase’s primary objective
is to identify and ﬁx any misspellings in the OCR system’s output [53, 54].
  Non-word error and real-word error are the two fundamental types of errors [53].
A non-word error happens when a word that the OCR system recognizes doesn’t
match any entry in the lexicon. For example, when ‘how’ is recognized as ‘huw’ by
the OCR system, then ‘huw’ is a non-word error since its presence is not present in the
English language [53]. And in case of real-word error, the OCR system’s recognized
word appears in lexicon entries, but its presence is grammatically incorrect for the
sentence. Consider an example, when ‘how was your day?’ is recognized as ‘how
was you day?’, then ‘you’ is considered as the real-word error [53].
   These two errors fall under three different classes: deletion error, insertion error
and substitution error [53]. In deletion error, one or more characters are deleted
from an original word. For example, recognizing ‘house’ as ‘huse’, ‘hose’, ‘hos’,
etc. [53]. When a word has an extra character, it is called an insertion error. For
example, considering the word ‘house’ again and recognise it as ‘hoose’, ‘huuse’,
or anything else [53]. Alteration to characters inside the word results in substitution
errors. For example, the word ‘house’ again is now recognized as ‘hause’ or anything
else [53].
  The algorithms and post-processing approaches are proposed to solve the errors
discussed above. These approaches or algorithms can be broadly divided into three
groups: manual error correction, dictionary-based error correction, and context-based
error correction [53].
  The manual error correction approach is sometimes referred to as proofreading,
a group of people is hired to sit and edit the output of OCR text manually with the

--- Page 529 ---
A Review in Assamese Handwritten Character Recognition                            535

continuous human intervention [53]. Dictionary based error correction approach is
referred to as lexicon error correction. A lexicon or a dictionary is used to check the
spelling of the words recognized by the OCR and correction is made if needed [53].
By using the grammatical context as a guide, context-based error correction ﬁnds
and ﬁxes errors [53].

Numerous datasets are available to facilitate the research of OCR. The table shares
details about a few datasets of various scripts in India. The details of the dataset
shared are only of ofﬂine handwritten characters be it text or numbers (Table 1).



5  Assamese Language and Properties of Its Script


Assamese is a language spoken mostly in the northeastern part of the country, majorly
in the state of Assam. Assamese is also spoken in Bhutan and Bangladesh [63]. Assam
was ruled by Ahom kings before the British era, with their capital based in Sibsagar
and later changed to Jorhat. In the year 1846 the American missionaries established
the ﬁrst printing press in Sibsagar and published a monthly named ‘Arunodoi’ using
the variety spoken in the nearby areas of Sibsagar, this led to the reason for acceptance
as a formal variety of the language [63]. The language is recognized by the 8th
schedule of the Indian Constitution on 17th December 1960 [64, 65].
  The Assamese script today is derived from an old Indian script called the Brahmi,
as suggested by the various excavated rocks with inscriptions from the fourth century
to the nineteenth century [66, 67]. The script is composed of 41 consonants, 11
vowels, 10 digits, and over 300 hundred compound characters [68, 69]. The characters
are formed below a head line also referred to as matra [67]. The vowels are presented
independently or with a consonant to manipulate the consonant’s pronunciation [67].
Consonants are mostly presented independently, if two or three characters are merged
then such characters are termed as compound characters [67].
  The words are formed by bringing the vowels and consonants together. Three
zones can be utilized for classifying the words [68, 69]: Upper Zone, comprises the
extensions of modiﬁers, seen above the headline. Middle Zone, lies the main body
of the characters. Lower Zone, other form of modiﬁers exists (Fig. 2).

7  Conclusion


The review conducted for this study concludes that, in comparison to alternative
methods, neural networks provide efﬁcient accuracy for handwritten character recog-
nition. Besides this, it also discusses various OCR types, its history, and the various
phases that are required to be performed. The paper also shares a glimpse of datasets
of handwritten characters, be it text or number, of various scripts in India in separate
tables. Then it shares brief information on Assamese script. Lastly, it shares numerous
studies that have been performed on the recognition of handwritten characters. As
a future work, recognition of Assamese handwritten characters will be carried out
as the number of research is very low. And, practical use for daily personal use will
always be kept in mind.

Inner Line Permit Using Hyperledger
Fabric


Prangana Das, Noni Deori, Apurba Dey, Imopishak Thingom,
Pankaj Shukla, and Dharitri Brahma





Abstract The inner line permit (ILP) system, widely employed in various regions
to regulate the entry of non-residents into speciﬁc areas, has historically operated in a
centralized manner. While this approach has facilitated permit issuance and control,
it has also introduced security concerns, data vulnerabilities, and inefﬁciencies. This
research paper delves into the existing centralized ILP systems, scrutinizing the
security challenges they face and proposing a transformative solution through the
implementation of Hyperledger Fabric, a permissioned blockchain technology. By
leveraging Hyperledger Fabric, ILP systems can ensure that permit issuance, veriﬁ-
cation, and associated records are tamper-proof, transparent, and accessible only to
authorized stakeholders involved in the ILP process. Additionally, the immutability
of blockchain records enhances auditability, aiding in compliance with legal and
regulatory requirements. Smart contracts are utilized to digitally authenticate and
verify permit applications, reducing the risk of fraud and unauthorized access. The
permissioned blockchain ensures data privacy and security by granting access only
to authorized parties. Furthermore, we analyze case studies and practical implemen-
tations of Hyperledger Fabric in ILP systems to highlight real-world beneﬁts, such as
reduced reliance on intermediaries, efﬁcient processing of permit applications, and
increased trust among users and authorities.

Keywords Blockchain · Smart contract · Immutable record · Distributed ledger ·
Hash · Application

1  Introduction


The movement of individuals across regions and territories is a critical aspect of
modern society. However, the diverse cultural, environmental, and geopolitical land-
scapes often necessitate the implementation of speciﬁc regulations to ensure the
orderly and controlled inﬂux of people. One such mechanism employed by many
jurisdictions is the inner line permit (ILP) system.
  An inner line permit is a document issued by a governing authority that grants
temporary permission to non-residents or non-citizens to enter and travel [11] within
designated regions or areas. The ILP serves as a tool to regulate population movement,
preserve cultural identities, protect fragile ecosystems, maintain security, and balance
socioeconomic factors. However, there is scope for fraudulence, tampering and/or
misrepresentation of data, with little to no accountability for ensuring the authenticity
of the managed records. It involves privacy concerns, potential misuse of personal
information, lack of transparency in security [4] checks, and risks of unauthorized
access. These practices may lead to violations of data protection laws and erode
public trust in government handling of sensitive data.
   This report focuses on harnessing the power of blockchain technology, speciﬁ-
cally Hyperledger Fabric, to create an efﬁcient and transparent Inner Line Permit
system. By employing the decentralized [2] and immutable nature of Hyperledger
Fabric [1], we aim to enhance the effectiveness and reliability of the ILP process,
ensuring accountability, reducing bureaucracy, and fostering trust among all stake-
holders. The ILP system built on Hyperledger Fabric offers a paradigm shift in
how authorities, applicants, and other entities interact. It facilitates a streamlined
and digitized approach to permit application, veriﬁcation, approval, and issuance,
signiﬁcantly reducing administrative complexities and turnaround times.
  One of the primary advantages of utilizing Hyperledger Fabric for the ILP system
is its inherent security. The decentralized nature of blockchain technology eliminates
the reliance on a central authority, thereby reducing the risk of fraudulent activities
and unauthorized modiﬁcations to permit data. Additionally, the use of cryptographic
algorithms ensures the privacy and integrity of sensitive information while allowing
for transparency in the overall process.
  By implementing a permissioned [3] blockchain network, the ILP system can
bring together relevant authorities, government agencies, and applicants as partic-
ipants. Each participant can be assigned speciﬁc roles and access levels, ensuring
the appropriate handling of data and maintaining the conﬁdentiality of personal
information.
   Furthermore, the transparency of the ILP system allows authorities to monitor
compliance with regulations, track the movement of individuals, and make data-
driven decisions. This transparency also enables applicants to have visibility into the
status of their permit applications, promoting a sense of fairness and accountability
within the process.

--- Page 546 ---
Inner Line Permit Using Hyperledger Fabric                                        553

1.1  Objectives

• Design a peer-to-peer tamper-proof and forge-proof network leveraged for ILP,
   using a permissioned blockchain such as Hyperledger Fabric.
• Develop smart contracts (chain code) that enforce the rules and conditions of
   the ILP process, ensuring consistency and transparency in permit application,
   veriﬁcation, approval, and issuance.
•  Establish a decentralized network of relevant authorities, government agencies,
  and applicants as participants, leveraging Hyperledger Fabric’s permissioned
   blockchain framework to ensure accountability and trust in the ILP system.
• Implement a robust identity management system to authenticate participants and
   control access to the ILP network, ensuring the privacy and integrity of sensitive
   permit-related information.
• Design a user-friendly interface for applicants, authorities, and other stakeholders
   to interact with the ILP system, enabling seamless application submission, real-
   time status tracking, and efﬁcient communication.


2  Motivation and Background


In a typical workﬂow for a user visiting an ILP state requires to either applying
ILP permit through the online state portal with the documents required or applies
manually after visiting the state at the border ofﬁce. After receiving the permit, the
user is given the permit ID for that period of time.
   Similar systems are there like checking of immigration [9] of veriﬁed passport
holders and walk to a Global Entry Kiosk to generate an exit pass. The kiosk scans
the passports and collects ﬁngerprints to authenticate the passport holders [8].
   Also, decentralized land record systems have been instrumental in empowering
local communities by providing them with the ability to manage and safeguard
their land resources effectively. Studies by Himani Mukne et al. has highlighted
how decentralized land records enhance transparency, reduce disputes, and promote
sustainable land use practices [10].
  The downside is that we now have additional vulnerabilities and security lapses
because of each of these systems. The primary issue with the existing entry/exit
technique is that data is centralized, which makes it vulnerable to attacks and means
that attempts at manipulation could result in the loss of all or some of the data.
If security holes are discovered in the system, data validation and data entry into
this centralized database could have severe consequences. Finally, there is always a
chance that the entry/exit records will be altered—either by hostile outside parties
or as a result of internal political pressures, etc. Thus data should be immutable to
avoid such issues.
  The communication between multiple stakeholders with a centralized database is
a serious cause of concern in terms of security and scalability.

--- Page 547 ---
554                                                                                               P. Das et al.

   In addition to security concerns, a simple error in information recording might
make someone an unauthorized entry into the state, depriving them of any entry
record and their means of exiting the state. The principal challenges facing the
proposed system are its centralized structure and the challenge of maintaining records
that are securely synced across entry points. Additionally, it clears the path for
stakeholders to easily obtain passenger information without relying on a third party.
  As a potential solution, blockchain technology has emerged as a promising avenue
for addressing these challenges. Existing literature demonstrates that blockchain’s
decentralized  [9] nature, tamper-proof record- keeping, and automated smart
contracts can enhance the efﬁciency, security, and transparency of ILP processes,
while also mitigating the deﬁciencies associated with centralized systems [13]. This
paper contributes to this growing body of research by exploring the practical implica-
tions of integrating blockchain in the ILP system, thus ensuring a more streamlined,
responsive, and secures approach to regulating access to sensitive regions.



3  Proposed System


A forward-thinking proposal seeks to rectify the drawbacks of a centralized inner
line permit (ILP) system by introducing a blockchain solution using Hyperledger
Fabric [5]. Centralized systems often suffer from bureaucratic delays and a lack of
local context, hindering efﬁciency and responsiveness. The proposed blockchain-
based system offers transparent, secure, and decentralized ILP management. Appli-
cants access a user-friendly portal powered by Hyperledger Fabric, reducing delays
associated with centralized processing. Smart contracts automate identity veriﬁca-
tion and security checks, enhancing efﬁciency. This innovative system ensures only
authorized stakeholders have access to ILP information while safeguarding sensi-
tive data from breaches. By leveraging Hyperledger Fabric, the proposal aims to
create a more transparent, secure, and responsive ILP process, preserving the cultural
and environmental heritage of sensitive regions while mitigating centralized system
limitations.



4  System Workﬂow


The inner line permit (ILP) system has been put in place to regulate the entry of
individuals from states into protected or restricted areas within a particular region. As
shown in Fig. 1, the process begins when interested individuals submit an application
form to the designated authorities, which can be done either online or in person at
designated ofﬁces. Once the application is submitted the local authorities thoroughly
examine the provided documents, which usually include proof of identity, address,
and the purpose of the visit. This careful examination is crucial to verify that the
applicant is genuine and has reasons for visiting these protected areas. Next, the

--- Page 548 ---
Inner Line Permit Using Hyperledger Fabric                                        555





Fig. 1 System workﬂow


application and supporting documents undergo a security check conducted by police
or security forces. This security check is essential to ensure that there are no security
risks associated with granting permission. Additionally background checks may be
carried out to validate the applicants’ credentials and guarantee that issuing the
permit won’t compromise security. If everything goes smoothly during veriﬁcation
and security checks an ILP will be issued to the applicant. The permit will clearly
state the duration of their visit. Specify which areas they are allowed to access.
This meticulous workﬂow ensures that individuals granted an ILP can visit these
designated regions safely and legally while maintaining standards of security and
compliance.



4.1  System Architecture


In the inner line permit (ILP) system, several key participants and technologies collab-
orate to facilitate a streamlined and secure application process. Figure 2 shows the
participants in this system which includes the Applicant, individuals seeking the inner
line permit, and Veriﬁer, ofﬁcials responsible for verifying applicant information. The
technology backbone of the system utilizes Hyperledger Fabric, incorporating Smart
Contracts [6], State Database, and a Consensus Mechanism. Smart Contracts, also
known as Chaincode Functions, serve as the business logic governing ILP appli-
cation processing and veriﬁcation. The State Database stores the current status of
ILP applications and permits, ensuring an organized record-keeping system. The
Consensus Mechanism within the Hyperledger Fabric network ensures unanimous
agreement among network participants concerning the validity of transactions and
state updates.
  The interaction ﬂow within the ILP system follows a structured process. Appli-
cants initiate the process by interacting with the ILP application interface, providing
the necessary information. The ILP application details are then transmitted to the





Fig. 2 System architecture

--- Page 549 ---
556                                                                                               P. Das et al.

Hyperledger Fabric network [7], where Veriﬁers, using appropriate permissions,
access this data. Veriﬁers meticulously validate the applicant’s information, updating
the application status on the network through the execution of smart contracts. The
Fabric network’s consensus mechanism plays a crucial role, guaranteeing unanimous
agreement on the veriﬁcation decision. Upon approval, ILP applications are marked
as “approved” within the state database, signifying the issuance of permits.
  To ensure transparency and keep applicants informed, a notiﬁcation service oper-
ates externally. This service accesses the updated ILP application status from the state
database and promptly sends notiﬁcations to applicants. These notiﬁcations convey
the approval or rejection status of their ILP applications, ensuring clear communica-
tion and enhancing the overall efﬁciency of the ILP system. Together, these compo-
nents and interactions form a robust, technology-driven process for inner line permit
applications, safeguarding accuracy and conﬁdentiality throughout the application
lifecycle.



4.2  Channel Creation


In the inner line permit (ILP) system, applicants initiate the process by submitting
their applications and receiving notiﬁcations. Figure 3 shows how we can specify
public and private channel. The applications undergo initial veriﬁcation and approval
on the Public Channel, where basic criteria are assessed, and consensus is reached.
Successful applications proceed to the Private Channel, which facilitates detailed
and conﬁdential veriﬁcation processes involving Veriﬁer A and Veriﬁer B. In this
secure environment, Veriﬁers conduct in-depth scrutiny of documents and engage
in private communication to determine the application’s ﬁnal approval status. By
excluding the applicant from the private channel, a higher level of conﬁdentiality is
maintained, ensuring a secure and private [12] ILP application process.

a Hyperledger Fabric blockchain network.

1.  CreateILPApplication(ILPChaincode cc, string id, string applicant, string details)



   function CreateILPApplication(ILPChaincode cc, string id, string applicant,
   string details):
   ILPApplication newApplication newApplication.ID = id
   newApplication.Applicant = applicant newApplica-
   tion.Status = "Pending" newApplication.Details = details
   cc.ILPApplications[id] = newApplication


   This function creates a new ILP application using the provided id, applicant infor-
mation, and details. It initializes a new ILPApplication object with the given data,
sets its status to “Pending,” and stores it in the ILP Applications map within the cc
(ILPChaincode) instance. This signiﬁes the initiation of a new ILP application with
a pending status for further processing.

   cc.ILPApplications[id]

It accesses the ILPApplications map within the cc (ILPChaincode) instance and
returns the ILPApplication object corresponding to the given id. This operation allows
querying the status and details of a speciﬁc ILP application.

6  Result


The proposed system is implemented on Hyperledger Fabric. As shown in Fig. 3,
we have created two channels. One channel is for the initial public processes and
another for the more detailed and conﬁdential veriﬁcations. Each channel serves a
distinct purpose in the ILP application process, with the Private Channel ensuring a
higher level of conﬁdentiality and privacy. The participants involved in our system
are Applicant, Veriﬁer A and Veriﬁer B. The dataset collected from the applicant
are Name, Address, State, Nationality, ID proof type and number, Contact Number,
and Purpose of Stay. The creation of a block begins with the submission of an ILP
application, treated as a transaction. This transaction undergoes basic veriﬁcation on
the Public Channel, where consensus is reached. Approved transactions are grouped
into a block, including a timestamp, reference to the previous block, and a unique
identiﬁer.
  The block is broadcasted, veriﬁed by network nodes, and, if applicable, under-
goes additional scrutiny on the Private Channel. Once consensus is reached on both
channels, the ﬁnal block is committed to the blockchain, forming an immutable and
transparent record of ILP transactions. This streamlined process ensures security,
transparency, and, when necessary, conﬁdential veriﬁcation within the ILP system.
   In this work the distinctions between the traditional Inner Line Permit (ILP) system
and the innovative blockchain-based ILP system are highlighted. Traditional ILP
systems, characterized by centralized authority and manual processes, are suscep-
tible to security vulnerabilities such as data tampering and single-point failures.
In contrast, our blockchain-based ILP system leverages decentralized ledger tech-
nology and smart contracts, mitigating these vulnerabilities through cryptographic
hashing, a distributed ledger, and consensus mechanisms, thereby enhancing security.
The traditional ILP system, reliant on centralized control, often lacks transparency
and faces challenges in terms of accessibility. In our proposed blockchain-based ILP
system, decentralization and transparency are intrinsic, addressing trust concerns and
providing a more accessible and secure platform for ILP management. Furthermore,
the integration of smart contracts automates and secures processes, contributing to
efﬁciency gains. Thus, this has transformative potential of transitioning from tradi-
tional ILP systems to the decentralized, secure, and transparent framework offered
by blockchain technology.



7  Conclusion and Future Work


In this article, our implementation of a dual-channel system on Hyperledger Fabric for
the ILP (Immigration and Legal Permanent Residency) application process signiﬁes
a signiﬁcant advancement in security, transparency, and conﬁdentiality. Through the
Public Channel, basic veriﬁcation processes are conducted with consensus, leading to
the creation of blocks containing crucial applicant information. These blocks undergo

--- Page 553 ---
560                                                                                               P. Das et al.

additional scrutiny on the Private Channel, ensuring a higher level of conﬁdentiality.
The collaboration of Applicant, Veriﬁer A, and Veriﬁer B in this streamlined process
results in the formation of immutable and transparent blocks, broadcasted, and veri-
ﬁed by network nodes. Achieving consensus on both channels validates the relia-
bility and integrity of ILP transactions. Our system addresses the complex balance
between transparency and privacy, offering a secure and efﬁcient solution for the
evolving needs of decentralized ILP system.
   Future research can expand on this work by examining the effects of additional
parameters, like the quantity of concurrent transactions, on performance. Further-
more, in a real setup of the solution, as the nodes would be dispersed geographically,
the network delay would play a crucial role. Therefore, a study on how the network
affects the overall latency of the transactions may ﬁnd it interesting.
   In summary, the integration of blockchain technology in ILP systems is still in its
infancy, and as it continues to evolve, there will be numerous opportunities for further
research, development, and implementation. Future work should focus on addressing
technical, regulatory, and societal challenges while capitalizing on the potential of
blockchain to revolutionize permit systems for the betterment of indigenous cultures,
environmental preservation, and administrative efﬁciency.
